In 1215, Innocent III. celebrated the tenth general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, being the fourth of Lateran, in which a variety of new penalties were decreed against the heretics of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. In particular it was ordained, that those who were condemned by the bishops as impenitent heretics should be delivered to secular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; that the goods of laymen condemned should be confiscated, and those of priests applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their churches; that the inhabitants suspected of heresy should be summoned to purge themselves in the canonical form, and, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of refusal, excommunicated; that if they <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> more than a year under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a>, without having recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of the church, they should be accounted heretics, and treated as such; that all persons who favoured or received into their houses heretics, should be liable to excommunication as well as the heretics themselves,—declared infamous, and as such excluded from all public employments,—deprived of the right of electing their own magistrates,—and rendered incapable of giving <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice, making testamentary dispositions, or taking up any succession, if at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of a year they had failed to perform their duties and satisfy the church. Pope Innocent III. died on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1216, and two days thereafter was succeeded by Honorius III., who resolved to continue the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which his predecessor had commenced. The new pontiff approved of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> founded by Dominic de Guzman, according to the rule of St Augustin, and having for its object to preach against the heretics; an institution which gave rise to the order of preaching friars, who were afterwards termed Dominicans. He wrote to Guzman, praising his zeal, and encouraging him to persevere in the enterprise in which he had engaged; he sent into the provinces of Languedoc and Provence, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Bertrand, with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of legate, the principal object of whose mission was to prosecute with new vigour the war against the Albigenses, to sustain the zeal of the missionaries, and to ensure the reconciliation of converted, as well as the punishment of obstinate heretics; and, lastly, he issued a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> addressed to all the bishops of Christendom, strongly recommending to their favour and support the order of preaching friars. Meanwhile St Dominic, who happened to be at Rome, had instituted an order for seculars who lived in the world, the members of which were to be bound to assist, as far as they could, those who preached against heresies, and to prosecute heretics with unrelenting rigour. This order has sometimes been designated the Third Order of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PENITENCE">Penitence</a>, but it was more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> denominated the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITIA">Militia</a> of Christ, because those who entered it were required to combat heretics, and to aid the inquisitors in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their ministry. They were in fact regarded as forming part of the family of the inquisition, and, for this reason, they bore the name of Familiars. Here, then, we have the two great elements of the Holy Office; first, the institution of St Dominic, or the order of preaching friars, called Dominicans; and, secondly, the Militia of Christ, an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> which afterwards gave rise to that which was known under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>; two orders which were soon confounded, and the members of which were denominated Familiars of the Holy Office of the Inquisition. Nor was it long ere the tribunal, thus organized, commenced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> operations against heretics. In 1224, the Inquisition had been established in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> Dominicans. This is proved by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Frederick II., published at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> in February 1224, which provided that heretics condemned as such by the church, and delivered over to the secular arm, should be punished in a manner proportioned to their crime; that whosoever, through fear of punishment, might be brought back to the unity of the faith, should be subjected to a canonical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> and shut up in prison for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; that the inquisitors established by the pope, or Catholics zealous for the purity of the faith, might require judges, in any part of the empire, to cause heretics to be seized, and detained as prisoners until, after being formally excommunicated by the church, they were judged and punished with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; that all who supported or protected heretics should undergo the same punishment; that heretics who had returned into the bosom of the church should be obliged to pursue those persons charged with heresy, discover, and bring them before the Inquisition; that he who, having made abjuration in articulo mortis, should relapse into heresy after recovering his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, should equally suffer a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> punishment; and that <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> against God was a much greater crime than treason against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This constitution contains other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> equally severe, and concludes by declaring that all those who should concur with the new religious order in delivering the empire from the contagion of heresy, would serve God and render themselves useful to the state. It appears, however, that the efforts of the Inquisition in Narbonne, were not attended with the success which the Pope had expected from them, probably because the events of the war were not always favourable to the crusaders. But it was reserved for Gregory IX., who ascended the pontifical throne in 1227, to fix the establishment of the Inquisition in the form of a tribunal, and at the same time to give it constitutions. With this view he convened a council at Toulouse, where new measures of severity were adopted against the heretics; he also issued a bull excommunicating them, and further, enjoining that the impenitent should be delivered over to the secular arm, and that all their supporters and adherents should be declared infamous. He next transmitted a brief to Esparrago, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, exhorting him to combat heresy; and at the same time addressed to the prior of the Dominicans of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> a commission, confiding to that religious order the execution of his bull against heretics. Councils were also held at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, and at Beziers, where new regulations were adopted for preserving the purity of the faith, by multiplying the severities against those by whom it was denied. But whilst this was passing in France, the heresy of the Albigenses penetrated even into the capital of the Catholic world. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> means of repression hitherto employed against these schismatics had totally failed, either in lessening their ardour, or in abating their enthusiasm. Several thousands of their number had perished at the stake in France and Italy; yet, so far from being discouraged, they had, in defiance of the power of the Pope, carried their doctrines into his very capital, and, by this conduct, proved how much they disregarded the anathemas of the church, and even the horrible torments with which Gregory had menaced them. Nor is it improbable that the pontiff would have abandoned the system of repression which he had adopted, if the opinions which originated in the fourth century, when Constantine embraced Christianity, had not from age to age acquired a new degree of force; namely, that sufficient reasons might be discovered in the Gospel for punishing heretics with death. Unhappily, however, men's minds, subjugated by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, and inflamed by bigotry, were rendered incapable of considering objects in their true <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Hence, so far from changing his system, or taking as his guide that spirit of meekness and benevolence which had distinguished the first three centuries of Christianity, Gregory fulminated against the heretics a bull in which he excommunicated all those belonging to certain classes that are therein named; ordained that the persons condemned should be delivered over to the secular power to receive the punishment due to their crime; regulated the mode of procedure to be adopted against persons accused of heresy; intercommunicated, declared infamous, and deprived of their civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, those inhabitants who should receive into their houses, protect, or defend reputed heretics; and provided that if any one desired to recant and renounce his errors, he should undergo such penance as might be prescribed, and thereafter be imprisoned for life. This bull, which contained many other penalties and disabilities, was enforced with the utmost rigour; whilst the senator Annibal, and other members of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Rome, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the Pope in the execution of the measures which he had ordained, passed different municipal laws, having for their object the detection and punishment of heretics, and being in spirit and character nearly the same with those which had been promulgated by Frederick II. Nor were these regulations confined in their operation to Rome. They were transmitted, along with those which Gregory himself had decreed, to the Archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, in order that he might cause them to be rigorously executed in his own diocese, in those of his suffragans, and in some other parts of Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, where heresy had already made alarming progress. Frederick II. also renewed the constitutions which he had published against heretics in 1224, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> against blasphemers, which condemned all heretics indiscriminately to undergo the punishment of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, or of having the tongue cut out, if the bishops thought proper to shew them mercy, in order that in future it might be impossible for them to blaspheme the holy name of God. Such is the general form which the Inquisition had assumed in France and Italy, when Gregory IX. introduced it into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. This event took <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> about the middle of the thirteenth century. Spain was then divided into four Christian kingdoms, viz. Castile, Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, besides the Mahommedan States; but, with relation to the Inquisition, that country was, in 1301, divided into two provinces, viz. those of Castille and Aragon. To the Dominicans, who had hitherto acquitted themselves with success in the ministry of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, Gregory confided the execution of the bull by which the Inquisition was established in Spain; and, at a subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> of this order had conferred upon him the right of nominating the local inquisitors, with the title and rank of provincial of Spain. Nor was it long ere this formidable institution, having for its object to extirpate heresy, and to preserve the purity of the Catholic faith, came into active operation. For the details of its proceedings, however, we must refer the reader to the work of Llorente, which, with all its faults of style and arrangement, contains a vast body of interesting and authentic information on this subject. We shall only remark here, that never did plant find a more congenial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. In France and in Italy it had required strenuous and persevering efforts to organize and establish this terrible tribunal; in Spain, however, it took root at once, and in time attained a magnitude which, from a variety of causes, it never reached in any other country. During the fourteenth century its progress was steady, whilst its vigour and energy were continually on the increase. Its jurisdiction was enlarged, and its ramifications multiplied; autos-da-fe were celebrated in various places; and many perished in the flames, or were condemned to suffer punishments of greater or less severity, for asserting the unalienable rights of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. But it was not until towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fifteenth century, when Isabella, wife of Ferdinand of Aragon, had ascended the throne of Castille, and when the different kingdoms of Spain were united under these sovereigns, that the Inquisition became general in that country, and assumed that form which it retained until the period of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> in 1808. The execution of the bull of Sixtus IV., which authorized Ferdinand and Isabella to establish the Inquisition in their states, was indeed for a time suspended; but this suspension must have been of short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, for in 1480 and 1481 we find it in full <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Severe measures were adopted against the Jews, who were accused of the most absurd and ridiculous crimes, and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> the new Christians, as they were called, emigrated in great numbers. The flames of persecution raged at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, where, in 1481, twenty-six persons perished at the stake; and already no less than two hundred and ninety-eight victims had shared a similar fate. From this period, indeed, may be dated the establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Inquisition, that is, of the Inquisition such as it existed even until our own time. This was effected by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> inquisitor-general; the appointment of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> council of the Inquisition, afterwards denominated the Council of the Supreme; the institution of subaltern tribunals in all parts of the kingdom; and, lastly, the enactment of organic laws, having for their object to give stability to the tribunal, as well as uniformity to its procedure, and efficacy to its exertions in the repression of heresy. By this organization there was created in Spain a jurisdiction in matters of religion, which, under the able but merciless direction of such men as Torquemada, Valdez, and their immediate successors, became the most effective and vigorous engine of persecution which had ever before been known in any age or country. Its character <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be best understood by stating the substance of the organic or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> laws of the modern Inquisition, which, under the name of Instructions, were published at Seville on the 29th of October 1484. The first of these regulated the manner in which the institution of the tribunal should be announced in those countries or places where it might be judged necessary to establish it. The second ordained the publication, in the church of the place, of an edict accompanied with the censures provided against those who, having committed the crime of heresy or apostasy, should not voluntarily denounce themselves before the expiration of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> which had been granted them, and also against those who should obstruct or resist the execution of the measures ordained by the Holy Office. By the third, a delay of thirty days was allowed to heretics to declare themselves, and thereby to prevent the confiscation of their goods, without prejudice, however, to the pecuniary fines to which they might afterwards be condemned. By the fourth, it was provided that the voluntary confessions of those who declared themselves should be made in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in the presence of the inquisitors and a registrar, so that the self-accused might be required to answer all the questions which might be addressed to them by the inquisitors on the subject of their confession, and also respecting their accomplices, and those whom they knew or suspected to be guilty of apostasy. The fifth prohibited giving secret <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a> to any one who had made a voluntary confession, excepting in the single case where no one had had knowledge of his crime, and where there was nothing to apprehend from its publicity. By the sixth article it was provided that part of the penance enjoined on him who had been reconciled should consist in his being deprived of the exercise of every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employment, and of the use of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, pearls, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. The seventh imposed pecuniary fines upon those who had made a voluntary confession. The eighth provided that the voluntary penitent who might present himself with his confession, after the expiration of the term of grace, should not be exempted from the penalty of confiscation of goods, which he would otherwise have incurred. In the ninth article, it was enacted, that if persons under the age of twenty presented themselves to make confession, after the expiration of the term of grace, and if it were proved that they had been led into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> by their parents, it would be sufficient to impose on them a slight penance. The tenth imposed on inquisitors the obligation of declaring, in the act of reconciliation, the time in which the reconciled had fallen into heresy, in order to ascertain what portion of his goods belonged to the fisc. The eleventh article bore, that if a heretic detained in the secret <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> of the Holy Office, were touched with due <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, and demanded absolution, it might be granted him, by imposing as a penance the pain of perpetual imprisonment. By the twelfth, it was provided, that if the inquisitors considered the confession of the penitent to have been simulated, in the case indicated in the preceding article, they should refuse absolution, declare him a false penitent, and condemn him as such to be relaxed, that is, delivered over to the secular arm. The thirteenth ordained that if a man, absolved after free confession, boasted of having concealed several crimes, or if it appeared, from information afterwards obtained, that he had committed more than he confessed, he should be arrested, and judged as a false penitent. The fourteenth provided, that if the accused, when convict- --- 1 *Histoire Critique de l'Inquisition d'Espagne*, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1816, 4 vols. 8vo. Llorente had been an inquisitor himself (at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALATAYUD">Calatayud</a>) and was probably on that account selected to prepare a digest of the materials for a history of the Inquisition, furnished by the archives of the Holy Office. Such is the substance of the Code of the Inquisition, as originally promulgated, perhaps the most extraordinary digest ever formed for consolidating a system of religious tyranny. From this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>, indeed, it must be evident, whether we examine the twenty-eight <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in detail, or consider them as a whole, that the judgments and sentences pronounced would depend upon the manner in which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> was prepared, and the particular views and feelings entertained by the judges, who were to decide as to the heresy or orthodoxy of the accused, according to inductions, analogies, or consequences, deduced from facts or isolated observations, reported with more or less of exaggeration and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. The code in question was, however, several times augmented, even in the early days of the Inquisition. In particular, there were added to it the instructions which had been prepared at Seville in the beginning of 1484, those of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a> in 1488, those of Toledo and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a> in 1498, and, lastly, those of Valladolid in 1561. But with all these modifications the forms of procedure underwent little or no change; nor was the arbitrary character which distinguished this cruel and odious <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> in any degree mitigated. It was scarcely possible for the accused, however innocent, to establish an effectual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Placed between the alternative of either recognising his innocence, or suspecting him of guilt, the judges constantly allowed themselves to adopt the latter course, which at once superseded the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, and left the accused entirely at their mercy. The additional acts of the inquisitor-general Torquemada also fall under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> which has already been given. They were eleven in number, and principally intended to regulate details. They provided that in every subaltern tribunal there should be two inquisitor-jurisconsults, a fiscal, an alguazil, registrars, and other officers if required; that every functionary who received presents either from the accused, or their families, should be immediately dismissed; that the Inquisition should maintain at Rome an able jurisconsult, with the title of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>; that contracts signed before the year 1479 by persons whose goods happened to be seized after that period, should be valid; that proprietors who might have afforded to fugitives an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> on their estates, should be held as having placed their whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> at the disposal of the government; that the notaries of the Inquisition should keep accounts of the effects of persons condemned; that the receivers of the Holy Office might sell that property, the administration of which they found troublesome, and collect the rents of such as was immovable; that each receiver should attend to the interests of the tribunal to which he was more immediately attached; that the goods of a person condemned could not be sequestrated without an order of the Inquisition; that the inquisitor and other officers should be paid their salaries quarterly by the receiver; and that, in regard to circumstances unprovided for in the new constitutions, the inquisitors should have a discretionary power to act as they judged best, but that, in matters of great importance, they should have recourse to the government for instructions. The crimes of which the Inquisition took cognisance were heresy in all its different forms, apostasy, Judaism, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MAHOMMEDANISM">Mahommedanism</a>, sorcery, offences against <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and polygamy; and the punishments consequent on conviction varied according to the presumed degree of delinquency, from temporary confinement and severe penance to the san benito and the auto-da-fe. This tribunal was not esta- --- 1. Que devait-on attendre de tels hommes, devenus les arbitres de la vie et de la mort de leurs semblables, en les voyant complètement aveuglés par leurs préventions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRE">contre</a> des accusés sans défense? L'homme simple devait succomber; l'hypocrite seul triompher."—(Llorente, Hist. Crit. de l'Inquisit. d'Espagne, i. 184.) 2. San benito is a corruption of sano bendito. Its true name in Spanish was sanatorio; but sano bendito, corrupted into san benito, became the vulgar name, because, since the time of the Hebrews, a sano was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of penitence. blished without great opposition. The first inquisitor of Aragon was openly assassinated, and all the provinces of that kingdom offered the most strenuous resistance to a jurisdiction which trenched so much on their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> rights and privileges. But their opposition proved unavailing, as did also an attempt made by the Cortes of Castille and Aragon to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the Holy Office after it had been established. The Inquisition triumphed over all its adversaries, and soon became so formidable, that parents delivered up their children, husbands their wives, and masters their servants, without a murmur. Terror, in fact, constituted the great element of its power; nor was this feeling diminished in force by the suddenness with which it pounced on its victims, and the impenetrable secrecy in which all its proceedings were involved. Its stroke was like that of fate. No man knew when it might descend on his own head; every one felt that resistance was vain, and escape impossible. Imagination <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LENT">lent</a> its aid to exaggerate the fearful reality; terror froze all hearts; even kings and princes trembled before it. Nor can it be denied that, in its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and palmy days, its proceedings were marked by a bold and fearless impartiality. It scrupled not to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> and proceed against <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Carlos of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, whom death alone placed beyond the reach of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. It instituted processes against <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., Philip II., the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, and other illustrious personages, the first of whom was accused of favouring Lutheranism, and the others were charged with want of zeal in the prosecution and extermination of heretics. Nor was it in any respect more lenient to the clergy than to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. Bartolomeo Carranza, archbishop of Toledo, a prelate of eminent learning, piety, and moderation, was accused of entertaining and countenancing certain opinions declared to be heretical, imprisoned for several years, and, after enduring the greatest sufferings, died before his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> was brought to a close, though it ended in a sentence of absolution. With regard to the inferior clergy, a charge of heresy, or even the suspicion of having shewn kindness to heretics, was almost <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a capital <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>. Neither rank, nor age, nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, afforded any defence against its watchful vigilance and its pitiless severity. It was instituted to preserve the uniformity of the faith, and, in Spain at least, it completely succeeded. Nor can it be doubted that the procedure of the Inquisition was eminently calculated to accomplish the objects for which it had been originally instituted. This consisted of several parts; namely, the denunciation, the inquest, the censure by qualificators, secret imprisonment, the primary audiences, the charges, torture, the requisitory, the defence, the proofs, the publication of the proofs, the definitive censure by qualificators, and the sentence. The procedure of the Holy Office commenced by denunciation, or something held equivalent thereto, such as a discovery incidentally resulting from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> made before the tribunal in another affair; and this, when signed, assumed the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, in which the delator, after having sworn to tell the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, designated by their names, or in some other manner, the persons whom he believed or presumed to be able to give evidence against the denounced. Then followed the inquest, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the persons named and designed in the declaration as cognisant of the facts and circumstances therein set forth, and who were made to promise upon oath that they would never reveal the interrogatories which they were to be called upon to answer. Next came the censure by the qualificators. When the tribunal had examined the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> instruction, and discovered therein sufficient grounds for further procedure; and when the registers of the other tribunals of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> had been examined, to ascertain if there existed in these any charges against the denounced; the whole was submitted by the inquisitors to certain theologians, called qualificators of the Holy Office, who indicated or qualified in writing the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> meriting theological censure, as heretical, savouring of heresy, or calculated to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to heresy: And in case the denounced was only suspected of this crime, they decided whether the suspicion was light, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, or violent. As soon as the qualification here described had been made, the procurator-fiscal demanded that the denounced should be transferred to the secret prisons of the Holy Office. The tribunal had three sorts of prisons; public, intermediary, and secret. The first were those in which the Holy Office caused to be confined persons who, without being guilty of any crime against the faith, were accused of some delict, the punishment of which belonged of right to the Inquisition. The second were destined for such servants or ministers of the Holy Office as had committed some crime or some fault in the exercise of their functions, without, however, incurring the suspicion of heresy. The third or secret prisons were those in which heretics, or persons suspected of being so, were confined, and where the prisoners could only communicate with the judges, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> provided and with the precautions enjoined by the constitutions. In the three days which followed the imprisonment of the suspected, they gave him three audiences of monition or advice, to engage him to speak the truth and the whole truth, without concealing anything which he had himself done or said, or which he could impute to others contrary to the faith. He was also told, that if he conformed faithfully to what had been prescribed to him in this particular, mercy would be shewn him, but that, in the contrary case, he would be treated with all the rigour of law. After the formality of the three audiences of monition had been gone through, the procurator-fiscal prepared the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> against the prisoner, in conformity with the heads of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> indicated or qualified in the instruction; and although there existed only a semi-plena probatio, he charged the facts deposed to as if they had been fully proved, and what was worse, he did not limit the articles or counts of his indictment to the number of facts declared, and dispensed with applying to each head of accusation the proper character or notion which distinguished it. The next part of the procedure was the most horrible, namely, the application of the torture. Although the prisoner, in the three audiences of monition, might have confessed as much as, or even more, than the witnesses had deposed to, the fiscal terminated his requisitory or accusation, by demanding that the accused should be subjected to the question, on the alleged ground --- 1 See Llorente, Hist. Critiq. de l'Inq. d'Espagne, tom. iv., and M'Crie's History of the Reformation in Spain. 2 "Il serait difficile de rien concevoir de plus affreux que ces réduits," says Llorente; "et non qu'ils soient à présent tels qu'on les a décrits, c'est-à-dire profonds, humides, sales et mal-sains; à ces traits il est plus facile de reconnaître les rapports inexactes et exagérés des victimes de l'Inquisition que le témoignage de la vérité. Je ne parlerai de ce qu'ils ont été autrefois, mais il est certain qu'aujourd'hui ces lieux sont de bonnes chambres voûtées, bien éclairées, sans humidité, et où il est permis de faire un peu d'exercice. Mais ce qui les rend un séjour vraiment redoutable c'est qu'on n'y entre sans être à l'instant flétri dans l'<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> publique; infamie à laquelle aucune autre, soit civile, soit ecclésiastique, n'expose les prisonniers; c'est qu'on y tombe dans une tristesse inexprimable, compagne inévitable d'une solitude profonde et continue; c'est qu'on n'y connaît jamais l'état de la procédure dont on est l'objet, et qu'on ne peut y jouir de la consolation de voir et entretenir son défenseur; enfin, c'est parcequ'on y est plongé pendant l'hiver dans des ténèbres de quinze heures par jour, car il n'est point permis au prisonnier d'avoir de la lumière après quatre heures du soir ni avant sept heures du matin; interrave assez long pour qu'une hypochondrie mortelle s'empare du prisonnier, au milieu du froid, dont il est saisi dans un séjour où le feu n'a jamais pénétré." (Hist. Crit. de l'Inquist. d'Espagne, t. 300.) of culpable concealment and denial of the truth. It is certain that for a long period the torture had not been applied by the inquisitors, either in Spain or in any other country, the mitigating and humanizing influence of time and improvement having virtually abolished this barbarity; but the form of procedure still remained unchanged. The requisitory or accusation of the fiscal was never communicated in writing to the accused, to enable him to prepare his defence. He was conducted into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of audience, where, in presence of the inquisitors and the fiscal, a secretary read over the charges one after another, stopping at each article, and calling upon the accused to answer at the instant, whether it was conformable to the truth or otherwise; thus laying a snare for the unhappy person who was about to be put on his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. After the accusation had been read, the inquisitors asked the accused if he wished to be defended. If he answered in the affirmative, they ordered a copy to be taken of the accusation and answers, and, from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of titularies of the Holy Office, appointed him an advocate. No prisoner was permitted to choose his own counsel, although there existed no law of the Holy Office which denied him this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> right. To the proof, and the publication of the proof, as it was called, both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> mockeries of justice, succeeded the definitive censure by the qualificators, or theologians of the Holy Office, to whom was remitted the original of the judgment they had pronounced on the summary instruction, together with an extract of the answers made by the accused in his last examination, and who were required to qualify for the second time the propositions upon which the accusation was founded, to consider the explanation given by the prisoner, and to decide whether he had, by his answers, eluded in whole or in part the suspicion of heresy with which he was charged, or whether, on the contrary, he had not fortified the suspicion of his guilt. The importance of this censure must be evident, since on it depended the definitive sentence. Yet says Llorente, "les qualificateurs se donnent à peine le temps d'écouter une lecture rapide de ce qui s'est passé: ils se hâtent d'établir leur opinion, et c'est là le dernier acte important de la procédure," all the rest being a simple formality. Lastly, came the sentence, which, as may easily be anticipated from the nature of the procedure, was generally condemnatory of the prisoner. In fact, before the reign of Philip III., sentences of absolution were so rare in the Holy Office, that in one or even two thousand judgments we scarcely find an instance where the prisoner was fully acquitted, because the slightest doubt as to the complete innocence of the accused led the qualificators to declare him suspected de levi, and this was sufficient to induce the inquisitors to condemn him to suffer pains more or less grave, according to circumstances, and to make a formal abjuration of all kinds of heresy, particularly of that of which he had incurred the suspicion. Devant l'Inquisition, quand on vient à jurer Si l'on ne sort rôti, l'on sort au moins flambé. The reading of the judgment formed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINALE">finale</a> of the procedure which we have been endeavouring to describe; and the execution of it always commenced in the same auto-da-fe where it was read and signified. We shall not attempt to describe a public and general auto-da-fe, because all the circumstances attending that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> may be found detailed in several works, and even represented in engravings, which exhibit to the eye a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the horrors of which no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a> can convey any adequate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. We shall only speak here of the san-benito, to which reference has already been made in a previous part of this article. This vestment was merely a kind of scapulary which was fitted close to the person, and descended only to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, in order that it might not be confounded with any form of the monastic habit. This last circumstance led the inquisitors to prefer for the san-benito an ordinary woollen stuff dyed <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, with crosses of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, by which means every trace of resemblance between the habit in which the penitents of the Inquisition were clothed, and that worn by any of the religious orders, was completely annihilated. Such was the san-benito in 1514, when Cardinal Ximenes de Cisneros caused the ordinary cross to be replaced by that of St Andrew. Afterwards, however, the inquisitors varied the forms of the san-benito, in order that one of these might be applicable to each class or description of penitents. But we shall only mention here those which were in common use. When a person had been declared slightly suspected of heresy, and condemned to make abjuration, if he demanded to be relieved from the censures <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> cautelam, he was made to assume a san-benito, which the Spaniards of the fifteenth century called zamarra, and which was merely the scapulary we have already mentioned, without a cross in saltier. But if the condemned abjured as one violently suspected, he bore one-half of this cross; and if he made abjuration as a formal heretic, he bore it entire. This, however, applied only to those who, after having been reconciled, had their lives spared. But there were other kinds of san-benito for those who were condemned to perish in the flames. He who, after having been once absolved from the crime of formal heresy, and reconciled to the church, relapsed into his former errors, was denominated relapsed, and incurred the pain of death. His fate was inevitable, however lively might be his repentance, and even notwithstanding a second reconciliation. The only advantage which this last act procured him, was that of not being burned alive. He was merely strangled, or put to death in some other manner less horrible than by fire, and then his corpse was delivered to the flames. Thus, as there were three kinds of san-benito for the three classes of condemned who were delivered to the secular arm, so also the inquisitors contrived an equal number for those who were doomed to suffer death. The first was that of prisoners who had repented before being condemned. It was formed of a simple yellow scapulary, with an entire red cross in saltier, and a round pyramidal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>, called coroza, of the same stuff as the san-benito, and garnished with similar crosses, but without any representation of flames, because the repentance of the accused having been manifested in time, had saved them from the penalty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CREMATION">cremation</a>. The second was destined for those who had been definitively condemned to be delivered to secular justice, in order to undergo the pains of fire and who had repented, after their condemnation, and before being conducted to the auto-da-fe. The san-benito and the coroza were made of the same stuff. On the lower part of the scapulary was represented a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bust on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRAZIER">brazier</a>, whilst the rest of it was covered with the resemblance of flames pointing downwards, to indicate that the criminal was not to be burned alive, because he had not been adjudged to suffer that punishment, but only to be thrown into the flames after being strangled. The same representations were painted upon the coroza. The third was for those who were treated as guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> impiety. It was made of the same stuff (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>) as the others. The lower part exhibited a human bust on a brasier, surrounded with flames; and the rest was covered with flames in their natural direction, to show that he who wore it was doomed to actual burning. On the vestment were also delineated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> figures of devils, which were painted thereon, to indicate that these lying spirits had entered and taken up their abode in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the guilty. The coroza was charged with similar figures. Such were the principal forms of the san-benito. The others were intended for those adjudged to suffer milder penalties, as confinement. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSCRIBED">Inscribed</a> and penance, and generally had inscribed on them the name, country, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of heresy, punishment, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of condemnation of the delinquent, accompanied with a cross in saltier or with flames, according to circumstances. As the Inquisition was the creation of an intolerant age, when religious zeal was envenomed by bigotry, and exasperated by schisms and divisions, so it has fallen before the humanizing influence of modern civilization, and is now, even in Catholic countries, only a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of history. In Spain and Portugal it has ceased to exist even in name; in Italy and other countries, where it has not been formally abolished, it is merely an obsolete institution, which henceforward no one will ever succeed in reviving. But the time was when it acted with fearful energy and efficacy, and when, like the Vehmgericht of the middle ages, it struck terror into all hearts. In Spain alone, according to Llorente, upwards of three hundred and forty thousand persons were judged and punished, one way or other, by this tribunal. The following is the general result of his statement in figures: - Burned alive, ........................................... 31,912 - Burned in effigy, ........................................... 17,559 - Subjected to rigorous pains and penances, 291,450 Total, 341,021 And if to the number of victims immolated by the Inquisition in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">Peninsula</a>, be added all the unfortunate who were condemned by the tribunals in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, together with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, Milan, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, whilst these countries were under the dominion of Spain, it would probably be found that more than half a million of human beings had been condemned by this inexorable tribunal to undergo various punishments, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of which inferred infamy.

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is said to be inscribed in another, when all its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> touch the sides <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> planes of the other figure.

INSCRUTABLE

Pages 303-303

Unsearchable, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, is usually understood of the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and the judgments of God, into which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason is unable to penetrate.

INSECTS

Pages 303-304

Insecta, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. See Entomology. Noxious Insects; Means of destroying them, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> preventing their increase. Of those substances which have been generally observed to be efficacious in driving away or in destroying insects, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, and its various preparations, may be reckoned the most generally effectual. Sulphur is also useful. Oils of all kinds have often been deservedly recommended; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> is not less remarkable for its utility. Mercury is known to kill or drive away <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; and it may probably be of equal efficacy in ridding other animals of insects. For instance, a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of mercurial ointment rubbed upon the skins of sheep, on the sides, between the fore-legs and the body, may kill or drive away the insect peculiar to these animals. Sulphur is recommended to be added to the mercurial ointment. Thus not only the insect peculiar to them, but also the scab, may be cured.1 Allway2 directed that, in the winter, the walls, frames, and other parts of his green and hot houses should be well washed with corrosive sublimate mercury, dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These houses had been greatly infested with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> spiders and ants. After having been washed with this solution, neither of these were to be seen next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. This wash, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made weaker, may be used on old garden-walls, and the roots of fruit-trees infested with insects. It may destroy the tender leaves of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, though not the roots. The same wash <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> effectually destroy that disagreeable insect the bug, and all other insects of a tender cuticle; and it will not in the least hurt the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>-furniture or hangings. Care must be taken that the wash be applied into every crevice or folding of the furniture with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. It will sometimes be necessary to repeat the wash, as the ova of bugs may remain concealed, notwithstanding the utmost care. Some of the West <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> were much infested with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ants, which greatly injured the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes. The remedy was, to dissolve corrosive sublimate mercury in rum, in the proportion of two drams to a pint of spirits. This solution was poured upon dry powdered sugar; and when the sugar was dried, it was laid in the paths of the ants. They ate it, and were destroyed. Might not this practice be imitated, by laying sugar thus prepared on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or pieces of thin boards near the roots of fruit-trees infested by insects, especially when the fruit is ripening? The papers or boards might be taken in during the night, or when it rained. The sugar should be coloured with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, or other substance, thereby to mark it as a substance to be avoided by curious idlers. We are informed that a person in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> employed brimstone in the following manner. Having cleared all round the roots of trees infested with caterpillars or other insects, he strewed some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of brimstone round the roots, and covered it with a thin sprinkling of fine mould, that it might not be blown away by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, yet so that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> might operate through the mould, and cause the brimstone to fumigate. In this manner he destroyed the caterpillars. One <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POUND">pound</a> he found sufficient for two-hundred trees. In that hot <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> the sun may perhaps have that effect; but it scarcely will in this. To drive insects from small trees, he also employed sulphur in the following manner. He split the end of a pole, and put in the slit some matches, set them on fire, and held them under the parts of the trees chiefly affected. A pole thus armed, he found, would answer for three or four trees. Brimstone mixed with damp straw, and set on fire, in hop-ground infested with the fly, for instance, might be of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in driving away that insect. The itch is supposed to originate from a very small insect which nestles under the skin, and proceeds no farther; and it is, therefore, attended with no dangerous consequences. Brimstone made into an ointment with hogs-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> is a sure remedy. Sheep are liable to an eruption on the skin, known by the name of the scab. Brimstone, when added to the mercurial ointment recommended for that disorder,3 might perhaps render the application more efficacious and less dangerous. The natives of hot countries are taught by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that an unctuous covering of their bodies prevents the bites of musquitos and all gnats. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> inhabitants in such countries are not sufficiently careful in preventing the least stagnant water near their dwellings, in which the musquitos are bred; they are produced even in the waste water thrown out. Dr Franklin, by a careful <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this circumstance, guarded his family in Philadelphia from such insects. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of musquitos in his library, he found on inquiry, that one of his servants had taken off the cover of a tub placed near his window for receiving <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-water. On such an occasion the remedy is --- 1 Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the Encouragement of Arts, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, vol. vii. viii. p. 90. 2 Ibid. vol. v. vi. p. 59. 3 Ibid. vol. vii. p. 90. Insects easy, namely, shutting up the room for the day, so that the musquitos cannot come at any water, in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> they die. Though this caution may seem trifling to us who live in a mild climate, it is far otherwise in hot countries. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> being known to be most efficacious in destroying insects, may not the use of it be extended to the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> in the bowels of horses, where they probably occasion the violent pain which these animals seem sometimes to suffer? If the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were for some time kept fasting, and a large quantity of oil, say a pint, were given, supposing worms were the cause, the oil might in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> destroy them. Flowers, leaves, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, are known to be devoured by caterpillars. But these are destroyed by oils, which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the lateral pores by which they breathe. For this purpose it is advised that, on the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, a cloth dipped in train oil be laid on those parts of the tree in which there is any appearance of them. We are informed in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Society of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that oil of turpentine, when applied to animals covered with insects, destroyed the insects without hurting the animal. The author tried it on several trees, mixed with fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> so as to incorporate therewith, adding water, till the whole was brought to some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fluidity. In this mixture he dipped branches of fruit-trees on which there were insects, and thereby destroyed not only the eggs but also the insects, without hurting the leaves. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> may be got off by washing, or the first heavy shower. From these experiments the author thinks, that oil of turpentine may with equal efficacy be employed for killing various kinds of lice on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals. We are informed that Mr Winter, amongst other experiments on turnip-seed, steeped the seed twenty-four hours in a sufficient quantity of train-oil. He then drained the oil from the seed, which he mixed with a quantity of fine sifted earth, and immediately sowed it in drills. When the plants began to appear on the surface, the ground was sown with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>. He found that seed steeped in linseed oil answered equally well.1 The turnips least injured by the fly, were those which grew from seed steeped in this way; they grew so luxuriantly as to produce rough leaves several days <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the most flourishing of any of his other experiments, and were the better enabled to withstand the attack of the fly. The leaves of these turnips were of a darker green, and appeared twice as thick in bulk and luxuriancy as the other turnips, and were considerably larger. The seed was drilled an inch and a half deep, and a foot distant in the rows. Train oil is apt to kill the leaves of plants which have been injured by insects, but linseed oil has not that effect, though equally destructive to the insects. The train oil seems to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> as an oil, and by its disagreeable smell to prevent insects approaching it. In this respect it may be successfully used to prevent field mice or other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> preying on acorns, chestnuts, or other seeds steeped in it before they are sown. When thus giving directions for preventing the fly on turnips, an experiment may be mentioned, by the disclosure of which a person gained a considerable reward. His secret was, running a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> over the ground early in the morning, whilst the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> remained on the ground, on the first appearance of the fly. The dew entangled the flies so much, that they could not make their escape, and were therefore crushed to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. But as the roller may leave the surface of the earth too hard, it was recommended to fix some boughs of elder in a gate or hurdle, to be drawn over the field; and if the boughs had before been fumigated with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of tobacco, or tincture of assafoetida, the success would be the surer. The most certain method of preventing the injury done by the fly is to raise the plants in a nursery, and at a proper <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> to transplant them, being carried to the ground in a wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARROW">barrow</a> filled with manure softened with water so as to admit the plants. This method will secure their more speedy growth. In the nursery the attack of the fly may be prevented by sprinkling soot or quicklime on the ground. The utility of transplanting turnips is evident by the practice of transplanting the turnip-rooted cabbage. They who are discouraged from having recourse to this practice by the expense attending it, do not reflect that the hoeing is prevented, and the plants grow the better, being set in fresh earth.

INSINUATION

Pages 305-305

denotes a cunning and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> way of creeping into any person's favour; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> it means something conveyed by implication or innuendo. **INSINUATION of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">Will</a>**, amongst civilians, is the first production of it, or the leaving it with the registrar, in order to its probate.

INSOLVENT

Pages 305-305

a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such persons as have not wherewithal to pay their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> debts. See **Bankruptcy**.

INSPECTOR

Pages 305-305

a person to whom the care and conduct of any <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is committed. **Inspectors**, in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, were such persons as examined the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and value of lands and effects, in order to the adjusting of taxes and impositions in proportion to every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s estate. The Jews have also an officer in their synagogue, whom they call ḥazan, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> inspector. His business consists principally in inspecting or overlooking the prayers and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, in preparing and shewing them to the reader, and in standing by him to see he reads correctly; and, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the latter make mistakes, he is to correct him.

INSPIRATION

Pages 305-316

amongst divines and others, implies the conveying of certain extraordinary and supernatural notices <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> intimations into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; or it denotes any supernatural influence exercised by God upon the mind of a rational creature, by which he is formed to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intellectual improvement, to which he could not or would not have attained, in his present circumstances, in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> way. Thus the prophets are said to have spoken by divine inspiration. Some authors reduce the inspiration of the sacred writers to that particular care of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, which prevented anything they had said from failing or coming to nought; maintaining, that these writers were not really inspired either with knowledge or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. According to M. Simon, inspiration is no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Holy Spirit, which never permitted the sacred writers to be mistaken. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the inspiration of the Holy Spirit regards only the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, not the style or words; and this seems to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in with M. Simon's doctrine of direction. Theological writers have enumerated several kinds of inspiration. These are, an inspiration of superintendence, in which God so influences and directs the mind of any person, as to keep him more secure from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in a various and complex discourse, than he would have been merely by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his natural faculties; plenary superintendent inspiration, which excludes any mixture of error at all from the performance so superintended; inspiration of elevation, where the faculties <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> in a regular, and, as it seems, in a common manner, yet are raised to an extraordinary degree, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> shall, upon the whole, have more of the true sublime or pathetic, than natural genius could have given; and inspiration of suggestion, when the use of the faculties is superseded, and God does, as it were, speak directly to the mind, making such discoveries to it as it could not otherwise have obtained, and dictating the very words in which such discoveries are to be communicated, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are designed as a message to others. It is generally allowed that the New <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> was written by a superintendent inspiration. Without this the discourses and doctrines of Christ could not have been faithfully recorded by the evangelists and apostles; nor could they have assumed the authority of speaking the words of Christ, or evinced this authority by the actual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of miraculous powers. Besides, the sacred writings bear many obvious internal marks of their divine original, in the excellence of their doctrines, the spirituality and elevation of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, the majesty and simplicity of their style, the agreement of their various parts, and their efficacy on mankind; to which may be added, that there has been in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, from its earliest ages, a constant <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> that the sacred books were written by the extraordinary assistance of the Spirit, which must at least amount to superintending inspiration. But it has been controverted whether this inspiration extended to every minute circumstance in their writings, so as to be in the most <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> plenary. Jerome, Grotius, Erasmus, Episcopius, and many others, maintain that it was not; whilst others contend, that the emphatical manner in which our <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> speaks of the agency of the Spirit upon them, and in which they themselves speak of their own writings, fully justify our believing that their inspiration was plenary, unless there be convincing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> brought on the other side to prove that it was not. If it be said we allow that there were some errors in the New Testament, as it came from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the apostles, there may be <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger of subverting the main purpose and design of that book; since there <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be endless room to debate the importance both of facts and doctrines. **Inspiration**, in **Physic**, is understood of that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> is admitted into the lungs; in which sense, inspiration is a branch of respiration, and stands opposed to **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">Expiration</a>**. **Inspirating**, in **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>**, an operation by which a liquor is brought to a thicker consistence, by evaporating the thinner parts. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSPRUCK">Inspruck</a>** or **Insbruck**, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tyrol, in the Austrian dominions. It is situated on the river Inn, where the Sill falls into that stream. Though not a strong it is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> city, containing twenty-one churches, two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, an orphan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, several monasteries, and within the walls 1925 families, consisting of 10,237 individuals; the suburbs also are extensive and populous. It contains a gymnasium, with a good library, and fifteen professors in the several branches of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, This diversity of opinion may easily be traced to its source. There are not many original thinkers in the world. The greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> even of those who are called philosophers implicitly adopt the opinions of certain masters, whose authority they deem sufficient to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of argument; and having chosen their respective guides, each maintains with zeal what his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> taught, or is supposed to have taught. When Locke so successfully attacked the doctrine of innate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and innate principles of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, he was thought by many to have overturned at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> all innate principles whatever; to have divested the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind of every <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, affection, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>; and to have left in it nothing but the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and intellect. Such, we are persuaded, was not his intention; nor is there any thing in his immortal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which, when interpreted with candour, appears to have such a tendency. In our opinion, great part of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Human Understanding has been very generally misunderstood. Much of its merit, however, was soon discovered; and mankind, finding <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> disencumbered of the barbarous jargon of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and built upon a few self-evident principles, implicitly embraced every opinion advanced, or which they supposed to be advanced, by the illustrious author; especially if that opinion was contrary to any part of the scholastic system which had so <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been employed to perplex the understanding, and to veil absurdity. Hence arose many philosophers of eminence, both at home and abroad, who maintained, as they imagined, upon the principles of Locke, that in the human mind there are no instincts, but that every thing which had been usually called by that name is resolvable into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. This doctrine was attacked by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a>, who introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of mind, as faculties derived from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; and these he considered as the tests of speculative truth and moral rectitude. His Lordship's principles were in part adopted by Mr Hutcheson of Glasgow, who published a system of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a>, founded upon a sense or instinct, to which he gave the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral sense</a>; and the undoubted merit of his work procured him many followers. Men generally run from one <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to another. It being now discovered, or at least supposed, that the human mind is endowed with instinctive principles of action, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers soon afterwards arose, who maintained with much vehemence that it is likewise endowed with instinctive principles of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; and who built a system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, if such it may be called, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of innate, distinct, and independent senses. The rise of this sect is well known. Berkeley and Hume had adopted Locke's doctrine respecting the origin of our ideas; and had thence deduced consequences supposed to be dangerous in themselves, but which, it was thought, could not be denied without refusing the principles from which they were inferred. The foundation of the instinctive system being thus laid, the system itself was rapidly carried to a height far beyond what seems to have been the intention of its excellent author; and reason was well nigh banished from the regions of philosophy. For such a proceeding it is not difficult to assign the cause. The instinctive scheme requires much less labour of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> than the systems of Locke. --- 1 As nothing is of greater importance in the philosophy of mind than accurate definitions, it may not be improper to observe, that throughout the whole of this article the word spontaneous is to be taken in the sense in which it is used in the following extracts from Hale's Origin of Mankind: "Many analogical motions in animals, though I cannot call them voluntary, yet I see them spontaneous. I have reason to conclude, that these are not simply <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>." "The sagacities and instincts of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> the spontaneousness of many of their motions, are not explicable, without supposing some <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> determinate power connected to and inherent in their spirits, of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> than the bare natural modification of matter." If this be attended to, our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of instinct will be found perfectly consonant to that which has been given by the author of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Metaphysic: "Instinct," he says, "is a determination given by Almighty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> to the mind of the brute, to act in such or such a way, upon such or such an occasion, without intelligence, without knowledge of good or ill, and without knowing for what end or purpose he acts." and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; for upon the principles of it, when carried to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, every phenomenon in human nature is thought to be sufficiently accounted for, by supposing it the effect of a particular instinct implanted in the mind for that very purpose. Hence, in some popular works of philosophy, we have a detail of so many distinct internal senses, that it requires no small strength of memory to retain their very names. Besides the moral sense, we have the sense of beauty, the sense of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, the sense of honour, the hoarding sense, and a thousand others which it is needless here to mention. This new system, which converts the philosophy of mind into <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or rather into a collection of facts and anecdotes, though it has made a rapid progress, is not yet universally received.
