The most esteemed edition of his works is that of Reiske, Leipzig, 1775, and of Schömann, Gryphiswald, 1831. They have been translated into English by W. Jones, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1779; into French by Auger, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1783; and into German by Schömann, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUTTGART">Stuttgart</a>, 1830. Another discourse of Isæus (*De Meneclis Hereditate*) was discovered in a manuscript of the Library of St Lawrence, at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and published by Tyrwhit, London, 1785. This Isæus ought not to be confounded with Isæus, another celebrated orator, who lived at Rome in the time of Pliny the younger, about the year 97.

ISAIAH

Pages 468-468
or the Prophecy of ISAIAH, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Isaiah is the first of the four greater prophets; the other three being Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. This prophet was of royal descent, his father Amos being brother to Azariah king of Judah. The first five chapters of his prophecy relate to the reign of Uzziah; the vision in the sixth chapter happened in the time of Jotham; the following chapters, to the fifteenth, include his prophecies under the reign of Ahaz; and those which were made under the reigns of Hezekiah and Manasseh, are related in the subsequent chapters to the end. Isaiah foretold the deliverance of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon by Cyrus, one hundred years before it came to pass. But the most remarkable of his predictions are those concerning the Messiah, which describe not only his descent, but all the remarkable circumstances of his life and death. The style of this prophet is noble, nervous, and sublime, insomuch that Grotius calls him the Demosthenes of the Hebrews. However, the profoundness of his thoughts, the loftiness of his expressions, and the extent of his prophecy, render him one of the most difficult of all the prophets; and the commentaries which have been hitherto written on his prophecy fall short of a full explication of it. Bishop Lowth's translation, published in 1778, throws considerable light on the composition and meaning of Isaiah.

ISARIA

Pages 468-468

a rugged and mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, touching Pamphylia and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, situated almost in Mount Taurus, and taking its name from Isaura; and according to some, extending by a narrow slip to the Mediterranean. Stephanus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and Zosimus, make no mention of places on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; though Pliny and Strabo do; but the latter are doubtful whether these are places in Isauria Proper, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> in Pamphylia, or in Cilicia.

ISAURA

Pages 468-468
or ISAURUS, in Ancient Geography, a strong city of Mount Taurus, in Isauria, which was twice demolished; first by Perdiccas, or at least by the inhabitants, who, through despair, destroyed themselves by fire, rather than fall into the hands of the enemy; again by Servilius, who thence took the surname Isauricus. Strabo says there were two Isauras, the old and the new, but so near that they were often confounded.

ISCA DUMNIORUM

Pages 468-468

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Lat. 5° 44', <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40' W. ISCA Silurum, in Ancient Geography, the station of the Legio Augusta Secunda in Britain; now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, on the Uske.

ISCALIS

Pages 468-468
or ISCALI, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Belgae in Britain; now Ilchester, in Somersetshire, on the river Ise.

ISCHIA

Pages 468-468

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west side of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, of volcanic origin, but fertile in wheat, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. It contains about twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The mountain Spomea, in height 2500 feet, is an extinguished volcano, but has woods and good pasture <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and several dairies are maintained, in which excellent cheese is made. It contains the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, of the same name as the island, with 3140 inhabitants. The whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 22,470 persons, who are <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in producing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, wine, excellent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and various kinds of fruit.

ISCHURIA

Pages 468-468

ἰσχυρία (formed from ἵσχω, I stop, and ἱπτιον, urine), in Physic, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> consisting in an entire suppression of urine.

ISELASTICS

Pages 468-468

a kind of games, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> combats, celebrated in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Roman emperors. The victors at these games had very considerable privileges conferred on them. They were crowned on the spot immediately after their victory, had pensions allowed them, were furnished with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> at the public cost, and were carried in triumph to their own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

ISELWORTH

Pages 468-468

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, in the Hundred of the same name, eight miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is pleasantly situated on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and contains <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, and several other mansions of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> respectability. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> industry is exercised in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, for the supply of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 4346, in 1811 to 4661, in 1821 to 5269, and in 1831 to 5590.

ISENBERG

Pages 468-468

now a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the principality of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, having been added to it when the former sovereign, who is still the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> proprietor, was mediatised. It is about 100 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, is a hilly district, with extensive woods, is watered by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Kinzig and Bracht, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> living in four market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and forty-four villages, to the amount of 47,500, subsist chiefly by agricultural occupations. None of the four towns in it, except Berstein, has a thousand inhabitants.

ISERE

Pages 468-469

a department of the south of France, formed out of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> divisions of Grisonsvaudan and Biensois, which were formerly portions of Dauphiné. It extends over 3564 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> assize, 841,230 hectares. It is divided into four arrondissements, and these into 45 cantons, with 558 communes, having 471,660 inhabitants. The latter mostly adhere to the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, but there are about 7000 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is a patois, composed of Celtic, Latin, French, Italian, and Greek, but in which the Latin words predominate. The pure French, with the southern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a>, is generally spoken in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is generally hilly, and in many parts mountainous, exhibiting most picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> scenery, rising gradually from the plain through which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> flows to the lofty elevations bordering on Savoy, where the highest of them, the Col de Saix, is 10,296 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Some of the numerous valleys which extend between the ranges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are of peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, especially the valley of the Isère or Grésivaudan, which is nearly fifty miles in length, and considered as the most delightful district of France. It resembles a well cultivated garden, through which, with many windings, the river flows, between meadows and corn-fields, where scattered mulberry and other fruit trees, fine vineyards, and small woods on the sides of the hills, are ornamented by country houses and neat villages intermingled amongst them. Though, from the elevation, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> portion of the department remains uncultivated, and is incapable of cultivation, yet the other portions are fertile and highly productive. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, mixed with small shells in the valleys, resting on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, and is easily worked; it is well irrigated, and adapted to almost every vegetable production. The only navigable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Rhone and the Isère, whose contributory streams are numerous. There are also some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, which serve the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a>. There are several mountain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> within the department, and some of them are 7548 feet in height. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> varies with the elevation; some of the eastern sides of the mountains are constantly covered with snow, whilst the valleys are in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> intensely hot. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> agricultural products are wheat, maize, barley, potatoes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, rapeseed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, wine, chestnuts, filberts, and some medicinal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, besides cattle and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> which yield small portions of silver, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and coal, but none of them is extensively worked. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are cotton, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and woollen goods, earthenware, gloves at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Grenoble, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities, fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, glass, liqueurs and brandy. There is also much <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> prepared for the glover's trade.

ISERLON

Pages 469-469

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARENSBURG">Arensburg</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Westphalia. It stands on the river Baaren, and is one of the first manufacturing places in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for silks, velvets, and ribbons, and also has manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> goods, with extensive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>. It contains two Lutheran, one Reformed, and one Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, 786 houses, and 5690 inhabitants. Lat. 51° 25' 6", and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 35' 22" E.

ISIAC TABLE

Pages 469-469

is one of the most considerable monuments of antiquity discovered at Rome in 1525, and supposed, by the various figures in bas-relief upon it, to represent the feats of Isis, and other Egyptian deities. There have been various opinions as to the antiquity of this monument. Some have supposed that it was engraved <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the Egyptians worshipped the figures of men and women; but others, amongst whom is Bishop Warburton, apprehend that it was made at Rome by persons attached to the worship of Isis. Dr Warburton considers it as one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> of the Egyptian monuments, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mixture of hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which it bears.

ISIACI

Pages 469-469

priests of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Isis. Dioscorides tells us, that they bore a branch of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> instead of olive. They sung the praises of the goddess twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, namely, at the rising of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when they opened her temple, after which they begged alms the rest of the day, and returning at night, they repeated their orisons, and shut up the temple. The Isiaci never covered their feet with any thing but the thin bark of the plant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPYRUS">papyrus</a>, which occasioned Prudentius and others to say that they went barefooted. They wore no garments except <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, because Isis was the first who taught mankind the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of preparing this commodity.

ISIDORUS

Pages 469-469

called DAMIATENSI, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> PELUSIOTA, from his having lived in a solitude near that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was one of the most famous of all St Chrysostom's disciples, and flourished in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held in 421. We have upwards of two thousand of his epistles in five books. They are short, but well written, in Greek. The best edition is that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in Greek and Latin, printed in 1638, in folio.

ISIS

Pages 469-469

a celebrated deity of the Egyptians. Some suppose her to be the same as Io, who was changed into a cow, and restored to her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where she taught <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and governed the people with mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, for which reasons she received divine honours after <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. According to some traditions mentioned by Plutarch, Isis married her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, and was pregnant by him even before she had left her mother's womb. These two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deities, as some authors observe, comprehended all <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and all the gods of the heathens. Isis was the Venus of Cyprus, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, the Cybele of the Phrygians, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, the Proserpine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and the Bellona of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Osiris and Isis reigned conjointly in Egypt; but the rebellion of Typhon, the brother of Osiris, proved fatal to this sovereign. The ox and the cow were the symbols of Osiris and Isis; because these deities, whilst on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, had diligently applied themselves to the cultivating of the earth. Since Isis was supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, as Osiris was the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, she was represented as holding a globe in her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with a vessel full of ears of corn. The Egyptians believed that the yearly and regular inundations of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> proceeded from the abundant tears which Isis shed for the loss of Osiris, whom Typhon had basely murdered. The word Isis, according to some, signifies "ancient," and on that account the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> were often in these words: "I am all that has been, that shall be; and none amongst mortals has hitherto taken off my veil." The worship of Isis was universal in Egypt, and her priests were obliged to observe perpetual chastity; their heads were closely shaved, and they always walked barefooted, and clothed themselves in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> garments. They never ate onions, they abstained from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> with their meat, and they were forbidden to eat the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of sheep and of hogs. During the night they were employed in continual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> near the statue of the goddess. Cleopatra, the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Egypt, was wont to dress herself like this goddess, and affected to be called a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Isis. Isis, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, a river that takes its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, and flows through only a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Wiltshire. It enters this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> near its source, and begins to be navigable for boats at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CRICKLADE">Cricklade</a>; but after running in a serpentine manner about four miles, it leaves Gloucestershire at a village called Castle Eaton.

ISJUM

Pages 469-469

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Ukraine in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name on the river Jszumez, which near to it falls into the Donez. It is surrounded with walls, but in a neglected condition; and contains four churches, 718 houses, and 4500 inhabitants, whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of corn and cattle. Lat. 49° 12' 30" N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37° 30' 5" E.

ISLA DE LA GENTE HERMOGA

Pages 469-470
or Island of Handsome People, an island in the Pacific Ocean, discovered by Mendana, about six leagues in circumference. Lat. 10° S.; Long. 175° 10' W.

ISLA DE LEON

Pages 470-470

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> generally containing 40,000 inhabitants, but from being within the line of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Spanish troops and the garrison of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, during the siege it was supposed to contain more than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. When the French armies were in possession of the rest of Spain, this city became the refuge of the loyal party, the place of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> for the national representatives, and the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. From being near the arsenal of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CARACCAS">Caraccas</a>, the officers and workmen employed there, found it convenient to take up their residence in this city. The streets are wide, the houses <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the public buildings splendid, and its whole appearance gives it an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magnificence. It is separated from the continent by the narrow but navigable river Sante Petri, over which is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> called Puente de Zuarzo, generally, but erroneously, believed to have been built by Julius Caesar; it is, however, known to have been erected by Cornelius Balbo the younger, seventeen years before the Christian era. The foundations are now the same as then existed, but the upper works, and some of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, were built in 1437. On both sides, but especially towards the continent, the river has extensive and boggy marshes, which can only be crossed by means of a narrow causeway, exposed to the attacks of several heavy batteries. The strength of this place, and the secure retreat from it to Cadiz, of still greater strength in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of emergency, made it the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and valuable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> of all that remained of freedom in Spain from the year 1810, till the result of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a> compelled the French to evacuate Andalusia. The marshes on the banks of the Sante Petri afford prodigious quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, crystallized by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. It is piled in heaps of a pyramidal form; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> dissolves the upper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, the sun crystallizes it again, and thus forms a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> cake of salt, and defends the heap from the future effects of any bad <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It is permitted to be exported on payment of a very trifling duty, and numerous ships are loaded with it. What is conveyed to the interior becomes the subject of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> monopoly, and is subject to a very heavy tax. Lat. 38° 53' 16" N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 40' 31" W.

ISLAM

Pages 470-470
or ISLAMISM; the true faith, according to the Mahommedans. See MAHOMMEDANISM.

ISLAMABAD

Pages 470-470

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, in the district of Chittagong, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It is situated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Chittagong, near about ten miles from its junction with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It carries on a considerable trade, and ships are also built there, and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. This town was early known to the Portuguese, by whom it was called Porto Grando. It was taken from the rajah of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARRACAN">Arracan</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> in 1656; and was at that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> well fortified with 1200 cannon. Its name was changed from Chittagong to Islamabad. In 1689, the English made an unsuccessful assault upon it. Since it was ceded to the British in 1760, the fortifications have been allowed to go into decay. The entrance to the river is dangerous without a pilot, as it has only four fathoms over the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and afterwards deepens to five to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fathoms. The entrance to the river is in 22° 13' N. The town stands in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 91° 42' E.; lat. 22° 22' N. This is also the name of a considerable town of Cashmeer, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river Ihytyur, over which is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> eighty yards in length. Its houses are built of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, with gardens on their roofs; and its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> manufacture is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHAWLS">shawls</a>. Lat. 34° 6' N.; Long. 74° 7' E.

ISLAMNAGUR

Pages 470-470

a town of Hindostan, in the Mahratta territories, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALWAH">Malwah</a>, five miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from Bossal, in lat. 23° 19' N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 77° 31' E. There are many small places of this name in Hindostan. ISLAMPOOR. There are two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this name in Hindostan, one in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AJMEER">Ajmeer</a>, seventy-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles north from Zeypoor. Lat 27° 4' N.; long. 75° 23' E. Another in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAHAR">Bahar</a>, district of Bahar, thirty-five miles south from Portna. Lat. 25° 7' N.; long. 85° 15' E.

ISLAND

Pages 470-470

a tract of dry <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands contradistinguished from CONTINENT, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> TERRA FIRMA.

ISLEBAINS

Pages 470-470

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name given to those who adopted the sentiments of a Lutheran divine of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, called John Agricola, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, and a native of Isleb, who, interpreting literally some of the precepts of St Paul regarding the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, declaimed against the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of good works. See ANTONINIANS.

ISLINGTON

Pages 470-470

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in the hundred of Ossulton, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It rises in a gentle declivity from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, but, by the houses connecting with it, appears to be only a prolongation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. It is chiefly occupied by persons carrying on trade in London, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> by those who have retired from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It contains no very splendid mansions, but a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of respectable and comfortable dwellings. It contains the hamlets of Upper and Lower Holloway, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Newington Green and Kingsland. Being on the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> are passing through it at all hours. Besides the parish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> it has three others, and chapels for sectaries of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. The New River passes through the parish, and the Regent's Canal. The latter, by a tunnel, goes under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street, and under the New River, and thus conveys coals and other heavy <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at a cheap rate. The New River head, from which a great part of the metropolis is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is in this parish, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> known as Sadler's <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>. A mineral water here was once frequented for its medicinal qualities, but the fashion seems to be changed, as it is now rarely resorted to. A collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> has been lately founded at Highbury in this parish, for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of dissenting ministers of the class of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the parish amounted in 1801 to 10,212; in 1811 to 15,065; in 1821 to 22,417; and in 1831 to 37,316.

ISMAELITES

Pages 470-470

the descendants of Ismael, dwelling from Havila to the wilderness of Sur, towards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and thus overspreading <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea; wherefore Josephus calls Ismael the founder of the Arabs.

ISMAIL

Pages 470-470

a town of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Bessarabia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name. It is situated on an arm of the Danube, is strongly fortified, and has become celebrated for the carnage which attended its capture in 1789 by Suwarow. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it has not recovered its former importance, and contains but few inhabitants, with little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> produce. Lat. 45° 21' 30"; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28° 44' 35" E.

ISMARUS

Pages 470-470

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cicones in Thrace, giving name to a lake, and by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> called Ismara.

ISMID

Pages 470-470

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NICOMEDIA">Nicomedia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bithynia. It retains no traces of its former <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, nor any antiquity, except the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It contains 750 families, and is situated on the side of a hill overlooking the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Nicomedia. Lat. 40° 39' N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° 34' E.

ISMIK

Pages 470-471

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Nice, which now contains scarcely 300 houses, yet exhibits numerous monuments of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. It is situated on a lake communicating with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> of Marmora, and carries on This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is famous in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, as the seat of two councils, in 325 and 387. During the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a>, it became the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> erected along the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Asia Minor. The old walls of the town may be still traced over a circumference of four miles. Lat. 46° 16' N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° 50' E.

ISOCHRONAL

Pages 471-471

is applied to such vibrations of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> as are performed in the same space of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; as are all the vibrations of the same pendulum, whether the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> it describes be longer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> shorter. ISOCHRONAL Line, that in which a heavy body is supposed to descend without any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a>.

ISOCRATES

Pages 471-471

one of the most celebrated rhetoricians of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, was born, b.c. 436, five years before the beginning of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, twenty-two years after the birth of Lysias, and fifty-four after that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>. He died b.c. 338. He was son of Theodorus, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> of musical instruments, but, though of humble parentage, he seems to have enjoyed the best <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> which Athens could furnish. His early years were spent under Gorgias of Leontium, one of the most celebrated sophists of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; Prodicus of Ceos, whose beautiful apologue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> between Virtue and Vice, has immortalized his name; and Theramenes, who was afterwards condemned to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the thirty tyrants, because, though their colleague, he refused to participate in their tyranny. With their assistance, Isocrates soon began to display the talents of which he was possessed, and became anxious to illustrate his name as a statesman and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, however, it would appear, had placed an impassable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against his entrance on public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, by furnishing him with a weak <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and timidity of nature which he found himself unable to overcome. Thus prevented from pursuing the path to which his inclination pointed, he determined to make his talents subservient to his fortune. He opened a school for oratory, and soon found himself surrounded by a numerous body of young men anxious to profit by his instructions. Amongst the more celebrated we may mention Theopompus, Ephorus, Isaeus, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMOTHEUS">Timotheus</a>, Philiscus, and Xenophon. So numerous were the disciples of Isocrates, that Hermippus composed a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in several books respecting them. The sophists of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> were accustomed to discuss subtle <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of logical casuistry; Isocrates first distinguished himself by discussing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> interests of the time, and examining important questions of morality. As his speeches were not intended to be delivered, but to be perused in the retirement of the closet, Isocrates was obliged to pay particular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of style, to the rounding of his periods, and avoiding whatever might prove offensive to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. He is said to have been employed ten years in polishing one of the most celebrated of his productions, entitled the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PANEGYRIC">Panegyric</a>. It might be expected that this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of proceeding would be attended with some defects; it occasioned a want of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>, a constant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>, and often an entebling of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which were enveloped in a multitude of words, useful only to round the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> and to produce the necessary rhythm and cadence. He was not always able to secure himself against the envy of his countrymen, and they even accused him of holding a suspicious intercourse with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon, with whom he kept up a constant correspondence; but he proved, by the closing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his life, that his intentions had always been pure, and that he had sincerely loved his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Charonea, b.c. 338, so fatal to the liberties of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, he determined no longer to drag on a life which would be embittered by seeing his country subject to the Macedonians. He preferred to starve himself to death. Of his works we still possess twenty-one orations and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> letters. The first is addressed to Demoricus, of whom we know nothing, and is a collection of remarks and maxims for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a young <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s conduct. It is attributed by some critics to Isocrates of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLONIA">Apollonia</a>, who is mentioned by Suidas and Harpocration. One of the finest of his productions is the Panegyric (Πανεγυρικός), which was written n. c. 380, with the view of putting an end to the internal dissensions of the Greeks, and inducing them to unite against the Persians. We may also mention the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> entitled Ἐπιστολῆς, as one of the best specimens of his peculiar style, though it was composed, n. c. 342, at the advanced age of ninety-four. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> panegyric on the Athenians and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Numerous editions of his works have been published. The editio princeps was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> in 1493, by Demetrius Chalcondylas, but the best is that by Coray, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1807. The Panegyric has been published separately by Morus, 1803, by Pinzger, Lips. 1825, and by Dindorf, Lips. 1826. Many of his other works have also been published separately. ISOPERIMETRICAL figures, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are such as have equal perimeters <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> circumferences. ISOSCELES triangle, in Geometry, one that has two equal sides.

ISPANAHAN

Pages 471-473

from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated as one of the most splendid cities of the East, though now nearly in a state of ruin and decay. Its original name is said to have been Sipahan, which it received from the Persian kings, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its having been the general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous for their armies. The origin of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is lost in a remote antiquity; but it is generally supposed to have arisen from the ruins of Hecatompylos, the capital of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>; whilst some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to stand on the site of the Aspa <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Aspadura of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. It is well adapted, from its central situation with the noble river Zeinderood flowing through it, for the capital of the empire. It was under the caliphs of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> that it rose to be the capital of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>, and under their powerful protection it soon increased in wealth, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and trade. The invasion of Timor gave a fatal blow to its rising prosperity. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol9.html#article-ISPAHAN">Ispahan</a> was taken by his conquering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the year 1387; and at first he contented himself with exacting a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> contribution from its inhabitants. But being apprised that the inhabitants meditated a nocturnal insurrection against his troops, he gave up the place to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> execution; and in the indiscriminate massacre which followed, it is computed that 70,000 inhabitants perished; indeed their heads piled up in heaps on the walls of Ispahan, attested the merciless severity of the conqueror. From this desolation, owing to its favoured situation, it quickly revived; and under the early <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOPHIS">sophis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> efforts were made to restore its former prosperity. But it was reserved for the renowned Shah Abbas to raise it to the height of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> magnificence, and to render it not only a luxurious capital, but the great emporium of the Asiatic world. During his reign it contained nearly a million of people, and to supply its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> required the labour of 1400 villages, whose inhabitants drew their subsistence from its prosperity. "Its bazaars," says Sir R. K. Porter, "were filled with merchandise from every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe, mingled with the rich bales of its own celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>." It was the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of industry, diligence, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>; whilst the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of ambassadors from the proudest kingdoms of the East, as well as from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and travellers visited it, to behold its splendours, and to enjoy the gracious reception bestowed by its monarch on the learned and ingenious of all nations. It was visited by Char din at the beginning of the eighteenth century, and its mag- --- 1 See Travels in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, &c., vol. i. p. 407, et seq. Ispahan. nificence was such, that no city of the East could compare with it, except the capitals of Hindostan and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. Such was the state of Ispahan during the reign of Abbas the First, and also during the subsequent reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Abbas. In 1722, it was taken by the Afghans, when all its prosperity and splendour were for ever extinguished by those merciless invaders. The people were massacred without mercy; the most superb edifices erected by the Persian kings were reduced to ruins; and the wall which formerly surrounded the city was entirely destroyed by them. In 1727 it was retaken by Nadir Shah, who took no pains, however, to restore its prosperity. Since this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, Ispahan has never again been a royal residence, the late sovereigns of Persia having preferred a more northern capital, particularly <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TEHERAN">Teheran</a>; and Ispahan, instead of being repaired and beautified as formerly, has gone more and more into decay, and now presents little else than a scene of ruin. Its people are in fact reduced to scarcely one-tenth of their former numbers; the streets are everywhere in ruin; the bazaars remain silent and unattended; the caravansaries are equally forsaken; its villages <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> waste; and its palaces are solitary, the sounds of revelry, which were wont to be heard in the festive halls, being now succeeded by the howling of jackals and famishing dogs. According to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> account of this city by Charadin, it was twenty-four miles in circuit, contained 172 mosques, 43 colleges, 1800 caravansaries, and 273 public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The most splendid edifice which adorned the city was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Shah Abbas. It is said to have been five miles in circuit, and was divided into gardens and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> grounds, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-houses and other elegant structures. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and elegance of the buildings, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the fountains dispersed through the gardens, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the royal halls in the interior, are said to have surpassed anything of the kind to be found in Europe. The walls and buildings of the palace remain still nearly entire; but it has been stripped of all its costly furniture, and every thing valuable that could be removed. The Meydun is a large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, nearly one-third of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, and about one-half in breadth. It was formerly surrounded by a canal, bordered by very fine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> trees; but all vestiges of both are now obliterated. Its original purpose, by Shah Abbas, was for the display of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and military exercises, but it is now entirely devoted to trade, being the place of the city where the finest shops are to be found, with a second storey, in which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> have their working apartments; and in the middle is a market for horses and cattle. In the centre of this immense <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> stand some edifices remarkable for grandeur or for character. In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west we find the great gate or rather tower of entrance to the bazaar, on which in former times stood the celebrated clock of Ispahan. The south-eastern side of the quadrangle shews the Mesched Shah, a superb mosque, which Shah Abbas built and dedicated to Mebedi, one of the twelve imams. On the north-east is the mosque of Looft Ullah; and on the south-west the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>-kapi, or gate of Ali, forms a majestic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the bazaar porch on the opposite side. This is the most perfect piece of fine brick-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be found in the Persian empire. Another remarkable object is the Chahar Bagh, or four gardens. The royal domain which bears that <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, is a very extensive tract, inclosed with four majestic walls, and divided into gardens with pleasure-grounds. The prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of all these is that of long parallel walks, shaded by even rows of tall and umbrageous planes; and interspersed with a variety of fruit-trees, and of every kind of flowering shrub. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">Canals</a>, which receive the waters of the Zeinderood, flow <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the avenues in the same undeviating <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and generally terminate in some large marble basin of a square or octagon shape, ornamented with sparkling fountains; the effect of the whole, though formal, being extremely <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>. Many magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and palaces opened into these gardens, which are now all destroyed. That at the east called Hooser Jereeb, one of the noblest edifices of Ispahan, was reduced into a heap of rubbish by the Afghans. Its garden, however, still remains, and is nearly a mile in extent. The object of this garden was to form a repository of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> which Persia produced, and which are still to be found there in the greatest perfection. The palace of Forty Pillars, which was the favourite residence of the Sefi kings, is said to exceed all our European <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of splendour, and to realize the wonderful tales of the Arabian Nights' Entertainments. At a considerable distance from the Chehel Setoon, or the palace of the Forty Pillars, to the left of the gardens, stands the Winter Palace, containing the harem, royal arsenal, and stables, where Ashraf, the second <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of the Afghan invaders, held his short and cruel sway, which he stained with the blood of its native <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the captive Shah Houssain. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to the winter palace stands a superb structure, lately erected by the Nimzam-a-Doulah, for the reception of his present majesty, should he ever visit the capital. The general style of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is the same with that of the neighbouring palaces, but executed in a more <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, simple, and elegant <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. There are several very handsome bridges in Ispahan across the Zeinderood. They were all the work of Shah Abbas, built of brick, and on the same plan, being perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, presenting the appearance of Roman <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>. Each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is formed of a long succession of small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, over which the causeway is laid; and on that run two lines of arcades on each side of the bridge, affording a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for foot passengers, and leaving the middle <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> open for horsemen and cattle. The bridge which joins the Chaur Bang with the suburb of Julpha, is 1000 feet long, and has thirty-four arches. The streets of Ispahan are narrow, winding, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; and being quite unpaved, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, in dry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, raises such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of dust, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> cannot be seen. Great pains are in consequence bestowed in watering the streets. The houses within, though they are handsome and convenient, have a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance from the street, being built merely of bricks dried in the sun, and covered with flat roofs. The walls by which the city was formerly surrounded, are now entirely obliterated. They were merely built of mud dried in the sun, and were never able to offer any effectual resistance against a vigorous assault. Ispahan, during its prosperity, was greatly distinguished by the extent and beauty of its suburbs. The suburb of Julpha was very wealthy and populous. It was chiefly inhabited by Armenians, who were transferred here from Old Julpha in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, on account of their skill in manufacturing industry. They were soon joined by others of their countrymen, as well as by a number of Georgians, Circassians, and other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, the suburbs being appropriated to the professors of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. The streets are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with well built houses and a numerous population, with walks of trees, cooling fountains, and pleasant gardens. It is now reduced to a complete ruin. Its 10,000 inhabitants have diminished to 300 wretched families, dwindling every year both in respectability and numbers; its thirteen churches are reduced to two, and these dirty and dark and dismal in their appearance. The worship of the Guebres, the ancient worshippers of fire, and that of Abbas Adab, formerly very extensive, have quite disappeared. Ispahan, after such a long period of misery and desolation from foreign wars and internal revolutions, has begun to revive from its low state, partly through the spontaneous efforts of its inhabitants, anxious to better their condition, and partly also through the exertions of Hajce <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAHOMMED">Mahommed</a> Hussein Khan, who, from the lowest situation, having acquired immense wealth, has employed it in the improve- ment of his native city and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. He has completed a royal palace, and has beautified and rebuilt many of the bazaars; repaired and added to the number of the fountains and aqueducts which supply the public gardens with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and inclosed and cultivated all the waste <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the vicinity of the city, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> fields, which are irrigated by the waters of the Zeinderood, and the cultivation of which is likely to supersede entirely its once abundant nurseries for cotton and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. Ispahan has still very extensive manufactures. It excels in silk manufactures and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BROCADE">brocade</a>; and it is also a great emporium of inland trade, and a depot of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> produce, being the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> medium of intercourse between <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CABUL">Cabul</a>, and the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and the countries round the Mediterranean, in the west. Lat. 32° 25' N.; Long. 52° 50' E.

ISPIRA

Pages 473-473

a town of Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hispiratis, now an inconsiderable town, but situated in a very fertile district, and surrounded by many fine and rich villages. It is ninety miles east of Trebisond.

ISRAEL

Pages 473-473

the name which the angel gave to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, after having wrestled with him all night at Mahanaim <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Penuel (Gen. xxxii. 1, 2, and 28, 29, 30, and Hosea xii. 3). It signifies "a conqueror of God," or "a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of God," or, according to many of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, "a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> who sees God." By the name of Israel is sometimes understood the person of Jacob; sometimes the whole people of Israel, or the whole <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Jacob; and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Israel, or of the ten tribes, distinct from the kingdom of Judah.

ISRAELITES

Pages 473-473

the descendants of Israel, who were at first called Hebrews, by reason of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, who came from the other side of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>; and afterwards Israelites, from Israel the father of the twelve patriarchs; and, lastly, Jews, particularly after their return from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, because the tribe of Judah was then stronger and more numerous than the other tribes.

ISSACHAR

Pages 473-473

one of the divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> by tribes, situated to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-ZABULON">Zabulon</a>, and by a narrow slip reaches the Jordan, between Zabulon and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> (Joshua, xix.). But whether it reached to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is uncertain. Some hold that it did; but this is an assertion not easy to be proved, as Joshua makes no mention of the sea in this tribe, nor does Josephus extend it farther than to Mount Carmel; and in Joshua (xvii. 10) Asher is said to touch Manasseh on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, which could not be <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Issachar extended to the sea.

ISSENGEAUX

Pages 473-473

an arrondissement of the department of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a> in France, extending over 1200 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is divided into six cantons, and these into thirty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> communes, which contain 76,306 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, which contains 1050 houses, with 6571 inhabitants, who subsist chiefly by agricultural operations.

ISSOIRE

Pages 473-473

an arrondissement of the department of the Puy-de-Dôme in France, extending over 758 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, divided into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cantons, composed of 116 communes, and inhabited by 95,500 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on the river Crouse, which a little below falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>. It contains 730 houses and 5,479 inhabitants, who manufacture some jewellery. Lat. 45° 33'; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 10' E.

ISSOUDUN

Pages 473-473

an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a> in France, extending over 466 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, divided into four cantons, and those into fifty-three communes, and containing 39,887 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> from which it takes the name, is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> which is situated on the river Thaëls, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>-rate stream. It is surrounded with ditches and walls, defended by towers, and contains 2050 houses, with 10,710 inhabitants. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> is cured in it, and there are many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> and stockings made. Lat. 46° 56' 53"; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 54' 5" E.

ISSUE

Pages 473-473

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, has various applications, being sometimes taken for the children begotten between a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> and his wife; sometimes for profits growing from mercerments <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> fines; sometimes for profits of lands and tenements; but more frequently for the point of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> depending in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, upon which the parties join, and put their cause to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. In all these occasions, issue has but one signification, which is, an effect of a cause preceding; as the children are the effect of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between the parents; the profits growing to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of any man's offence, are the effect of his transgression; and the point referred to the trial of twelve men is the effect of pleading, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>.

ISSURDU

Pages 473-473

a town of Hindostan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Asmeer, in the Rajput territories. It is surrounded with a wall and ditch, has a citadel in the centre, and is one of the best built <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in the province. Lat. 26° 26' N.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76° 10' E.

ISTAKHAR

Pages 473-473

a castle of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, formerly one of the citadels of Persepolis. It is situated on a very lofty and steep rock, and completely commands the surrounding plains. On the top is abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

ISTHMIA

Pages 473-473
or ISTHMIAN Games, one of the four solemn games which were celebrated every fifth year in Greece. They derived their name from the isthmus of Corinth, where they were celebrated. In their first institution, according to Pausanias, they consisted only of funeral ass="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RITES">rites and ceremonies in honour of Melicertes; but, as Plutarch informs us, Theseus, in emulation of Hercules, who had appointed games at Olympia in honour of Jupiter, afterwards dedicated these to Neptune, his reputed father, who was regarded as the particular protector of the isthmus and commerce of Corinth. The same trials of skill were exhibited here as at the other three sacred games; particularly those of music and poetry. These games, in which the victors were only rewarded with garlands of pine leaves, were celebrated with great magnificence and splendour as long as Paganism continued to be the established religion of Greece; nor were they omitted even when Corinth was sacked and burned by Mummius the Roman general; at which time the care of them was transferred to the Sicyonians, but was again restored to the Corinthians when their city was rebuilt.

ISTHMUS

Pages 473-473

a narrow neck <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> slip of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which connects two continents; or joins a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the terra firma, and separates two seas. The most celebrated isthmuses are that of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, which joins <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; that of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, which connects <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; that of Corinth, which unites the Morea with Western <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; that of Crim-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, otherwise called Taurica Chersonesus; and that of the peninsula Romania, and Erissos, or the isthmus of the Thracian Chersonesus, twelve furlongs <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, being that which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> undertook to cut through.

ISTRIA

Pages 473-473

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, situated in the northern <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It is bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and on the south, east, and west, by the sea. It produces wine, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and pastures; and there are quarries of fine marble. One part of it belongs to the Venetians, and the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. Capo d'Istria is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ITALY

Pages 495-500

Italy. It is about thirty-five miles in length, and in no part exceeds three miles in breadth, but it is of very great depth. It is formed by the river Adda and 195 smaller streams. It issues forth by the river, which bears the same name as at its entrance, but with an increased volume of water, and serves to fructify a great extent of land. At Bellagio it divides into two branches, one of which terminates at the city of its own name, and the other at Lecco. Lago d'Iseo is about twenty miles long and six broad; it is chiefly supplied by the streams of the Oglio, which issues from it again and runs to the Po. Lago d'Idro is small, being only seven miles in length, and through it the river Chiese passes before it joins the Oglio. Lago di Garda is the most extensive of all the lakes of Italy, covering a space of 315 square miles, or 201,600 English acres. It receives the water of the Sarta, and its only issue is at Peschiera, into the Mincio. It is of sufficient depth to carry vessels of the greatest draft of water. These vast reservoirs are of unspeakable advantage, both to the internal connection of one part of the country with the other, and to the several occupations of agriculture. As the slope of the land is regular and gentle from these lakes to the river Po, nature has thereby formed the means of distributing, with comparatively little cost of labour, the water over an extensive portion of the land, and in that due proportion which the nature of the soil or the description of the crop may require. In many parts streams of water are made to pass rapidly over the fields that require it, and what is not absorbed by the earth is received again into canals, and, at lower elevations, again passed in a similar manner over other fields, till the surplus fluid at length reaches the river Po. As these modes of disposing water to the greatest advantage are almost peculiar to Upper Italy, and by their extension have been productive of the most beneficial effects on the fruitfulness of the soil, as well as on the internal communication, a sketch of their commencement and early progress can scarcely be destitute of interest. After the decline of the power of the German emperors of the Saxon race, who had succeeded to Charlemagne, several free states were formed, of which Milan became one of the most flourishing; but war having been kindled amongst these states, most of the others combined with the Emperor Frederick I. against Milan, and, in 1162, captured and almost destroyed the city, laying waste the fields; but, during the continuance of hostilities, a change of fortune favourable to Milan, and the gaining of a battle, led to a peace in 1176. The energy and industry which this free state had displayed in war became equally manifest in peace. The canal then, as now, called Naviglio Grande, was begun to be constructed in 1178, or rather perhaps restored, for it is probable that the citizens of Pavia, eighty years before, had dug the canal, which had been partly filled up and rendered altogether useless during the continuance of hostilities. The canal was at first only carried to Abbiategrasso, but the benefit was found to be so great, that, in the year 1220, the canal of Muzza was added to it. In 1269 the canal of Vettabia was extended and lengthened. It had been originally constructed in 1037, but, as is stated by Giuleni (Storia di Milano, vol. iv.), was long neglected. In 1350 the canal of Treviglio, or Fosso Bergamasco, was begun; and, in 1460, the Duke Francesco Sforza first planned that of Artesana. These, though in some degree designed for the purposes of navigation, were chiefly planned and regulated to administer to irrigation. Navigation was only permitted two days in the week, and the other five days the water was used to enrich the land. It seems very probable that advantage to the soil from irrigation was known prior to any of the dates here stated as the commencement of these canals. That some progress was made as early as the year 1138, appears from a contract made in that year by the monks of Chiavarella and Vicoboldone, in which are the following conditions: "Ut monasterium possit ex Vectabia trahere lectura (a canal) ubi ipsum monasterium voluerit, et si fuerit opus licet facere eadem monasterio fossa super terram ipsius Johannis (the vender), ab una parte viae et ab alia, &c. possit firmare et habere clausum (sluice) in prota ipsius Johannis." A similar contract of the following year, and several of subsequent dates, are still in existence. The whole water of the Vettabia belonged to those monks, having been granted to them by a charter of the Emperor Frederick II.; and the fame of their skill in the management of water was so great, that the chief of Milan, Napoleone della Torre, intrusted to their care the construction of works for draining the environs of that city, whilst Rinaldo, archbishop of Cologne, employed them in improving the marshes in his dominions.
