The following are some of the methods practised at present. **Mix up some vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> with naphtha or spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> and turpentine, and let it sour for a night; then add as much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JAPAN">japan</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> not take away the body of the black. After the article has been freed from rust, coat it with this, and put it into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>. When dry, let it be coated with japan; two coats are sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the japan be rich or old. If the article is intended to be polished, another coat or two may be given, according to the surface of the article; and let it be gently cooled between each coat. To polish the above, take a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-grained pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, ground <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a smooth and perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> surface, and with this slightly rub down all the knots. When this is effect- In japanning tin, care must be taken to deprive the article of any rosin or grease. It then receives one coat of black and two coats of japan, as in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of cast or sheet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. If it has to be polished previously to being coated, it is rubbed smooth lengthways with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>-comber's card, or coarse sand-paper. This will greatly aid the polisher, and in some instances may <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a coat of japan. The article is then polished and oiled as before described. Clean the tin as before mentioned, and give it one coat of japan. Let it then be put into the stove, and when dry give it another. If a dark <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> is required, it is subjected to a strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and if a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> brown, a coating and a gentle heat only is necessary. Care must be taken that each coat is well settled or stiffened in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it upside down to keep it from flowing all one way, before putting it in the stove. Grind some Venetian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> in spirit of turpentine very fine, to which add three parts of mixing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> with one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of japan, that is, as much as will not take away the body of the red. Coat the article, and put it into the stove till it dry. Then give it one coat of japan pretty fluid, and let it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the air, as mentioned above. Put it again into the stove, and when dry it will appear of a fine brown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. All metals may be japanned in this way, especially old tin <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. If a polish is required, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> instead of Venetian red, as it will require more coats. Another brown, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called chocolate, may be produced by using purple brown in the same way. In japanning wood in the same way as metal, it ought to be dried or seasoned well in the stove before coating. A black is obtained by using the same black as that already mentioned. After the article has been dried in the stove and taken out, it is coated with japan; and this is repeated until the surface becomes smooth. Care must be taken not to let the article cool between the periods of each successive application of the japan, else the air may insinuate itself into the pores of the wood, and cause it to blister when put into the stove again. The article made or turned must be in one piece. In japanning <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> tops, the best Spanish mahogany, planed and smoothed with sand-paper, must be used. First put it in the stove between two plates of iron, with a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> on it to keep it from casting or warping, till it be properly seasoned. Take it out and coat it with black as above mentioned. Afterwards put it into the stove to dry. Then coat it with japan until it has a flowing appearance. Should it blister between the coatings, rub the blisters down with fine sand or glass-paper. After the last coat has been applied, allow it to become perfectly hardened, and then polish it in the same way as metal is polished. This method is not generally known or practised, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> existing that it will not stand the heat; but Spanish mahogany, three fourths of an inch thick, will stand the same heat as tin. Small fire-screens made of plain-tree and other kinds of wood may be japanned in the same manner; but as they are done on both sides, it requires a frame made of tin, tapered inwards, so that the screen may rest gently on the edges of it. Flat <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, which cannot stand the necessary temperature, are japanned in the following manner. Grind fine some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>-black with turpentine, then add two parts of japan and two parts of drying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COPAL">copal</a> varnish; and after the wood has been well dried, coat it over three times. When it is dry, smooth it down with wet rag and ground pumice-stone. The smoothing being finished, take extra quick copal varnish, tinged with ivory-black, and give the article two coats. When these are hardened it may be polished. If <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care be taken in laying on the varnish, polishing may not be necessary. To a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ground in turpentine add one part of drying copal varnish, and mix them together. Coat the japanning wood till the pores be filled up, and then rub it down as before described. Then take flake-white ground in turpentine, and add to it three parts of fine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> varnish; strain it grounds on through fine muslin, and let it stand for five or six hours; White, after which, coat the wood over twice, and let the first coat be properly hard before the other is applied. When sufficiently hardened, take a piece of fine <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> dipped in rotten-stone ground in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and rub it till smooth, when it is rendered fit for working on. But if it is to be finished in the white, let it be rubbed all over with a mixture of sweet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and flour, and then dusted with dry flour, which is afterwards wiped clean off with both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, leaving a fine glossy surface. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ground may be filled up in the same way as the above with the lead. When it is filled up, take chrome-yellow ground in turpentine, and add three parts of fine drying copal varnish; strain this, and coat the article with it, as in the above case, and varnish and polish it in a similar manner. Take common vermilion ground in turpentine, to which add one part of quick-mixing varnish. Fill up the ground with this, and then take Chinese vermilion ground in fine drying oil, thick, adding to it a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine mixing varnish, to make it free in working. With this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> the article is twice thinly coated, which method is preferable to laying on only one thick coat. When dry, it will be fit for working on. But if it is intended to be polished, give it two coats of fine quick-polishing varnish, and let the first coat be very hard before it receives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. After it is properly hardened, take a woollen rag dipped in ground pumice-stone and water, and rub the ground all over. When it is smooth, take a flannel rag dipped in ground rotten-stone, and finish it, as in the case of the white. Fill up the blue ground in the same manner as the Blue-white is filled up; and a little Prussian blue may be added to it. When filled up, Prussian blue and white lead are ground by themselves upon the same stone, and afterwards mixed together in proportions varying according to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> required. The after-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for polishing is the same as that already described. Fill the green ground as in the case of the white, adding <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-black to make it of a lead colour, the quantity employed being in proportion to the shade required. When filled up and smoothed, take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>-green ground in turpentine, and add a small quantity of mixing varnish to it, so that the green may be flat, for it will require three coats, as the green has a very little body. It is then smoothed and rendered fit for working on. If a dark hue is wanted, take <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> green, which may be made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> by adding a little chrome-yellow; or darker, by adding Prussian blue and black. This green is more easily produced than any other. Varnish and polish the article as before described. Take white lead ground in turpentine, and add crimson-lake and Prussian blue, according to the shade wanted. The article is then coated, varnished, and polished, in the same way as the red. All the above grounds may be enriched by giving each a coat of thin primitive colours ground in turpentine, and mixed up with fine clear mixing varnish. These are crimson-lake for red, yellow-lake for yellow, Prussian blue for blue, verdigris for green, and lake and blue for purple. To produce damask grounds for white, when the ground is fit for working on, take fine dial varnish for size, so that it may not discolour the ground, and size the device. Let it stand till it slightly attaches itself to the finger; then take a piece of shamoy leather, dip it in silver powder, and shade the device with it, when it will appear like damask. For obtaining red or crimson, after the ground has been smoothed with the common vermilion, take japanners' <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> size, thin, and size the device; when it adheres to the finger, take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> and shade it as above. This being dry, coat it with crimson lake ground in turpentine and mixed with fine polishing varnish; polish it as usual, and a rich damask ground will appear. This ground must be a very light yellow. Use size and silver powder, the same as in the case of the white; coat it with yellow-lake ground in turpentine and mixed with polishing varnish; coating, varnishing, and polishing it as usual. Make the ground a very light blue, almost approaching to white; use the size and silver as in the above case; take Prussian blue ground in turpentine and mixed with polishing varnish, and coat it to the shade required, then varnish and polish it as usual. Make a light bluish-green with verdigris and white lead ground, use size and silver as in the case of the white, then take verdigris ground in turpentine, and mix it with slow-drying varnish, to prevent it from cracking, as the verdigris is very brittle; coat it to the shade wanted, and varnish and polish it as usual. Make a ground of crimson lake and Prussian blue mixed with white lead, very light; then take lake and blue ground in turpentine and mixed with polishing varnish; coat it to the shade required, size and silver it as in the case of white, and varnish and polish it as usual. Beautiful grounds are produced with the silver powder; and devices on black grounds with either of the above colours, which greatly enrich the appearance of the deep or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PALE">pale</a> gold ornaments that are wrought upon them. All the above coloured grounds may be produced on metals in the same way, with the exception of the white. In filling up metals, take Venetian red ground in turpentine or tar spirits, add as much japan as will give it body enough, so as not to crack, and afterwards coat the article till it is filled up; then smooth it down with lump pumice-stone. Put it into the stove till dry every time it is coated, then lay on the ground colour as before mentioned. With regard to sizing and gilding on japan grounds, take the gloss off the part that is to be worked on, by which means the size will be better seen. In ornamenting any article, as, for instance, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-tray, with various golds, bronze, and colour, proceed thus: After tracing or drawing out the ornaments, size the parts for your deep gold first, and then gild them, the parts for the pale gold being also gilt; and care must be taken that the size has but a slight adhesive feel before the gold is put on. If bronze shaded is introduced, size the part first, and then take a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> and dip it into the bronze or gold powder gently; then rub the sized part, and it will produce a soft shade. If it is to be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bronze, let it be nearly dry; rub the sized part gently over with a piece of shaggy leather dipped in bronze, then warm the tray, and rub the part over smartly, when it will appear solid with a metallic lustre. After all is gilt and bronzed, take a common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and etch up all the finer parts of the ornament with it; but for the stronger parts take a fine camel-hair pencil dipped in black, to open up the ornament. The gold may be shaded with terre senna, and then put into the stove till dry, when it may be varnished and polished in the usual way. In putting on raised <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, take Chinese vermilion two parts, and white lead two parts; mix them thick together with turpentine, adding a small quantity of japan so as to make it adhere to the ground. Then take a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> hair pencil and dip it amongst the raising, keeping the pencil upright so as to feed the point. Although the raising appear flat or dull, it will take a bright polish by rubbing it with the finger, after which it is sized and gilt. In imitating Japanese or Chinese, this must be done on Japan gloss or polished ground. As this kind of work is not varnished, a little oil-colour may be mixed with the gold size, such as white lead or chrome-yellow, which will enable the fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> to be better seen, and make the work more closely resemble gilding. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> on japan work, either oil or varnish colour may be used. The varnish colour looks clearest, and is most showy, but it requires great practice to blend the colours so as to appear soft; oil-colour is at present that most frequently used. In varnishing white wood-work, or work covered with paper, take sheep-skin size in a liquid state, dip into it a camel-hair flat <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and come over the work swiftly with it, so as not to wash up the painting. When this is dry, take hard white spirit varnish and a camel-hair flat brush, and coat the work over smartly. It will appear whitish at first, but it will become clear as it dries. After it has received four coats, let it stand for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, until small cracks appear all over it. Rub the gloss off the work, or any knots, with the dry fingers, and then wipe it clean; after which give three or four coats more, when the varnish will appear full and flowing. Allow it to stand for a day or two, then take a piece of woollen cloth wet with water, dip it in ground pumice-stone, and smooth down the work with it, and then wipe it clean. After this take a piece of woollen cloth and dip it in rottenstone ground in sweet oil, with which rub the work till a glass appears. After wiping it, dip a piece of fine flannel in sweet oil mixed with flour, and rub the work smartly; powder it with dry flour, then rub it quickly off with the palms of the hands, and a brilliant gloss will appear. In japanning paper after it comes out of the dip-stove, it must be coated till a full flowing body of japan is produced. In polishing the above, care must be taken that the ground is not overheated in the rubbing. If it be brought up with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> varnish, it must stand till it be thoroughly cool, otherwise the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the ground will draw the size out of the pencil before the work can be executed. As black japan is generally the colour that paper-grounds are filled up with, it greatly depends on the japan or varnish being rich or old, as either will produce a good gloss to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of coats given. For any other colour that is required, rub down the above ground smooth; for the first coat let it be white, but tinged a little with the colour wanted, unless it be maroon. The first coat must be a light-olive colour smoothed down, thinly coated with crimson lake; if a dark maroon, purple-lake is the pigment employed. The best polishing varnish ought to be used in the finishing. Paper trays are brought up in boards, sheet above sheet, with paste, to the thickness required, with the exception of the edges, which are done upon iron <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, and then taken off, planed, glued, and nailed together, like a piece of wood. With regard to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> board, or any other paper, it is japanned in the usual manner, with a first coat of sheep-skin size to make it bear out.

JAPETUS

Pages 534-534

a son of Cœlus and Terra, who married <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Asope, Theonis, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Clymene, and had four sons, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, Menetius, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, and Epimetheus. He was thus considered as the author of the Hellenic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. (Apollod. i. 1, 2; Diodor. v. 65, 67; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, Theog. 134. Iapetionides, a son of Japetus; Atlas, Ovid, Met. iv. 631). He is supposed to be the same as Japheth, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>.

JAPHETH

Pages 534-535

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. His descendants possessed all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Mediterranean, as well those which belong to Europe, as those which depend on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. They had all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, and the northern parts of Asia above the sources of the Tigris and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Noah, when he blessed Japheth, said to him, "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a> shall be his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>." This blessing of Noah is supposed to have been accomplished when the Greeks, and after them the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, carried their conquests into Asia and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, where were the dwellings and dominions of Shem and Canaan.

JAPYDES

Pages 535-535
or Iapodes, a people who stretched along the coast of the Adriatic, from the Gulf of Quarnero, as far as Zara, the ancient Jadra, for a distance of 1000 stadia. They occupied the valleys of Mons Albius, which form the extreme point of the Alps to the east, extending in the interior to the Pannonia and the Ister or Danube. They were finally subdued by Augustus after they had twice defeated the Romans within twenty years, attacked Aquileia, and plundered Tergestum or Trieste. Their towns were Metulum, Arpennum, Monetium, and Veudum. They were in the habit of tattooing their bodies. (Strab. vii. 315; Appian. Illbr. 18, 19.)

JAQUELOT

Pages 535-535
Isaac, a learned French Protestant divine, was born on the 16th December 1647, at Vassy in Champagne, of which place his father was minister. The revocation of the edict of Nantes having obliged him to quit France, he took refuge first at Heidelberg, and then at the Hague, where he procured an appointment in the Walloon church. Here he continued till that capital was taken by the king of Prussia, who, having heard him preach, appointed him his French minister in ordinary at Berlin, to which city he removed in 1702. During his residence at Berlin he entered into a warm controversy with M. Bayle on the doctrine advanced by him in his dictionary concerning Manicheism, which dispute continued until death imposed silence on both parties. It was in this controversy that M. Jaquelot openly declared in favour of the Remonstrants. His reputation as a writer rests principally on the following works, viz. 1. Dissertation sur l'Existence de Dieu, Hague, 1697, in 4to; 2. Dissertation sur la Messe, où l'on prouve aux Juifs que Jesus-Christ est le Messie promis, et prédit dans l'Ancien Testament, Hague, 1699, in 8vo; 3. Traité de la Vérité et de l'Inspiration des Livres du Vieux et du Nouveau Testament, Rotterdam, 1715, in 8vo; 4. Select Sermons, Geneva, 1721, in two vols. 12mo.

JARCHI

Pages 535-535
Solomon, otherwise Isaki Solomon, a famous rabbi, born at Troyes, in Champagne, who flourished in the twelfth century. He was a perfect master of the Talmud and Gemara; and he filled the postils of the Bible with so many Talmudical reveries, as totally extinguished both the literal and the moral ass="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense of it. The greater part of his commentaries are printed in Hebrew, and some have been translated into Latin by the Christians. They are generally esteemed by the Jews, who have bestowed on the author the title of prince of commentators.

JARDYN

Pages 535-535
or Jardin, Karel du, a painter of conversations, landscapes, and such like subjects, was born at Amsterdam in 1640, and became a disciple of Nicholas Berchem. This painter, in colouring and touch, resembled his master Berchem; but he added to that manner a force which distinguishes the great masters of Italy; and it is observed, that most of his pictures seem to express the warmth of the sun, and the light of mid-day. However, some of his subjects are often more extensive, containing a greater number of objects, and a larger design. His works are as much sought after as they are difficult to be met with. He died at the age of thirty-eight.

JARENSK

Pages 535-535

a town of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Wologda, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of its own name, extending over 23,936 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, but containing no more than 31,500 inhabitants. It is generally a neglected district, covered with woods, marshes, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The town is situated on the river Wytscheda, which is usually closed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> from the beginning of November to the middle of April. It contains 200 houses, and from 1000 to 1100 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 47. 33. E. Lat. 61. 20. N.

JARGEAU

Pages 535-535

a town of the arrondissement of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LOIRET">Loiret</a>, in France. It stands on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, over which is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It contains 428 houses, and 2690 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 1. E. Lat. 47. 50. N.

JARMERITZ

Pages 535-535

a town of the circle of Znaym, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, and situated on the river Rokitna. It has near it a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> belonging to the family of Questenburg, with a very extensive library. The town contains 272 houses, with 1650 inhabitants.

JARNAC

Pages 535-535

a town of the arrondissement of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COGNAC">Cognac</a>, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, in France, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river. It contains 1560 inhabitants, amongst whom are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> dealing very extensively in brandy for foreign countries. It is celebrated for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought there in 1569, between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> and the Catholics, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Condé was taken prisoner.

JAROSLAV

Pages 535-535

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the circle of Przemysl, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, and situated on the river San. It contains a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a> and six other churches, for Catholics, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, with 1400 houses, and 6975 inhabitants, occupied in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and in distilleries. It was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and is still the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Czartoryski, a nobleman of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 47. E. Lat. 49. 59. N.

JAROSLAW

Pages 535-535

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of European Russia, formerly in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, to the eastward of Twer, extending over 15,202 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It comprehends twelve cities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 554 parishes, 7705 villages, and 1,022,900 inhabitants. It is an elevated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> district. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally marshy, but mixed with portions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> or clayey <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. It is miserably cultivated, and though all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> are chiefly occupied in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, it scarcely produces sufficient corn (chiefly rye and barley) for their subsistence. Both <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> succeed tolerably well; and the conversion of these into the various kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> is a means of affording to the inhabitants of the towns occupation and subsistence. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> of their cattle also form a branch of employment to the people, as does the fishery on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The river Wolga enters the province from Twer, and receives the waters of numerous streams that flow through it. There is a lake of eight miles in length and three in breadth, called Rostow, out of which the Kotorosla runs to the Wolga; and thirty-six smaller lakes, all, like the streams, abounding in fish. The Wolga is navigable in its whole progress through the province, as are also the Mologa and the Schekissa, which run into it. The province is divided into ten circles. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Jaroslav, is also that of the circle of the same name. It stands at the junction of the Kotorosla with the Wolga. It has no other fortification than palisades, but is defended by a fortress. It contains forty-four churches, several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, 2754 houses, and 24,200 inhabitants, whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> subsistence arises from the linen trade, and Russia <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. 4. 55. E. Lat. 57. 57. 30. N.

JASHER

Pages 535-536

THE BOOK OF. This book is mentioned by Joshua, and referred to in the following passage: "And the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> stood still, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOON">moon</a> stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies: is not this written in the book of Jasher?" It is difficult to determine what this book of Jasher, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> "the upright," is. St Jerome and the Jews believed it to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, or some other book of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, in which God had foretold that he would do wonderful things in favour of his people. Huetius supposes it to have been a book of morality, in which it was said that God would subvert the course of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in favour of those who put their trust in him. Others pretend that it was public annals, or records, which were styled <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a>, or upright, because they contained a faithful account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Israelites. Grotius believes that this book was nothing else than a song, composed to celebrate the miracle, and victory therewith connected. This seems the more probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, because the words cited by Joshua as taken from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon, and thou moon in the valley of Ajalon," are such poetical expressions as do not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> with historical <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>; besides that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Samuel (i. 18), mention is made of a book under the same <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, on account of a song composed on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>.

JASLO

Pages 536-536

a circle of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Gallicia, extending over 1354 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It contains five cities, eleven market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 366 villages, inhabited by 195,200 individuals, occupying 28,562 houses. It consists of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is for the most part <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and stony; but it produces corn equal, with the aid of potatoes, to the consumption. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated at the junction of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Jastel and Wisłoka, and containing 224 houses, and 1463 inhabitants.

JASON

Pages 536-536
chief of the Argonautic expedition, was son of Æson, king of Iolcos, and of Alcimede or Polymede. His father was obliged to yield to the superior power of his brother Pelias, and was driven from his kingdom. Jason was secretly carried by his mother to the valleys of Mount Pelion, and there delivered into the hands of Chiron the centaur. By him he was trained to the arts of war, and began his adventurous career by joining in pursuit of the Calydonian boar. Then, in obedience to the orders of an oracle in Magnesia, he presented himself at Iolcos to reclaim the kingdom, covered with the skin of a leopard, and armed with two javelins. Pelias had been warned by an oracle to beware of a man who should appear with one foot shod and the other uncovered. Jason, by some accident, entered Iolcos in this manner, and the suspicions of Pelias were of course immediately excited. He boldly demanded the kingdom, to which he was the rightful heir; but Pelias prevailed on him to proceed to Colchis to get possession of the golden fleece, promising on his return to resign the crown. He was accompanied in this expedition by all the bravest of the Greeks (see Argonauts); and, after many curious adventures, they all arrived in safety in Colchis. Jason proceeded to present himself at the court of Æetes, and explained to him the object of his voyage. The king agreed to restore the golden fleece, provided he submitted to certain conditions the former would impose on him. He must tame brazen-footed bulls, whose nostrils breathed flames, and plough with them a field sacred to Mars. He must then kill a dragon which kept watch day and night over the golden fleece, and sow in the field which he had tilled the teeth of this serpent, from which armed men would spring, ready to attack him. The destruction of Jason seemed inevitable, but he was extricated from his difficulties by Medea, the king's daughter. His lofty bearing, and the intrepid nature of the enterprise, had captivated the heart of Medea, and she determined to deliver her lover from all his dangers, if he promised her eternal fidelity. By her magic herbs, he performed the conditions, to the astonishment of Æetes and his subjects; and, having obtained possession of the golden fleece, returned to his native country, accompanied by Medea, whom he afterwards married. Medea, however, carried along with her Absyrtus, her brother; and when she heard that her father was in pursuit, she tore him to pieces, and scattered his limbs in different places, that she might escape whilst her father was employed in collecting the mangled body of his son. They arrived in safety in Iolcos, where they were received with the greatest joy. Æson was restored to youth again by the magic power of Medea; and Pelias, the usurper of the crown, wishing to be restored to the flower of youth, allowed himself to be cut up by his daughter at the persuasion of Medea, and thrown into a boiling caldron. Thus Pelias perished by a miserable death. But Jason was obliged to fly with Medea, and proceed to Corinth, where they lived in great harmony for four years. At the end of that time, having divorced Medea, he married Glaucus, or Creusa, daughter of Creon, son of Sisyphus, king of Corinth; but his inconstancy was severely avenged. Medea slew his sons in his presence, and burnt Creusa, together with Creon and Jason. Another tradition states that they returned to Colchis, and reinstated on his throne Æetes, whom a faction had expelled.

JASPER

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mineral belonging to the siliceous genus of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and of which there are many varieties, some of them extremely beautiful, which are much sought after, and employed as trinkets and ornaments. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>.

JASPONYX

Pages 536-536

an obsolete <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, importing, as appears from the name, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of jasper and onyx.

JASSY

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a>, the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, of a Greek archbishop, and of many of the wawodes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. It stands on a lofty situation, but is surrounded with hills still higher. It is watered by brooks forming a stream ending in the Pruth. The town is composed chiefly of wooden houses, and is said to be excessively filthy, and by no means healthy. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the prince is plain, small, and badly situated. The city contains no less than forty-three churches, with twenty-six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and nunneries of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. It has also a Catholic and a Lutheran chapel. The houses are stated to be six thousand in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the inhabitants from twenty-five to thirty thousand. It is not a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of any other trade than such as arises from providing for the luxuries of a voluptuous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and a petty sovereign. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 27. 24. 55. E. Lat. 47. 8. 30. N.

JASTROW

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Deutschkrone, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of East <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, situated on a brook running to the river Kuddow. It contains 296 houses, and 2380 inhabitants, of whom more than 400 are Jews. There is a manufactory for arms and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> clothing.

JAUER

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the same name, in the circle of Herschberg, of the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>. It stands on the river <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEISSE">Neisse</a>, is surrounded with walls and ditches, and contains one Lutheran and five Catholic churches, 604 houses, and 5230 inhabitants, chiefly occupied in the several branches of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture.

JAULNAY

Pages 536-536

a town of the arrondissement of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a>, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, in France, on the river Elain, with 245 houses and 1476 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to this town was fought, in 1356, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> usually called that of Poitiers, and sometimes Maupertuis, in which Edward the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> defeated the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> John a prisoner.

JAUNDICE

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> consisting in a suffusion of the bile, and a rejection thereof to the surface of the body, whereby the whole exterior <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is discoloured.

JAUTS

Pages 536-537

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, who have at different times made some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in its annals. The first historical mention of them occurs at the beginning of the eleventh century, on the invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> by Mahmoud the Gaznevide. That conqueror found them established on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>, prepared to oppose his passage. For this purpose they had mustered a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fleet of boats, to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, according to some accounts, of eight thousand. They were completely defeated, however, and driven into the mountainous districts in the interior of India. From this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Jauts remained in obscurity, till the reign of Aurungzebe. Churamana, a Jaut of some distinction, collected then some troops of banditti, with whom he began to commit depredations on travellers. Popular and enterprising, he gradually rose from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of robbers to be a powerful chieftain; and, availing himself of Aurungzebe's absence in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a>, became the terror of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round. He had even the audacity, on one occasion, to plunder the rear of that monarch's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and, when pursued, took refuge among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NARWAR">Narwar</a>, where he eluded all attempts to extirpate his force. Under the growing imbecility of Aurungzebe's successors, the Jauts continually extended their power, till at length, during the weak reign of Mahommmed Shah, and under their enterprising head, Sooraje <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, it rose to its utmost height. That <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> wrested continually new concessions from the weak <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, till he was able almost to dictate the councils of the Mogul <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. A reverse, however, took <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the invasion of Northern India by Ahmed Shah, the sovereign of Caubul. Sooraje Mull, having opposed that invader, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his territory overrun, and was obliged to seek aid from the Mahratta power. When the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, however, invaded <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, the Jaut chief went over to Ahmed Shah, and offered to atone for former hostility by his services on that critical occasion. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PANNIPUT">Panniput</a> followed, in which the Mahrattas were totally routed, and their power for the time entirely broken. Ahmed Shah rewarded the services rendered by his new ally in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of need, by the important cession of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a> and its district. Sooraje Mull, and his son Jowalier Sing, made repeated attempts to obtain possession of Delhi, but were always baffled by untoward circumstances. Jowalier Sing was assassinated by an impostor, who had undertaken to initiate him in the secret of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. He left his son an infant; a circumstance which, affording an open field to the dissensions of the chiefs, weakened the Jaut power, and rendered it unable to contend with the other fierce competitors for the spoils of the Mogul. In their contests, particularly with Nujeeph Khan, they were gradually stripped of all their possessions, and at length reduced to the fortress of Bhurtpore, with a small surrounding district. When the British power became predominant in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of India, Runjeet Sing, rajah of the Jauts, sought security by concluding a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lake, by which, on engaging to assist <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> against all enemies, he not only retained the internal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of his territories, but was even exempted from paying any tribute. Yet, in 1805, after the defeat of Holkar, he received that chief, with his discomfited army, into Bhurtpore. The place sustained a most desperate siege, and cost the British army an immense number of lives. At length the rajah, despairing of effectual resistance, agreed to compel Holkar to quit the place, and to give it up to the British, on condition of retaining the government of his territories, and the fortress of Deeg. He was obliged, however, to pay twenty lacs of rupees, and to give ample security for a more faithful observance of this treaty than of the former.

JAVA

Pages 537-543

This <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> geographers denominate the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. It extends eastward, with a slight deviation on the south, from 105.11. to 114.33. of east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, and lies between the latitudes of 5.52. and 8.46. south. It is in length, between Java Head and the south-east point of the island, 666 statute miles; and its breadth varies from 135½ miles, between the south-west point of Pachitan <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> point of Japara, to fifty-six miles, between the mouth of the Serayu River and the Marabaya. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is estimated at 50,000 miles. On the south and west it is washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean; to the north-west by a strait called the Straits of Sandsa, which separates it from the island of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> at a distance, at the narrowest point, of only fourteen miles; and on the south-east by the Straits of Bali, only two miles wide, which divide it from the island of that name. These islands, and others stretching eastward, form with Java a gentle curve of more than 2000 geographical miles. From the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, Java is distant 140 leagues, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a> about fifty-six leagues, and from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> 200. The island of Java is of a rectangular form, so that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were divided into five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> six parts, each would form a parallelogram. It is extremely diversified on its surface. An uninterrupted range of lofty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, varying in elevation from 5000 to 11,000 and even 12,000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and exhibiting in their round bases or pointed tops their volcanic origin, extends almost east and west through the whole length of the island. They rise to their greatest elevations towards the centre, which is much broken. The tops of these mountains were formerly the craters of volcanoes, which are now extinguished, though many of them emit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> after heavy rains. From this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chain other innumerable ranges of hills of inferior height run in various directions, and serve to form and confine plains and valleys of different elevations and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. These mountainous regions present all the most romantic and highly diversified scenery which is to be found amid waving forests, never-failing streams, and constant verdure, heightened by a pure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and the glowing tints of a tropical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The aspect of the northern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is low, in many places swampy, and overgrown with mangrove trees and bushes, particularly towards the west. But in advancing five miles inland a sensible improvement is experienced in the atmosphere and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. Every step in advance leads to a purer <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> and a brighter <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. Here, amid the mountains, are found elevated and fertile plains, the seat of industry and skilful cultivation. "Here," says Sir <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> Raffles, "stupendous mountains are clothed with abundant harvests, impetuous cataracts tamed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>. Here is perpetual verdure; here are tints of the brightest hue. In the hottest season the air retains its freshness, in the driest the innumerable rills and rivulets preserve much of their <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> directs in endless conduits and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, to irrigate the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which he has laid out in terraces for its reception; it then descends to the plains, and spreads fertility wherever it flows, till at last, by numerous outlets, it discharges itself into the sea." The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> harbour is that of Sourabaya, in the eastern districts, formed by the approaching extremities of Java and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, which is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and spacious, and secure against the violence of the sea and the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The next in importance is that of Batavia, more properly the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of Batavia, which --- 1 See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Java, by Sir Stamford Raffles, vol. i. p. 24. Java are sheltered by several islands lying in the outer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bay. There are other positions along the northern coast which might be improved into convenient harbours, though the whole coast affords excellent anchorage at moderate depths during nearly all seasons of the year. In the smooth sea and moderate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> which usually prevail, the native vessels and small craft always find sufficient shelter at the change of the monsoon, when it is dangerous to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> on the coast, by running for shelter under some of the islands which are scattered in those seas, or passing up the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which, though presenting a difficult entrance, from the mud banks, that form a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAR">bar</a> at their mouth, are mostly navigable for small vessels as far up as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> capitals through which they run. The south coast, which rises into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and rugged cliffs, is inaccessible, with the exception of a few bays, on account of its exposure to the open sea, and the violent surf which in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> dashes against it. From the mountains of Java numerous streams pour <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the plains. There is no space, indeed, for the formation of large rivers. But there are probably no less than fifty which in the wet season bear down rafts of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and other rough produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and not less than five or six at all times navigable to the distance of some miles from the coast; and those which are useful to the agriculturist for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a> of the lands cannot be numbered. The principal rivers are the Solo, the largest in the island, which discharges itself on the north side by two principal outlets into the sea near Gresseck, and by which the produce of an extensive country is carried down in flat-bottomed boats to the sea. The river of Sourabaya, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in magnitude, falls into the sea by five outlets near Sourabaya. There are several smaller rivers in these eastern districts, which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the ocean on the northern shore, and which are highly useful for the conveyance of teak timber from the interior forests to the coast; or which, being directed into canals, tend to improve the inland <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the country. Towards the west, the principal rivers which fall into the sea on the northern coast are the Chikandi, the Chidani, the Chitaran, and the Chimanok. Those which discharge themselves by the south coast are the Chinamandiri, which falls into the sea at Wyn-Coop's Bay, the Chitandui, the Serayu, and others. Along the northern coast almost every district has its principal river, but they have all the disadvantage of being blocked up at their entrance by the accumulation of mud banks, an evil which is increasing with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> necessarily washed down in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of irrigating the land for the cultivation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. Java contains no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of any considerable size, though there are several very beautiful lakes of small dimensions among the hills, many of which are the craters of extinguished volcanoes. There are also extensive swamps, which, though they are filled with water during the wet season, are for the rest of the year dried up or choked by vegetation. Java possesses a soil that is extremely rich, and remarkable for its depth, owing, as Sir Stamford Raffles conjectures, to the exclusively volcanic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the country, and the quantity of new mould that is constantly washed down the sides of its mountains. The best soil resembles the richest garden mould in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The seasons, as in all tropical countries, are distinguished into wet and dry, and depend on the periodical winds, or the monsoons. The west monsoon, which brings on the annual rains, begins in October, and becomes more steady in November and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>; it continues till the latter end of February or the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. It often blows with great violence, and is accompanied with heavy rains, which renders this the most unhealthy season. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April ushers in the easterly winds and fair weather, which continue for the remaining half year. But the rains, though they often fall in torrents, are not so constant nor so violent as on the continent of India. During the rainy season there are days free from showers; while, again, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, occasional rains refresh the atmosphere, and preserve the brightest verdure of the landscape throughout the year. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a>-storms are frequent, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> very vivid. The thermometer on the northern coast, at Batavia, Semarang, and Sourabaya, occasionally rises, about three in the afternoon, to 90°, which it rarely exceeds; but in general it has been found to range between 70° and 74° in the evenings, and 83° at noon, or at Semarang 87°. At thirty or forty miles inland from Batavia, on the mountains, it ranges between 60° and 70°, above which it seldom rises. On the hills of Semarang, where Europeans frequently reside during the dry season, at an elevation of about 4000 feet, it is frequently, in the mornings, as low as 45°, and ranges between 50° and 62°; and on the summit of one of the highest mountains, Sindoro, it has been seen as low as 27°. From its insular situation, Java enjoys the benefit of the land and sea breeze; and its diversified surface affords the choice of climate, and a regular diminution of temperature, in proportion to the elevation. With the exception of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Batavia, where the climate is the most baneful in the world, and the low marshy flats on the northern shore, the island of Java is, in point of salubrity, equal to the healthiest parts of British India, or of any tropical country in the world. This fact is attested by the medical registers of the different British regiments stationed in this island. From the 1st November 1813 to the 1st November 1814, the deaths among 7470 British troops, who were exposed to many disadvantages and privations, did not exceed 504, which was only in the proportion of 1 to 14. From November 1814 to November 1815, out of 7487 troops, 252 died, 63 by fever, 123 by dysentery, and 65 by other diseases, which is only in the proportion of 1 in 30 in a year; a low estimate for climates that have borne a better character for salubrity than that of Java. This island abounds in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and extraordinary variety of its vegetable productions. Between the tops of the mountains and the sea-shore is comprised almost every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of temperature, and hence the produce of every region finds here some congenial spot. Rice, of which there are a hundred varieties, is cultivated on all the low grounds and ravines along the sea-coast, and in other situations commanding a supply of water. It is the great staple of agriculture in Java, to which every other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of husbandry is subordinate; and this island is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> of the eastern archipelago, from which all the other adjacent islands and states of Sumatra, Molucca, Borneo, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>, and the Moluccas, have been <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> supplied; while every year about six or eight thousand tons were formerly sent by the Dutch to Ceylon, Coromandel, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, and their other settlements. Notwithstanding this abundant produce, it is calculated that about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> eighths of the island are either neglected or badly cultivated; and such is the fertility of the soil, that it is from the remaining one eighth that these great supplies are derived. Maize or Indian corn ranks next in importance to rice, and is principally cultivated in the higher regions, and in those tracts where there are no mountain streams for the irrigation of the soil. Its cultivation has of late been extended in Java, and is becoming more and more a favourite article of food. Wheat has been introduced by the Europeans, and cul- --- 1 See Raffles' History of Java, vol. i. p. 30; Batavian Transactions, vol. viii. Introductory Discourse. tivated with success to an extent required by the European inhabitants. It thrives well in the interior of the country. Oats and other grain thrive in those parts of the island, and would be produced in great abundance were due <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> given to their culture. Potatoes have been cultivated during the last forty years, in elevated situations, near all the principal European establishments, and are found of a good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; also most of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> culinary vegetables of Europe, though their quality is apt to degenerate unless fresh supplies of seed be procured from Europe. Other species of grain, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEGUMINOUS">leguminous</a> vegetables, and a variety of pulses, are raised as green crops in intervals between those of rice; and in times of scarcity the natives make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of various kinds of the plantain, also the yam and the sweet <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>. But in general Indian corn is the only article used by some as a substitute for rice. Cotton of an inferior quality to the Indian cotton is cultivated in almost every part of the island, and its cheapness occasions a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. The coffee plant thrives luxuriantly in Java. It was first introduced about the year 1723 by the Dutch, who established a monopoly of the article, and forced the natives to cultivate it, and deliver it into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> stores at a reduced price. During the French administration of Marshal Daendels this cruel oppression was carried still further, and in certain districts every family was forced to take care of a thousand <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and deliver the produce into the government stores. Under the more humane rule of the British governor, Sir Stamford Raffles, the free cultivation of coffee was permitted to the inhabitants, and all compulsory labour was abolished. The quality of the Java coffee is reckoned superior to that of the West Indies, and ranks with that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> in the European <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>; its cultivation, for which many parts of the island are eminently adapted, has therefore been greatly extended; and it is exported to the amount of twenty-six millions of pounds, which is about two sevenths of the produce of the West Indies. The soil is very favourable to the growth of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, which was introduced by Europeans, and is now extensively raised for exportation in the central districts of the island, about five millions of pounds being sent to the rest of the archipelago. In some parts it forms, after rice, the most important article of cultivation. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEPPER">Pepper</a> was at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the principal export from Java; but it was strictly monopolized by the government, and the most oppressive modes were resorted to in order to enhance its price. For some time past it has ceased to be cultivated to any extent. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIGO">Indigo</a> is raised in most parts of the island; and both the climate and soil of Java offer peculiar advantages for the extensive cultivation of this plant. The natives prepare the indigo very unskilfully, and hence it is of very indifferent quality. But if it were more carefully manufactured, it might form a most valuable and important export for the European market. Notwithstanding the extent to which cultivation has been carried in many districts of the island, large portions of the surface are covered with primeval forests, affording excellent timber for almost every purpose. Extensive forests of teak are found in almost all the eastern provinces, but especially in the central districts of the island. There are great varieties of other kinds of timber, as the suran (the tana of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>), of which the wood is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, strong, and durable, having something of the smell of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, and which, as the grain is not fine, is used for making chests, trunks, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. The wengu is often used instead of teak. It is of a somewhat finer grain, and, when in full blossom, is the most beautiful tree existing. The wadang or layur, a light wood, is well adapted for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> and spars of small vessels. There are several other similar woods, of which are formed the handles of spears and pikes. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and ponderous wood, the nangka, which is used for beams and rafters in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of houses, and sometimes for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture. There are other woods, heavy, hard, and close in the grain, which are used for the anchors of small vessels, for ships' blocks, for naves of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, for handles of tools for carpenters and other artificers, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CART">cart</a>-wheels, for machinery, and such like purposes. There are other light woods, which are useful for canoes, for the handles of axes and other like tools, and which are manufactured into planks. There are various descriptions of woods that are well adapted for household furniture, cabinet <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c. of a deep-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and which take a fine polish; others of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> colour, and finely grained, that are used for inlaying. There are other kinds of woods of various colours, variegated, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and black, or of yellowish or brown colours, and very heavy, which are employed for canes, handles, and spears. The bamboo flourishes in great luxuriance and variety. The rattans of Java are, however, inferior to those of Sumatra and Borneo. Many woods afford excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; and amongst the useful trees may be reckoned the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> tree, of which the fruit is very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in the washing of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; the kasenak, from the bark of which is made a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> for umbrellas; the oompong, from the resin of which the natives prepare a shining varnish for the wooden sheaths of krises; the cotton-tree, from which a silky <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is obtained for stuffing pillows and beds; the wax-tree, from the kernel of which an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is expressed, which some time after becomes hard, and bears a resemblance to wax, and may be burnt in lamps or converted into candles, affording when <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> an agreeable odour; the shrub is also produced which yields the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> from which the India rubber is prepared. This substance is converted into torches, which are employed in searching for edible <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-nests in the caves of the rocks. Few of the trees in Java exude the odoriferous resins which abound in Sumatra, Borneo, and the eastern islands. The camphor tree is unknown. None of the finer kinds of spices, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>, the clove, or the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, are indigenous to Java; but the few trees planted by Europeans in gardens have thriven well, and there is little doubt that the nutmeg and the clove might be extensively cultivated throughout the island. The vine would also thrive well in some of the eastern provinces; but its growth was always discouraged by the narrow policy of the Dutch, who were afraid lest it should interfere with the wine trade of the Cape of Good Hope. The cottage of every peasant is surrounded with plantations of cocoa-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> trees, which constitute an inheritance that is transmitted from father to son, and which it is reckoned a sacred duty to transmit, and to augment by new plantations. The various species of the palm-tree are found in Java; and, besides the cocoa-nut, there are many trees growing spontaneously, of which the seeds and kernels are used as food. The true sago of Amboya and the eastern islands is found in a fair, low, and marshy situation, though the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of it from the pith of the tree is not known to the inhabitants of Java; but from the aren or sagurus rumphi, which abounds in all parts, and, from its various and extensive uses, ranks next in importance to the cocoa-nut, a substance is prepared similar in all respects to the true sago of the eastern islands. Other trees exude <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and balsamic oils. The kubah yields a balsamic oil or jelly, which is much esteemed, which has the smell and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of camphor, and is taken inwardly for violent coughs, or disorders in the stomach. The benzoin-tree produces an odoriferous gum, of an <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour, which is a valuable article of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The upas or famous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POISON">poison</a>-tree of Java has long attracted the curiosity of naturalists, and has been the subject of many wonderful, and, as now appears, fabulous tales. It is one of the largest trees in the forests of Java, and rises with a completely naked stem to the perpendicular height of sixty, seventy, and eighty feet, when it sends off a few stout branches. The bark, which in old trees is almost half an inch thick, on being cut yields a milky juice, from which a poison is prepared equal in fatality to the strongest animal poisons hitherto known. The inner bark resembles a coarse piece of linen which is worked into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and which, after much bruising, washing, and immersion in water, is worn by the lower classes when working in the fields. But it is remarkable, that after being exposed to a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, this dress produces an intolerable itching, the effect of a small portion of the poison still adhering to the bark. The story of the tree poisoning the surrounding atmosphere is altogether a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. It is extremely difficult to penetrate into the forests of Java, from the quantity of underwood and creeping plants with which they are entangled. "No region of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>," says Marsden, "can boast of a greater abundance and variety of indigenous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> than Java. The mangustin, pre-eminent for delicacy of flavour amongst all the fruits of the East, of a round form and a purple colour, is found in great abundance. The dorian, a large fruit, like the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> fruit in appearance, of a disgusting smell, and of a flavour like a custard, is said, when seasoned with garlic, to become by frequent use extremely fascinating. The rambutan, a cool and agreeable fruit, of a delicate sub-acid flavour, grows on a showy and elegant tree. The lanesh or lanesh, much relished by the lower classes, grows in clusters like <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and has a pulpy substance, with a delicate sub-acid flavour. The pumplemoos, the Batavian lembu or vine of Bengal, and the shaddock of the West Indies, is in Java of an exquisite flavour; as also the pine-apple, which is much superior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>. There are besides extensive varieties of the atrocarpus or jack-fruit, which grows wild in abundance; of the mango, of which no less than forty varieties are enumerated; the plantain, the guava, the rose-apple, the custard-apple, the papaw, besides dates, pomegranates, tamarinds, figs, annanas, oranges, lemons, citrons, melons, pumpkins. In some of the mountainous tracts are to be found peaches, Chinese pears, and other fruits imported from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, the Cape of Good Hope, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. Of the oil-giving plants there are many. From the palma christi is obtained most of the oil that is burned in lamps. There are numerous trees, plants, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, which supply, from the bark or the leaves, fibres that are converted into ropes, threads, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> used for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, thread, and finally cloth, or spun into a kind of stuff resembling <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, &c.
