KEMPIS, THOMAS a pious and learned regular canon, was born at the village of Kemp, or Kempen, in the diocese of Cologne, in 1380, and took his name from that village. He performed his studies at Deventer, in the community of poor scholars established by Gerard Groot; and there made great progress in the sciences. In 1399 he entered the monastery of the regular canons of Mount St Agnes, near Swol, of which his brother was prior. Thomas à Kempis there distinguished himself by his eminent piety, his respect for his superiors, his charity to his brother canons, and his continual application to labour and prayer. He died in the year 1471, at the age of ninety. The best editions of his works, which consist of sermons, spiritual treatises, and lives of holy men, are those of Paris in 1649, and of Antwerp in 1607. The well-known book De Imitatione Christi, which has been translated into all the languages of the civilized world, though it has commonly been numbered amongst the works of Thomas à Kempis, is also found printed under the name of Gerson; and, on the credit of some manuscripts, it has been since ascribed to the abbot Gerson, of the order of St Benedict. This occasioned a violent dispute between the canons of St Augustin and the Benedictines. KEMPTEN, a city of Bavaria, in the province of the Upper Danube. It is situated on the river Iller, which is navigable nearly to its site, and is surrounded by hills. It is the seats of the revenue and police boards of the circle, and of the local courts of justice, both for civil and criminal affairs. The trade is inconsiderable, but consists in small linen and woollen manufactures. It contains 850 houses, and 5640 inhabitants, chiefly Catholics. Long. 10. 13. 25. E. Lat. 47. 44. 10. N. KEN, THOMAS, a deprived bishop of Bath and Wells, descended from an ancient family established at Kenplace, Somersetshire, was born at Berkhamstead, Hertfordshire, in the month of July 1637. At the age of thirteen he was sent to Winchester School, where he remained some time, and thence removed to New College, Oxford, of which he became a probationer-fellow in 1657. He took his degrees regularly; pursued his studies closely for many years; and in 1666 became a fellow of Winchester College, soon after which he was appointed domestic chaplain to the Bishop, and obtained the rectory of Brixton in the Isle of Wight. In 1674, he made a journey to Rome, and after his return took his degrees in divinity. Not long afterwards, having been appointed chaplain to the Princess of Orange, he went to Holland, where his piety and prudence gained him general esteem; but

KEMPEN

Pages 700-700

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Clevees-Juliers. It contains 520 houses, with 3120 inhabitants, who carry on <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and tapes. It is also the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the celebrated divine, Thomas à Kempis.

KEMPIS

Pages 700-700

THOMAS a pious and learned regular canon, was born at the village of Kemp, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KEMPEN">Kempen</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, in 1380, and took his name from that village. He performed his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> scholars established by Gerard Groot; and there made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the sciences. In 1399 he entered the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of the regular canons of Mount St Agnes, near Swol, of which his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a>. Thomas à Kempis there distinguished himself by his eminent piety, his respect for his superiors, his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to his brother canons, and his continual application to labour and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. He died in the year 1471, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of ninety. The best editions of his works, which consist of sermons, spiritual treatises, and lives of holy men, are those of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1649, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1607. The well-known book De Imitatione Christi, which has been translated into all the languages of the civilized world, though it has <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> been numbered amongst the works of Thomas à Kempis, is also found printed under the name of Gerson; and, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, it has been since ascribed to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Gerson, of the order of St Benedict. This occasioned a violent dispute between the canons of St Augustin and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>.

KEMPTEN

Pages 700-700

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Upper Danube. It is situated on the river Iller, which is navigable nearly to its site, and is surrounded by hills. It is the seats of the revenue and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> boards of the circle, and of the local courts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, both for civil and criminal affairs. The trade is inconsiderable, but consists in small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It contains 850 houses, and 5640 inhabitants, chiefly Catholics. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 13. 25. E. Lat. 47. 44. 10. N.

KEN

Pages 700-702

THOMAS, a deprived bishop of Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, descended from an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family established at Kenplace, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, was born at Berkhamstead, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1637. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of thirteen he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> School, where he remained some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and thence removed to New <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, of which he became a probationer-fellow in 1657. He took his degrees regularly; pursued his studies closely for many years; and in 1666 became a fellow of Winchester College, soon after which he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to the Bishop, and obtained the rectory of Brixton in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight. In 1674, he made a journey to Rome, and after his return took his degrees in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> afterwards, having been appointed chaplain to the Princess of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where his piety and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> gained him general esteem; but having offended the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, afterwards William III., by obliging one of his favourites to espouse a young lady of the princess's train whom he had seduced by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, Ken returned to England, and was employed to attend <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a>. Having returned with this nobleman in 1684, he was immediately appointed chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>, and not long afterwards nominated, without solicitation, to the bishopric of Bath and Wells. He attended the king in his last illness, and did his utmost to awaken the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; speaking, says Burnet, "with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> elevation of thought and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and like a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> inspired." The sudden <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the king delayed his admission to the temporalities of the see of Wells; but, on the accession of King James, new instruments were prepared for that purpose, and Ken entered upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his episcopal functions. In 1685, he published an exposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> Catechism; and, the same year, he gave to the world Prayers for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Bath. He took no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the popish controversy which was then so warmly agitated, though, in his discourses from the pulpit, he frequently took occasion to notice and confute the errors of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>; nor did he hesitate, when preaching in the chapel-royal, to set before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> the dangerous policy of its projected coalition with the sectaries. Some attempts were made to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> him over to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the popish party; but these proved completely abortive; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> was ordained to be read, in virtue of the dispensing power assumed by the king, Ken was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> who openly opposed it, and who were in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> sent to the Tower. But though he ventured to disobey the mandate of his sovereign for the sake of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he refused to transfer his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; and, accordingly, on the arrival of the Prince of Orange, he suffered himself to be deprived, and withdrew to Longleate, a seat of Lord Weymouth, in Wiltshire, where he composed many pious works, and amused himself with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> verses, which, however, have but little of the spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in them. Eventually he had settled on him a pension of L200 a year, which was punctually paid out of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> as long as he lived. Dr Ken, who had long been afflicted with colic pains, experienced, in 1710, a paralytic attack, which deprived him of the use of one side; and, after lingering for some time in a hopeless state, he expired at Longleate, upon the 19th <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1711. His works, consisting for the most part of devotional pieces, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> as well as in prose, were published in 1721, in four volumes. Ken, a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a>. It possessed at one time a flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and is still capable of supplying refreshments to vessels, being better planted than most of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Its ancient name was Kataia. It has a low and rocky <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in some parts, and must be approached with caution in the night. Long. 53. 40. E. Lat. 26. 27. N. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-KENANY">Kenany</a>, a small island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, situated about thirteen miles south of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, and two and a half from the mainland. In 1678 Sevaje, the Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, took possession of it, and from this station he greatly annoyed the trade of Bombay. It has a small harbour for vessels <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> little <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, on the eastern side. Long. 72. 56. E. Lat. 18. 42. N. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a>, a market-town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of the same name, 260 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on the river Ken, in a pleasant valley, and, by inland <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, comes into connection with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and with the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Morrey, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and Avon. There is much industry applied to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are the inferior kinds of woollen cloths and stuffs. It is a corporate town, under a mayor, twelve aldermen, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, but returns no members to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. There are guilds <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> companies for several branches of trade, which now scarcely exist. The church is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and there are chapels for the various denominations of Protestant dissenters, and for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. It is one of those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> which have been much increased and improved of late years. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 6892, in 1811 to 7505, in 1821 to 8984, and in 1831 to 10,015. Kenilworth, a town of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, in the hundred of Knightlow, 100 miles from London. It is celebrated as the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, the favourite of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and for the entertainments given in the castle, the ruins of which attest their former splendour. There is a market which is held on Wednesday. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 1968, in 1811 to 2279, in 1821 to 2577, and in 1831 to 3097. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KENNEL">Kennel</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> used indifferently for a puddle, a water-course in the streets, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for a pack of hounds, and the pack or cry of hounds themselves. See <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">Hound</a> and Hunting. Kenneri, a collection of remarkable caverns excavated in the rocky hills of the island of Salsette, near to Bombay, one of which had been fitted up by the Portuguese as a church, and they consequently thought it their duty to deface all the most pagan-looking sculptures. The fine teak ribs for supporting the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> are almost gone, and the portico is not so elegant as that at Carli. On the sides are two gigantic erect figures, each twenty-five feet in height, with their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to their bodies, which resembled the figures of Buddha seen at Ceylon. On each side of the great cave are smaller ones, apparently unfinished. The origin of these singular excavations is lost in obscurity. There is not even the slightest gleam of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> to guide the antiquarian in his researches into these curious memorials of Hindu or Buddha <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and in what age of the world, or by what people, they have been completed, is a question now likely to remain for ever unknown. Kennet, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, a learned English writer, and Bishop of Peterborough in the eighteenth century, bred at St Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, Oxford, where he soon distinguished himself by his vigorous application to his studies, and by his translations of several works into English, and other pieces which he published. In 1695 Kennet published his Parochial Antiquities. But a sermon preached by him on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1703, at Aldgate, exposed him to great clamour. It was printed under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of A compassionate Inquiry into the Causes of the Civil <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">War</a>. In 1706 he published his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">Case</a> of Improprations, and two other tracts upon the same subject. In 1706 he brought forward the third volume of the Complete <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, the two former volumes having been compiled by Mr Hughes. In 1709, he published a Vindication of the Church and Clergy of England from some reproaches rudely and unjustly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon them; and a true Answer to Dr Sacheverel's Sermon. When the great point in Dr Sacheverel's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, namely, the change of the ministry, was gained, and strange proceedings took <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> upon it, an artful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> by the bishop and clergy of London was to be prepared, and they who would not subscribe it were to be represented as enemies to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> and the ministry. Dr Kennet fell under this imputation. He was exposed to great odium as a low churchman, on account of his conduct and writings. When he was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> of Peterborough, an uncommon method was taken to expose him by Dr Walton, rector of the church of Whitechapel. In the altar-piece of that church, which was intended to represent Christ and his twelve apostles eating the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> and last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, Judas the traitor was drawn sitting in an elbow <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, dressed in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> garment, with a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> and appearance of Dr Kennet. It was generally said that the original sketch was intended for a bishop under Dr Walton's displeasure; but the painter being apprehensive of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of scandalmagnum, leave was given to drop the bishop and paint the dean. As this gave general offence, however, the Bishop of London ordered the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to be taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. In 1713 he presented the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for Propagating the Gospel with a great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books suitable to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; published his Bibliotheca Americana Primordia; and founded an antiquarian and historical library at Peterborough. In 1715 he published a sermon entitled The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">Witchcraft</a> of the present Rebellion, and afterwards several other pieces. In 1717 he was engaged in a dispute with Dr William Nicholson, bishop of Carlisle, relating to some alterations in a sermon by the Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>; and he disliked the proceedings of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> against that bishop. Upon the death of Dr <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, bishop of Peterborough, he was promoted to that see, to which he was consecrated in the year 1718. He sat in it more than ten years, and died in 1728. He was an excellent philologist, a good preacher, and well versed in the history and antiquities of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>.

KENNET

Pages 702-702
Basil, a learned English writer, brother of the preceding, was educated in Corpus Christi College, in the university of Oxford, where he became fellow. In 1706 he went as chaplain to the English factory at Leghorn, where he met with great opposition from the Papists, and was in danger from the inquisition. Kennet died in the year 1714. He published Lives of the Greek poets, Roman Antiquities, a volume of Sermons preached at Leghorn, and a translation into English of Puffendorf's Treatise of the Law of Nature and Nations. He was a man of most exemplary integrity, generosity, piety, and modesty.

KENNICK

Pages 702-703

WILLIAM, an author of considerable ability, was the son of a citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and brought up, it is said, to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> employment. This, however, he seems early to have abandoned, and to have devoted his talents to the cultivation of letters, by which he supported himself during the rest of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which might be said to have passed in a state of warfare, as he was seldom without an enemy to attack <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> to defend himself against. He was for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> a student at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he received the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in both laws. Not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> after his return to England, he attracted some notice as a poet by Epistles Philosophical and Moral, 1759; addressed to Lorenzo; an avowed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, written whilst under confinement for debt, and with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> that he was "much less ambitious of the character of a poet than of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>." From this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he became a writer by profession; and the Proteus shapes under which he appeared it would be a fruitless attempt to trace. He was for a considerable time a writer in the Monthly Review; but having quarrelled with his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, he began a new review of his own. When Dr Johnson's edition of Shakspeare first appeared in the year 1765, it was followed in a fortnight by a pamphlet, entitled a Review of Dr Johnson's new Edition of Shakspeare, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> or inattention of that editor is exposed, and the poet defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of his commentators. This pamphlet was followed by an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of it, and that by a Defence in 1766, in which year he produced his pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of Falstaff's Wedding, at first intended to have been given to the public as an original play of Shakspeare retrieved from obscurity, and which, it must be acknowledged, is a happy <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dramatic bard. With the celebrated English Roscius Dr Kenrick was at one time on terms of the strictest intimacy; but he took occasion to quarrel with him in print, and in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> too unmanly to be mentioned. In politics also he made himself not a little conspicuous, particularly in the dispute between his friends Wilkes and Horne. He was the original editor of the Morning <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>; but being ousted for neglect, he set up a new one in opposition. He translated in a very able manner the Emile and the Héloïse of Rousseau; the Elements of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England by Millot; and produced several dramatic performances, together with an infinite variety of publications both original and translated. To him also the public are indebted for the collection, imperfect as it is, of the poetical works of Robert Lloyd, 1774, in two vols. 8vo. Dr Kenrick died on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1777.

KENNICOTT

Pages 702-702

Dr Benjamin, well known in the learned world for his elaborate edition of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> and other valuable publications, was born at Totness, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, in the year 1718. His father was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> clerk of Totness, and once <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school in that town. At an early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> young Kennicott succeeded to the same employment in the school, being recommended to it by his remarkable sobriety and premature knowledge. It was in this situation he wrote the verses on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mrs Courtney from a dangerous illness, which recommended him to her notice, and that of many neighbouring gentlemen, who, with laudable generosity, opened a subscription to send him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In judging of this performance, they may be supposed to have considered not so much its intrinsic merit, as the circumstances under which it was produced. For although it might justly claim praise as the fruit of youthful industry struggling with obscurity and indigence, yet as a poem it never rises above mediocrity, and generally sinks below it. But, in whatever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> these verses may be considered, the publication of them was soon followed by such contributions as procured for the author the advantages of an academical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. In the year 1744 he entered himself at Wadham <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>; and it was not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he distinguished himself in that particular branch of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in which he afterwards became so eminent. His two dissertations, on the Tree of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, and the Oblations of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a>, came to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition as early as the year 1747, and procured him the singular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a bachelor's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> conferred upon him gratis by the university a year before the statutable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The dissertations were gratefully dedicated to those benefactors whose liberality had opened his way to the university, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> whose kindness had made it a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> not only of manly labour, but of honourable friendship. With such merit and such support, he proved a successful candidate for a fellowship of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> College; and soon after his admission into that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, he distinguished himself by the publication of several occasional sermons. In the year 1753 he laid the foundation of that stupendous monument of learned industry, at which the wise and the good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> gaze with admiration, when the cavils of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, and envy, and ingratitude, shall no longer be heard. This he did by publishing his first dissertation, on the state of the printed Hebrew text, in which he proposed to overthrow the then prevailing notion of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> integrity. The first blow, indeed, had been struck long before by Capellus, in his Critica Sacra, published after his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by his son, in 1650; a blow which Buxtorf, with all his abilities and dialectical skill, was unable to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">ward</a> off. But Capellus having no opportunity of consulting <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, though his arguments were supported by the authority of the Samaritan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> versions, could never absolutely prove his point. Indeed the general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was that the Hebrew manuscripts contained none, or at least very few and trifling variations from the printed text; and with respect to the Samaritan Pentateuch, the most opposite opinions were entertained. Those who held the Hebrew verity, of course condemned the Samaritan as corrupt in every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it deviated from the Hebrew; and those who believed the Hebrew to be incorrect, did not think the Samaritan of sufficient authority to correct it. Besides, the Samaritan itself appeared to very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage; for as no Samaritan manuscripts were then known, the Pentateuch itself was rashly condemned for errors which ought rather to have been ascribed to the incorrectness of the editions. In this dissertation, therefore, Dr Kennicott proved that there were many Hebrew manuscripts extant, which, though they had hitherto been generally supposed to agree with one another, and with the Hebrew text, yet contained many and important various readings; and that from those various readings considerable authority was derived in support of the ancient versions. He announced the existence of six Samaritan manuscripts in Oxford alone, by which many errors in the printed Samaritan might be removed; and he attempted to prove, that even from the Samaritan, as it was already printed, many passages in the Hebrew might undoubtedly be corrected. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as might reasonably be expected, was examined with great severity both at home and abroad. In some foreign <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the Hebrew verity, on its being attacked by Capellus, had been insisted on as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. "Ista Capelli sententia adeo non approbata fuit fidei sociis, ut potius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a> theologi, et speciatim Genevenses, anno 1678, peculiari canone caverint, ne quis in ditione sua minister ecclesiae recipiatur, nisi fatetur publice textum Hebraicum, ut hodie est in exemplaribus Masoreticis, quoad consonantes et vocales, divinum et authenticum esse." And at home this doctrine of the corrupt state of the Hebrew text was opposed by Comings and Bate, two Hutchinsonians, with as much violence as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> had been at stake. The next three or four years of Dr Kennicott's life were principally employed in searching out and examining Hebrew manuscripts, though he found leisure not only to preach, but also to publish several occasional sermons. About this time Dr Kennicott became one of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>'s preachers at Whitehall; and in the year 1759 we find

KENSINGTON

Pages 703-703

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, whose boundary joins to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the hundred of Ossulston, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. It is chiefly remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and gardens, the latter of which forms the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the recreation of the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The palace is an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> brick <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, purchased by William the Third, and by him and his successors enlarged in various styles. Though with little exterior <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, it has good suites of apartments allotted to junior members of the royal family, and to other persons. The gardens have received all the advantages of which their situation is capable, and form a most pleasing promenade. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> and other mansions are objects of remark within this parish, as well as the numerous smaller buildings erected within the last twenty years. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 8556, in 1811 to 10,386, in 1821 to 14,428, and in 1831 to 20,902.

KENT

Pages 703-706

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England, and, reckon- ing its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and fertility, perhaps the first in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is in a peninsular form, being bounded by the British Channel on the south; by the German Ocean on the east; by the river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> on the west. Its length is sixty-six, and its breadth thirty-six miles. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is calculated at about 1300 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The divisions of Kent are into five laths, which are subdivided into sixty-three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> and fifteen liberties, and contain two cities, thirty-six <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 414 parishes. The population, at the four decennial enumerations, amounted in 1801 to 307,624, in 1811 to 373,095, in 1821 to 426,016, and in 1831 to 479,155. At the last census the males were 234,572, and the females 244,583. These are comprehended in 97,142 families, of whom 31,667 are chiefly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, 29,419 are occupied in trade, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and handicraft, and 36,056 are not included in either of the other classes. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of males above twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> employed in retail trade <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> in handicraft, or masters or workmen, was 34,257. The baptisms, burials, and marriages, show the following proportion at different periods, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>: | One <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">Baptism</a> | One <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURIAL">Burial</a> | One <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> | |-------------|------------|--------------| | 1796 to 1800 | 30 | 31 | 116 | | 1806 to 1810 | 29 | 38 | 115 | | 1816 to 1820 | 31 | 51 | 130 | | 1826 to 1830 | 34 | 49 | 143 | Thus it is seen that the increase of population has been going on rather by a greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> than by the increase of births. The only <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of morals which our present statistical knowledge supplies is that regarding chastity, by showing the proportion which the number of illegitimate children bears to the whole of the births. The illegitimates in Kent have only been one in twenty-four, whereas in the whole of England they were one in twenty; in the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, one in thirteen; and in England and Wales taken together, one in nineteen. | 685 | 4,348 Bromley | 669 | 4,002 Faversham | 737 | 3,982 <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRANBROOK">Cranbrook</a> | 639 | 3,844 Folkestone | 719 | 3,638 Bexley | 601 | 3,206 <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENTERDEN">Tenterden</a> | 548 | 3,177 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> | 595 | 3,136 By the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of 1832, entitled an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> to amend the representation of the people of England, the county of Kent has been divided into the eastern and western parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> for the first of these is held at Canterbury, and the other polling places are Sittingbourne, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASHFORD">Ashford</a>, New Romney, and Ramsgate. The election for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or western <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is held at Maidstone, and the other polling places are Bromley, Gravesend, Tonbridge, and Cranbrook. By the same act, the boroughs of New Romney and of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEENBOROUGH">Queenborough</a> have been disfranchised; and the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, which before returned two members, can in future elect but one, and, to make up the competent constituency, the town of Folkestone has been added to it. Greenwich has by the same law been erected into a borough, and returns two members; and Chatham is also a borough returning one. The other places, viz. Canterbury, Rochester, Dover, Maidstone, and Sandwich, return, as before, two members each. Thus the representation consists of four members for the county, and fourteen for the cities and towns. The extent of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the county appears to be 996,480 acres when the whole area is included; but, from some not ascertainable cause, the returns from the several parishes show only 972,240 acres. The annual value of the land, including that of the houses, was taken in 1815, for the purpose of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> tax, at £1,644,179. The whole of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RATES">rates</a> levied in 1833 amounted to £450,851; and it had not much varied in the few preceding years. The appearance of Kent is generally acknowledged to be equal, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, to that of any other British county. Its surface is gently undulating; none of its hills, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, rise abruptly, nor reach a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> elevation. In all the valleys there are streams of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the woods and trees enrich the scenery, and the mixture of pasture and corn land, interspersed with orchards, fruit-trees, and hop plantations, give to its beauties a character of softness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. The Thames may be considered as a Kentish river, as it washes its whole northern boundary, and empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on its shores. The river next in importance is the Medway, formed by the junction of four small streams, one only of which rises within the county. It becomes navigable for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barges at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and continues its course by Maidstone to Chatham, where ships of the largest size can approach the shore; and there terminates its course, by joining the Thames at the Nore, beyond the arsenal of Sheerness. The Greater Stour, the Lesser Stour, the Rother, the Cray, the Darent, and the Ravensbourne, are small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, none of them navigable, but all of great benefit, by the fertility they communicate to the meadows on their banks, and by the power they afford to the many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> erected upon their banks. Kent is almost exclusively an agricultural county; and though the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fertile, and though there are few extensive tracts of barren or uncultivated land, yet no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> exhibits within so small a compass so great a variety of soils, of productions, and of modes of cultivation. It has been judiciously divided into eight districts for the purposes of agricultural <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. The first of these, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Thanet, is in the north-west <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the county. The soil is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> mould on a chalky bottom, and has been highly enriched by the marine substances that have been administered as manure. The whole island contains 23,000 acres of arable and 3500 acres of rich marsh land. The most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of crops is fallow, sometimes with, sometimes without, a crop of peas; this is followed by barley, clover, and wheat; and on some soils rather heavier, the course pursued is beans, wheat, and barley. The barley of this district is very much esteemed, and sought for as seed in other countries. Besides the common grains, seeds of various kinds are raised for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> seedsmen, particularly canary, radish, spinach, mustard, and onion seed. The soil in the marshy parts of the island is a mixture of clay, sea sand, and small shells, and yields most abundant pasture. The upland farms of East Kent, which surround Canterbury, and extend to Dover on one side and Ashford and Rochester on the other, are an open and dry tract of corn land, intermixed with woods. The soils are very various, all resting on a subsoil of chalk. Some of them are very heavy loamy clays, with a great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of flint <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a> on the surface; these are usually cultivated on a four-course rotation of fallow, barley, beans, and wheat; when the soil is somewhat stiffer, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> occurs of fallow, wheat, beans, and oats. In this district the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> usually commences from twelve to fourteen days later than in the Isle of Thanet. The woods in this district usually supply <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> to the hop-planters in the vicinity; they are cut <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> after from ten to fourteen years' growth. There are in this division some few hop grounds, but they are confined to three or four parishes. In the vicinity of Sandwich, Faversham, and Deal, a portion of land, of a rich <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> loam, receives an almost uniform cultivation; it is nearly all under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, and a four-course rotation is practised, of wheat, beans, barley, and oats, after a fallow, or sometimes canary occupies the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of wheat. Some portions of this land are alternately cropped with beans and wheat, or beans and canary. In the vicinity of Sandwich are many orchards, the apples of which are partly sent to London, and partly furnish return cargoes to the vessels that come laden with coals from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> and Sunderland. The district extending from Maidstone to Canterbury, and thence to Sandwich, is the great garden-tract for the growth of hops. The soils on which hops are produced are very various; the most productive are those which have a deep loam surface, with a subsoil of deep loamy brick <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; some of these have a considerable quantity of flint-stones mingled with the soil, and, when it becomes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, almost covering it. Another soil, provincially called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> shalten, is very good for the growth of hops; it is mixed with many small portions of stone and sand, and rests upon the basis of the stone called Kentish rag, which is burned into excellent lime. The cultivation of hops is a very fluctuating pursuit, as the produce varies in different years from two to fifteen hundredweight per <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and the prices have varied from three to fifteen pounds. The expense of cultivation is very great, from the quantity of manure that is required, from the great expense of the poles round which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> twine, and the labour of keeping the ground clear and of picking the hops. Besides hops, the district is very productive of apples, cherries, and filberts, to the growth of which many fields, from one to ten acres in extent, are devoted; part of the apples are made into cider; the remainder, with the cherries and filberts, are principally conveyed to the different <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> in London. The Isle of Sheppey is separated from the rest of Kent by an arm of the sea called the Swale, which is navigable for ships of 200 tons burden. Its length is eleven, and its breadth eight miles. About four fifths of this island is either marsh or dry pasture-land; upon the former many oxen are fattened, and the latter is appropriated to the breeding and feeding of sheep. About 10,000 acres of this island is arable land, of great fertility, usually cultivated with beans and wheat in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> years, with occasionally a fallow before the beans. This land is highly fertile, the wheat raised on it being considered as the best that is brought to London, a bushel frequently weighing sixty-four pounds. This great productiveness may be in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing to the practice of applying to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> heavy clayey soil a frequent dressing of the cockle shells which are washed on the beach by the sea. It is not unusual to apply thirty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CART">cart</a>-loads of these shells to an acre of land. The uplands of West Kent are extensive and various in their soils. This part is more woody and enclosed than East Kent. The ridge of the chalk hills, about six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in breadth, consists of a stiff clay, with many surface flints, and requires six horses frequently to plough it. On these soils the most common rotation is a year's clean fallow, then wheat, clover, wheat, and oats. Many large flocks of South Down sheep are kept on this hilly range. The valleys and the sides of the hills are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> soil and easier to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, but do not produce better corn; some of this, but not to a great extent, is cultivated for hops. The district known as the Weald of Kent was, in former times, an immense forest, desolate of inhabitants, and only occupied by wild swine and deer; and though it is now filled with towns and villages, and well peopled, the woods that remain are extensive; exhibiting some pleasing landscapes, where seats, farms, and villages, are mixed with cultivated fields, and woods of spreading oaks. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in this district are very bad, many of them impassable for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> in the best seasons; and, in winter, horses can only travel by keeping on the narrow paved tracts that are formed by the sides of the highways. The soil is principally clay, with a substratum of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>, in some places very heavy, but in others sufficiently light to be ploughed with oxen. This district produces wheat, oats, barley, rye-grass, clover, and beans; but so various are the rotations, that it is scarcely possible to generalise them. The pastures are very rich and fertile, and fatten annually great numbers of cattle. In the western part of this district, and in the adjoining Weald of Sussex, there were formerly many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-works; the ore is found, and the abundance of wood made the manufacturing of it profitable; but the substitution of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COKE">coke</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> in making iron has put a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> stop to all the iron-works of Kent and Sussex. The last agricultural division is a rich, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, extensive tract of land, on the southern coast, containing about forty-five thousand acres of the richest pasture in the united kingdom. This level is protected from the violence of the sea, and from inundations, by a dyke of earth of very great thickness, called Dimchurch-wall. The whole is alluvial land, consisting of a fine, soft, rich loam, with portions of sea-sand and broken shells intermixed. The subsoil consists of alternate layers of sand and clay mixed with shells, amongst which are sometimes found large oak trees in various positions, the wood of which is as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and as hard as ebony. On this plain there are two towns, Romney and Lydd, but scarcely any villages, and few other houses than those of the shepherds and herdsmen who attend upon the numerous cattle that graze on the marshes. As there are no other fences but dykes, or posts and rails, from the surrounding heights it has the appearance of one large verdant field covered with sheep and oxen. The breeding and fattening of sheep is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> purpose to which this level is appropriated, and the number bred is greater than on any other tract of the same extent in the kingdom. The sheep take their denomination from the district; they are larger than the South <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>, but not of a size equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> sheep. Their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is highly esteemed in the London markets, and their <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is both fine and of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the fleeces being about five pounds. The landed property of Kent is much divided; there are some noblemen that have large, but none such vast estates Kent as to give a preponderating <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> influence. The number of freeholders exceeds ten thousand, enjoying estates from the smallest value that can give a vote, and gradually rising to L7000 or L8000 per annum. The copy-hold tenures are very few, and the peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of Kent, known as gavel-kind, is very much diminished by various legal operations. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufactures carried on in this county are those connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and equipping of ships and boats. The males above twenty years of age employed in the several branches of ship-building, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, rope, and sail making, amount to 2120; to which are to be added, nearly as many plumbers, glaziers, painters, joiners, ironmongers, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-smiths, and other trades who are occupied more in shipping than in other kinds of business. The larger operations of the kind are carried on in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>'s yards at Deptford and Woolwich; but there are many private yards for building and repairing ships on the south <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Thames. At Woolwich, the great manufactory of warlike stores, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> chiefly, gives occupation to many labourers exclusively of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. There mortars and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> cannon are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, bored, and mounted, the different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> prepared, and all the various combustibles used in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> compounded; and in the dockyard at that place, some of the largest ships of war are always building or repairing. In Chatham, and at Rochester, the chief manufactories are those of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, either for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> or for the ordnance department. The private manufacturing establishments are not either numerous or extensive. The largest in value is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, which is made at Maidstone and near Dover, of the best <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; but in other parts, where the water is adapted for the purpose, that trade is carried on; some especially near Westerham. The whole number of males above twenty years of age employed in making paper are 531, of whom 147 reside in the town of Maidstone. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> of wheat is a considerable trade, from the goodness of the wheat grown here, and the slight expense of conveying the flour by water to the great market of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of calicoes is carried on, upon the banks of the river Cray. The principal of these works are at Crayford, where 124, and at Bexley, where forty males, above twenty years of age, are employed; but this trade, like that of making paper, gives occupation to many more females than males. At Dartford there are some large manufactories of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>; at Deptford, of several chemical preparations; at Greenwich, of machinery and of combs; and at Maidstone, of bagging for hops. One of the proudest ornaments of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, Greenwich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, for the relief of disabled or aged seamen, is in this county; and, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> contiguous to it, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, to which the eyes of all the navigators of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> are directed, as the place from which issues the nautical ephemeris, which all nations depend on when traversing distant seas. Though Kent is bounded on three sides by the ocean and the river Thames, it has scarcely any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The harbours are none of them good; those of Dover and Ramsgate are formed by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> piers, and the former is dry at low water when the sluices are open. The only trade from Dover is to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, for such light goods as can bear the expense of land-carriage. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery conducted from Folkestone; besides which, the principal foreign trade consists in smuggling those various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duties offer a temptation to encounter such perilous adventures. The sea-shores in this county invite numerous visitors, who frequent and fill various towns during the warm months of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The principal of these are Margate, Ramsgate, and Broadstairs; but, besides these, many of the smaller places on the coast are resorted to for purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> or amusement. On the western side of the county, the waters of Tunbridge have long been celebrated; and though the influence of fashion has erected into rivals several other Spas, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> that still <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to it is both numerous and respectable. (See Marshall's Survey; Boys's Survey; Brayley's Beauties of England and Wales; and Hasted's Kent.)

KENTIGERN

Pages 706-706

St., <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> St Mungo, a famous saint of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who flourished in Scotland in the sixth century, and is said to have been of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood of both Scotch and Picts, being the son of Thameitis, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Loth <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Picts, by Eugene III. king of Scotland. The bishoprics of Glasgow and St Asaph were founded by him in 560. He obtained the appellation of Mungo from the affection of his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> St Serf or Servanus, bishop of Orkney, who called him Mongah, which in the Norwegian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies dear friend. KENTISH <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Pancras, in the hundred of Ossett, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. It has of late so much extended its buildings, that it almost forms a suburb to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. It is finely situated in a valley, beginning between the hills of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMPSTEAD">Hampstead</a> and Highgate; and being deemed a remarkably healthy spot, is much occupied with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> residences of persons connected with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and within the last ten years it has assumed an elegant appearance. There is a chapel of ease, and some dissenting places of worship.

KENTON

Pages 706-706

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Devon, in the hundred of Exminster, 178 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on the river Ex, where the Ken falls into that stream. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 1639, in 1811 to 1793, in 1821 to 1891, and in 1831 to 2050.

KENTUCKY

Pages 706-709

one of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is bounded on the north by the river Ohio, which separates it from Ohio, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ILLINOIS">Illinois</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIANA">Indiana</a>; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; on the south by Virginia and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENNESSEE">Tennessee</a>; and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. It extends from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 81. 50. to 89. 29. W., and from lat. 36. 30. to 39. 10. N. Its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> length is 380 miles, its medium breadth is about 100, and it contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 38,000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Kentucky is said to possess larger quantities of fertile <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> than any other western state; and, for beautiful variety of hill and dale, the general excellence of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and picturesqueness of landscape scenery, including fine forests, and numerous streams and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, few countries surpass it. Yet there are in this state <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sterile tracts, and a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of land either too mountainous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> too <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> for cultivation. The Alleghany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> stretch along its eastern and south-eastern boundary, and branches from that chain penetrate into the counties contiguous to Tennessee and Virginia, rendering them broken and hilly. These offshoots from the larger mountains <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> round the basis of the small <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> hills, and open up into frightful chasms, shaded by the gigantic poplar. A tract from five to twenty miles wide along the banks of the Ohio has the same character, but it is interspersed with fertile valleys. Between this strip of land, Green River, and the eastern counties, lies what has been called the garden of the state; it is the most populous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and is distinguished for its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and fertility. It has a finely diversified or rolling surface, the soil is excellent, and there is abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and grape vines. It is about one hundred and fifty miles in length, and from fifty to one hundred in breadth. From three to ten feet beneath the surface, there is a substratum or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of this mineral in a dissolved state is intermixed with the soil, and imparts to it a warm and forcing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, highly favourable to the progress of vegetation. Much of it belongs to that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of soil technically called "mulatto land." Through this beau- Kentucky, tiful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> meander the Little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">Sandy</a>, Licking, Kentucky, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> Rivers, with their numerous tributaries. There are a few precipitous hills, but no elevations of a magnitude sufficient to entitle any part of it to the character of mountainous. The woods have a very fine appearance, and seem as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been promiscuously arranged for a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> ground. Grape vines of vast size climb the trees, and overshadow the verdure beneath with their umbrageous leaves. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> walnut, black cherry, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-locust, buck-eye, pawpaw, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-tree, mulberry, elm, ash, hawthorn, coffee-tree, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> poplar trees which indicate the richest soil, are everywhere abundant. When the country was first settled, it was covered with a thick <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANE">cane</a> brake; but this has now given <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to a beautiful grass sward. In the early part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the May-apple throws out its rich and beautiful verdure in abundance, which, along with the purple and redundant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> bud, and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> blossoms of the dogwood, impart a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> to the landscape. The trees are not in general large, but tall, straight, and tapering at the top. Innumerable branches wind amongst the copses; and in the declivities numerous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, impregnated with lime, gush forth. In the south-western part of the state, between Green and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> Rivers, there is a large tract of country, called "barrens," covered with grass like a prairie, and affording a fine range for cattle. Within these few years it has been planted with different kinds of trees, which, however, do not check the growth of the grass, or an infinite variety of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which enamel the sward, and during spring and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> flower in all the wild and luxuriant beauty of a western wilderness. Spread over this district are an immense <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small conical hills, called "knobs," covered with shrubby and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> oaks. The soil is of an excellent quality, being a mixture of clay loam and sand; and fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> is raised by many of the farmers. Of this state in general, an American writer observes: "For variety of hill and dale, for the excellence of the soil, yielding in abundance all that is necessary for comfortable subsistence, for amenity of landscape, beauty of forest, the number of clear streams and fine rivers, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and the finest development of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, and patriarchal simplicity of rural opulence, we question if any country can be found surpassing Kentucky." A long <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the northern frontier of this state is washed by the Ohio River; and the Mississippi passes a considerable part of the south-western boundary. Most of the rivers which have their origin within the limits of Kentucky rise in the southern part of it, and flow in a northerly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> into the Ohio. The river from which the state derives its name rises in the south-eastern portion, and interlocks with the head waters of Licking and Cumberland Rivers, the former having its origin in the north-east, and the other in the south-east corner. The Kentucky is an important stream, navigable for one hundred and eighty miles during winter, with a rapid current, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and in some parts perpendicular, banks of limestone. It takes a north-west course, and joins the Ohio at Port William, seventy-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles above Louisville, after receiving various tributary streams. Licking waters a rich and well-settled country, and, after a sinuous course of two hundred miles, enters the Ohio at Newport, opposite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINCINNATI">Cincinnati</a>. Cumberland River waters eighty miles of this state, when it enters Tennessee; but crosses again into Kentucky, and, after running fifty miles in it, once more returns to Tennessee, which it leaves a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the sister state. The river Big Sandy rises in the Allegany Mountains, and forms the eastern boundary of the state for nearly two hundred miles. Kentucky. During its progress it receives a great number of large creeks, and, before it enters the Ohio, separates into two branches or forks. It is navigable for a considerable distance. Green River is boatable for two hundred miles, and receives a great number of tributaries in its course. Salt River is boatable for one hundred and fifty miles, and, traversing four counties, enters the Ohio twenty miles below Louisville. There are a great many mineral springs, possessing medicinal qualities, some of which are really valuable. A fountain of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, vulgarly called mineral <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, was discovered at the depth of one hundred and eighty feet, whilst the ground was being pierced to obtain salt water. When the auger was withdrawn, the unctuous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> sprung perpendicularly upwards in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> stream, more than twelve feet above the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The rocks of this state are said all to belong to the secondary formation. Limestone and marble of the most beautiful species abound. Coal has been discovered in some places, especially along the Ohio. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> ore is very abundant, and wrought to a considerable extent. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>, copperas, and aluminous earths are likewise found. There are a number of salt springs, from which salt was formerly obtained; but it is now found more profitable to import it from other states. The soil of Kentucky is strongly impregnated with nitre; and it has been affirmed that fifty pounds of that salt, in a crude state, have been obtained from only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity of earth. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities and antiquities in this state; the limestone caves in particular excite the astonishment of all who visit them. One, styled Mammoth Cave, in the south-western part, one hundred and thirty miles from Lexington, on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> leading to Nashville, is said to be eight or ten miles in length, with a great number of avenues and windings. The famous cave of Antiparos is nothing to this stupendous subterranean cavity. A number of the rivers have excavated the earth, so as to form abrupt precipices, deep glens, and frightful gulfs. The precipices formed by Kentucky River are in many places awfully sublime, presenting perpendicular banks of three hundred feet of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> limestone, surmounted with a steep and difficult ascent four times as high. Amongst the antiquities of Kentucky are great numbers of those <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> mounds which are scattered over all the western territory. Human bodies have been found in a state of entire preservation in several caves; they are said to be considerably smaller than the men of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times.
