a town of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a>, surrounded with gardens, and supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> described by Xenophon, in the plain of Cayster, where <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> first met the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. It is ninety-eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Konieh.

KETOIE

Pages 715-716

one of the Kurile <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, near the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KETTERING">Kettering</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, about twenty miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is covered with wood, which affords shelter to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> foxes, seals, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-calves.

KETTERING

Pages 716-716

a town of the hundred of Orlingbury, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, with a market on Saturday. It is seventy-five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and is a manufacturing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where some worsted and woollen goods are made. It is not a well-built town. The sessions for the county are held in it. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 3011, in 1811 to 3242, in 1821 to 3668, and in 1831 to 4099.

KETTLE

Pages 716-716

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> which the Dutch apply to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of mortars, because it is sunk underground. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KETTLE_DRUMS">Kettle-Drums</a> are formed of two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basins of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, rounded at the bottom, and covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> or goat-skin, which is kept fast by a circle of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and by several holes fastened to the body of the drum, with a like <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of screws to screw up and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KEY">key</a> for the purpose. The two basins are kept fast together by two straps of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> which go through two rings, and are fastened the one before and the other behind the pommel of the kettle-drum's saddle. They have each a banner of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or damask, richly embroidered with the sovereign's arms, or with those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>, and are fringed with silver or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and, to preserve them in bad <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, they have each a cover of leather. The drumsticks are of crab-tree or of any other hard wood, of eight or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with two knobs on the ends, which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the drum head and produce the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. The kettle-drum with trumpets is the most martial sound of any. Each regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> has a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>. Kettle-Drummer, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> on horseback appointed to beat the kettle-drum, from which he takes his name. He marches always at the head of the squadron, and his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> is on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> when the squadron is drawn up.

KEVELS

Pages 716-716

in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, a frame composed of two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, whose lower ends rest in a sort of step <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> foot nailed to the ship's side, whence the upper ends branch outward into arms or horns, serving to belay the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> by which the bottoms of the main-sail and fore-sail are extended.

KEVERN

Pages 716-716

St., a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of the hundred of Kerriar, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall, 277 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 2104, in 1811 to 2242, in 1821 to 2505, and in 1831 to 2437.

KEW

Pages 716-716

a village of the hundred of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, six and a half miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is a pleasant village, with many highly respectable houses, but chiefly distinguished for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the favourite residence of George III. The palace is of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, built of brick faced with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the Gothic style. It is, however, inferior to the gardens, which are laid out with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and judgment, and contain almost every curious vegetable production of various countries and climates. There are in these gardens a variety of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> connected with classical and historical subjects. One of the most remarkable is the Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a>, about 170 feet in height, said to be an exact copy of one in the celestial empire, from the top of which is a fine prospect over the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 424, in 1811 to 560, in 1821 to 683, and in 1831 to 837.

KEY

Pages 716-716

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for the opening of locks. Molinus, in his treatise of keys, De clavibus veterum, printed at Upsal, derives the Latin name clavis from the Greek κλαμος, clamo, I shut, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> from the adverb clam, privately; and adds, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of keys is yet unknown in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of keys is due to one Theodore of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, according to Pliny and Polydore <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>; but this must be a mistake, as the use of keys was known before the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, whilst mention is even made of them in the nineteenth <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>. Molinus is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that keys at first served only for untying certain knots wherewith they ancienly secured their doors; but the Laconic keys, he maintains, were nearly akin in use to our own, consisting of three single <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and made in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an E; a form of which there are still some to be seen in the cabinets of the curious. There was another key called Bakawaya, made in the manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> screw, which had its corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> in a bolt affixed to the door. Key has hence become a general name for several things serving to shut up or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> others. Key, or Key-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a> or Vault, is the last stone placed on the top thereof, which, being wider and fuller at the top than bottom, wedges, as it were, and binds together all the rest. The key is different in the different orders. In the Tuscan and Doric it is only a plain stone projecting; in the Ionic it is cut and waved, somewhat after the manner of consoles; in the Corinthian and Composite it is a console enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, foliages, and other ornaments. Key is also used for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> jurisdiction, particularly for the power of excommunicating and absolving. The Romanists say the pope has the power of the keys, and can open and shut paradise as he pleases, grounding their opinion on that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ to St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, "I <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> give thee the keys of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven." In St Gregory we read that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the popes to send a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> key to princes, in which they enclosed a little of the filings of St Peter's chains, kept with a world of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> at Rome; and that these keys were worn in the bosom, as being supposed to contain some wonderful virtues. Key, in Music, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> or tone, to which the whole piece, be it in cantata, sonata, or concerto, is accommodated, and with which it usually begins, but always ends. Key, or Quay, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> wharf, usually built of stone, by the side of a harbour or river, and having several storehouses for the convenience of lading and discharging merchant ships. It is accordingly furnished with posts and rings, by which the latter are secured; together with cranes, capstans, and other engines, to lift the goods into or out of the vessels which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> alongside. The verb cojare, in old writers, according to Scaliger, signifies to keep in or restrain; and hence came our <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> key or quay, the ground where they are made being bound in with planks and posts.

KEY'S ISLES

Pages 716-716
three s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands in the Eastern Seas, of considerable extent, and named Key Watchs, Little and Great Key Islands, the first forty-five and the second sixty miles in circumference, and the third fifty miles in length and from five to twelve in breadth. They are situated about the 133rd degree of east longitude and between the 5th and 6th degrees of north latitude.

KEYDEE

Pages 716-716

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bhar, district of Nagpoor, 235 miles west by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 84. 49. E. Lat. 22. 46. N.

KEYNSHAM

Pages 716-716

a market-town in the hundred of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Somerset, 114 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on the south <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Avon, midway between Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. There is little trade, but a small market on Thursday. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 1591, in 1811 to 1748, in 1821 to 1761, and in 1831 to 2142.

KEYSLER

Pages 716-717

JOHN GEORGE, a learned German antiquary, was born at Thournex in the year 1689. After studying at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a>, he was appointed preceptor to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Maximilian and Christian Charles, the young counts of Giech-Buchau, with whom he travelled through the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of Germany, France, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, gaining <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation amongst the learned as he went along; Kharkoo by illustrating several monuments of antiquity, particularly some fragments of Celtic idols discovered in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Having acquitted himself of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, he was, in 1716, appointed to superintend the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of two grandsons of Baron Bernstorff, first minister of state to his Britannic majesty as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a>. However, having in 1718 obtained leave to visit England, he was elected a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, for a learned <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> de Dea Nehelennia, numine veterum Walachorum topico. He also gave an explanation of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monument on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> Plain called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a>, with a dissertation on the consecrated mistletoe of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>. These detached essays, with others of the same kind, he published on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Antiquitates selectae Septentrionales et Celticae. He afterwards made the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> tour with the young barons, and to this we owe the publication of his travels, which were translated into English, and published in 1756, in four vols. 4to. Mr Keysler, on his return, spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of his noble pupils, who committed their fine library and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> to his care, with a handsome income. He died in 1743.

KHANAKEE

Pages 717-717

a handsome little town of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> Arabi, on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMADAN">Hamadan</a>. In the vicinity are some magnificent ruins, supposed to be those of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Chosroes. It is ninety miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Bagdad.

KHANDESH

Pages 717-717

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a>, situated between the 21st and 23rd degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. To the north it is bounded by the Nerbuddah, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALWAH">Malwah</a>; to the south by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AURUNGABAD">Aurungabad</a> and Berar; on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-GUNDWANA">Gundwana</a> and Berar; and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a>. Its limits have never been accurately defined, though they may be estimated at 210 miles in length by eighty in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth. Khandesh was one of the small soubahs formed during the reign of Akbar, from conquests made south of the Nerbuddah. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> subdivisions are: 1. Gaulina; 2. Khandesh proper; 3. Meiwar; 4. Bejagur; 5. Pattneemaur; 6. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDIA">Hindia</a>. This province is remarkably strong by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, containing, within one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, nearly twenty fortresses, all in sight in different directions. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is well watered. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are, the Nerbuddah, Tuptee, and other tributary streams; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOORHANPOOR">Boorhanpoor</a>, Asseerghur, Hindia, Nundoorbar, and Gaulna. The surface of the province is very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, though it is not mountainous. The ridge of the western Ghautes extends along the Tuptee, from which passes descend into the lower country. This river has deep and steep banks, and the adjacent country is curiously intersected with ravines from thirty to forty feet deep, and sometimes winding along for a distance of several miles. As the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> frequently leads through these chasms, which are remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and hot, it is not uncommon to see an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> on its march through the country disappear in these deep valleys, and afterwards emerge half suffocated with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and covered with dust. This country was once flourishing and populous; but at present, owing to the devastations of different plundering tribes, such as the Bheels, Pindarries, and Arabs, joined to the oppressions of its Mahratta rulers, it is now desolate and overgrown with jungle, the towns are in ruins, the villages have been destroyed, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though fertile and well watered, lies neglected. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is estimated at two millions, five sixths of whom are Hindus. Khandesh was governed in the beginning of the fifteenth century by independent sovereigns, who, claiming <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the Khalif Omar, resided at Asseerghur; but, towards the close of the century, it was subdued, and annexed to the Mogul empire. Since the decline of the Mahratta power, the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the province of Khandesh was taken possession of by Arab colonists, whose soldier-like qualities gave them <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. In 1818 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KHARKOW">Kharkow</a> the whole of Holkar's territories in India were ceded to the British, to whose dominion the Arab colonists evinced a decided aversion; and as it was resolved to re-transport them to their own country, they determined to resist to the last extremity. The last body of these brave adventurers surrendered in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1818; but many of the Bheel chiefs, trusting to their mountainous and jungly recesses, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> refractory. They were dislodged from many of their retreats by the vigilance of British officers, who were for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> engaged in this harassing warfare. The province was formerly famous for the manufacture of cotton cloths called baftas.

KHARKOW

Pages 717-717
or Charkow, a city of the province Ukraine, in Russia, the capital of a circle of the same name. It is situated on the Donetz, where that river receives the waters of the Lepanka and the Charkow. It contains 1532 houses, and 15,000 inhabitants. It is the seat of a university founded in 1813, with twenty-five professors, and 250 students. It enjoys some considerable trade, especially at four great fairs, to which the Asiatics and Turks equally resort. Long. 36° 50'. 55". E. Lat. 49° 59'. 20". N.

KHARSHOT

Pages 717-717

a river of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, which, flowing through a narrow and beautiful valley, falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> near Tereboli.

KHASGUNGE

Pages 717-717

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, sixty-four miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west from the town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FURRUCKABAD">Furruckabad</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 36'. E. Lat. 27° 52". N.

KHATANGA

Pages 717-717

a considerable river of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, which has its rise in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOMSK">Tomsk</a>, and, after a course of 500 miles through a low and marshy territory, falls into the Northern Ocean, forming a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> to which it gives name.

KHEMLASA

Pages 717-717

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> walled town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, with a fort adjoining, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALWAH">Malwah</a>, ninety-four miles south-west from Chatterpoor. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 36'. E. Lat. 24° 15". N.

KHEROO

Pages 717-717

a town of Thibet, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Himalaya ridge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but now an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, having been laid waste, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to 1790, by an incursion of the Tartars, who occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the north of Joongale. A considerable trade is carried on between <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEPAUL">Nepaul</a> and this place.

KHILLIS

Pages 717-717

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, situated at the foot of Mount Taurus, where there is a celebrated market for cotton. It is twenty-eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>.

KHIVAH

Pages 719-719

an independent territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which extends on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a> a distance of between 100 and 200 miles, and on all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> is surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. The town of Khivah, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, is about fifteen miles from the Oxus, or 240 miles from Mungushluc, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> upon the banks of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. This tract of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, however confined and unpromising, was at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the seat of the Khwarezmian sovereigns, who maintained a very flourishing empire, well known in the annals of the East. This empire embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Western Asia, and the country around was populous and prosperous. But all is now changed. The country has been ruined by the invasions of different conquerors; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Khwarezm or Ourgunge, like the most celebrated cities of the East, has become a ruin; and the seat of the petty power that now exists has been transferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> town of Khivah. The modern city of Khivah was totally ruined by Nadir Shah, at the time when he overran all Turkestan, on his return from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; its youth were enlisted in his armies, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many were put to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and numbers were transported to distant parts. The Usbeck Tartars at length obtained the ascendency in this country, and maintained on the throne a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> said to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Ghenghis. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> from one of their tribes still rules in the country.

KHOEE

Pages 717-717

a town of Azerbaijan, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a rich and extensive district, situated on the borders of the lake Urumea. There is no town in Persia more beautiful and better built; the walls are in good repair; the streets regular, and shaded with avenues of trees; and the ceilings of many of the houses tastefully painted and embellished. These paintings are not <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>; and as the immediate predecessors of Shah Ismael frequently held their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, they were probably executed about that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. It is the emporium of a considerable trade carried on between <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and Persia. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 25,000. The plain in which it is situated is famous for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in 1514, between Shah Ismael and Selim I, in which 30,000 Persians encountered 300,000 Turks.

KHOOSHGAL

Pages 717-718

a well-built small fort in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bejapoor, and district of Bancapoor, strongly situated on a rising ground in the middle of an extensive plain. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 13'. E. Lat. 15° 29". N. KHORASSAN is, strictly speaking, a province of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. In its more extended <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, however, it comprehends Khorassan, an extensive tract of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, of which the boundaries have been differently defined, and indeed have greatly varied. In the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> revolutions which have occurred in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Khorassan has been the centre of a great empire, and the seat of mighty monarchs, and more frequently the dependency of a fallen state, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of invasion, rebellion, and anarchy. It was a constant subject of dispute between the independent monarchs, whose territories lay respectively on the east and on the west; and it sometimes fell into the power of one, and sometimes of the other. In these circumstances, its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> boundaries were continually varying, as the fortune of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> inclined to one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> other of the surrounding potentates. At one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> they comprehended the whole country to the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a>, including the steppe of Khwarezm, Balkh, and all the intervening country to the east; on the south-east, not only the cities and dependencies of Herat, but those of Subzawur, Farrah, Geeresh, and even Candahar itself; on the south it was always bounded by Kerman and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEISTAN">Seistan</a>; on the west it included the district of Yezed, but its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> was bounded in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> by the districts of Isphahan, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CASHAN">Cashan</a>, and Rha, in the vicinity of Semnann; and beyond the Elburz <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, the districts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRABAD">Astrabad</a> and of Goorgum were also considered as the dependencies of this vast territory. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Khorassan be merely considered as a province of Persia, its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> would be very inconsiderable indeed. But if, with Fraser, we take into consideration the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> features of the country, the following boundaries may be assigned. According to this traveller, a line, skirting the districts of Isphahan and Cashan, and meeting the Elburz Mountains near Dehimmuck, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> divide Khorassan from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> on the west. This line prolonged eastward to the desert on the eastern side of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, in the steppe of Khwarezm, will form its northern boundary; and we cannot positively decide, nor is exactness in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of great importance, in what <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the great desert that occupies the whole space between the foot of the Elburz range and the Oxus, this boundary should be placed. In a political view, it does not extend at present beyond the base of the Elburz Mountains. To the eastward it may properly be allowed to include the districts of Serrukhs, Hazarah, and Balai Moorghaib; and a line running between these and the dependencies of Balkh, in east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 68°, in a direction nearly south, including the district of Herat, and touching Seistan, would be the boundary of Khorassan on the east; whilst on the south it is bounded by Kerman and Fars. The surface of this extensive country is, like other parts of Persia, much diversified by plains and mountains; a very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion is quite unfit for the habitation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and consists of arid rocks, destitute of vegetation or fresh <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and deserts either of salt-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> or sand, among which may be found a few spots, like <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the sea. The following is a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, chiefly compiled from Fraser's Narrative of a Journey into Khorassan. The Elburz range of mountains, which is connected with the great chain of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, runs, in an easterly course, through the northern parts of Khorassan, sending forth various ramifications to the southward. From the base of these mountains a desert of barren sand, chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, stretches northward to an immense extent, including the steppe of Khwarezm, and forming a part of that mighty plain which extends eastward as far as the Jaxartes and the Oxus. In this plain are found many fertile districts; but in that portion which is included in the limits now assigned to Khorassan, there is no permanent habitation, and the scanty sprinkling of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> which it possesses consists of a few tribes of wandering Toorkomans. These mountains, though they present their loftiest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> to the desert, still <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a manner so gradual, as to enclose rich and well-watered valleys, which were formerly well peopled and cultivated, and once contained several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, which are now in ruins, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> attacks of the Toorkoman plunderers. The only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of any consideration that remains is Serrukhs, 120 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSHED">Mushed</a>, a very <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, the remains of which are now inhabited by Toorkomans and Usbecks. To the south, the Elburz Mountains send forth ramifications which penetrate the plain to the distance of from sixty to one hundred miles. Beyond this is the vast salt desert, which extends southward, with occasional fertile tracts, very nearly to the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a>. This desert varies very much in its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in different parts. In some places the surface is dry, and even produces a few of those <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that thrive in a salt <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; in others it consists of a crackling crust of dry <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, covered with a saline efflorescence. There are extensive marshy tracts, in the lower parts of which water accumulates during the winter months, which is evaporated by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, leaving a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of salt in cakes, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a> of mud. In some places the soil is a hard-baked and perfectly barren clay; again, in certain districts, extensive plains of sand are found, which is occasionally heaped up in hillocks in the form of waves, and frequently so <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as to be raised aloft by the winds in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, under which travellers are frequently buried, as in the Arabian deserts. The saline desert, however, according to Fraser, predominates in Khorassan. It is of a considerably higher level than the desert to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the Elburz Mountains; but still this traveller is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that they are connected. The only fertile parts of Khorassan are where the country is penetrated by the Elburz Mountains; and in the north-east corner of Khorassan there is a long stripe of country, consisting of the lower parts of these mountains, from ten to twenty miles in breadth, which bear some inconsiderable traces of cultivation, and give shelter to a few miserable hamlets, but contain no village of any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The valley of Mushed, amongst the Elburz Mountains, is of great length. It commences ten or twelve miles to the north-west of Sheerwan, extends, without interruption, for fifty miles beyond Mushed, and continues for the greater part of the way to Herat. It varies from twelve to thirty miles in breadth, and contains in its extent, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mushed, the towns of Chinnaran, Radean, Kabooshan or Cachoon, Sheerwan, and their dependencies, with a great extent of cultivated land. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Mushed to Herat must also <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through several well-peopled and well-cultivated districts. The extensive valley here spoken of contains a considerable portion of the district known by the appellation of Koordistan, being inhabited by Koordish colonies. The country which we have described above, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Khorassan, may be estimated to extend between 500 and 600 miles east and west, and between 300 and 400 miles north and south.

KHOZDAR

Pages 718-718

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELOOCHISTAN">Beloochistan</a>, the residence of Meer Murad <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Beloochee ameers of the Kumburance tribe. It is situated in a small romantic valley of the same name, between two tremendous ridges of bare <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, tolerably well cultivated, and watered by a stream flowing through the centre. The town is walled, and has a good bazar. It is a Mahommedan town, though the Hindus are held in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is severe; and at the approach of winter the richer classes retire to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTCH">Cutch</a> Gundava, to avoid the intense <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It is distant from Kelat, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of Beloochistan <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Baloochistan, three days' journey. Its situation is not exactly ascertained, but is nearly in latitude 36° 30' N. and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 67° E.

KHUAR

Pages 717-717
or Hawari, a town of Irak, in Persia, 200 miles north of Ispahan. It is situated on a mountain which separates the province of Irak from that of Mazanderan, and through which there is a narrow pass that takes its name from the town.

KHYPOOR

Pages 718-719

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SINDE">Sinde</a>, and the residence of the chiefs of the aristocracy who govern the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It carries on a considerable trade, and is noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> of cloths. Latitude not ascertained.

KIAHING FOU

Pages 719-719

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tchekiang. It has extensive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, there being scarcely a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in which silk-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> are not bred. It carries on a considerable trade, for the convenience of which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are cut in every street. It is 130 miles south-east of Nanquin. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 120. 14. E. Lat. 32. N.

KIAKHTA

Pages 719-719

a town of Asiatic Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Irkoutsk, and district of Verschnei-Oudlinsk. It is situated in a uniform and rather elevated plain, traversed by a river of the same name, and is surrounded by a lofty range of granitic and wooded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of a bleak aspect. It was visited in 1822 by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cochrane, the celebrated pedestrian traveller, who mentions that it is a neat and regularly-built town, containing 450 houses, with 4000 inhabitants. Owing to the narrow and jealous policy of the Chinese, no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> buildings are by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> allowed to be erected, excepting only a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> for public worship. Beyond the fortress, and immediately opposite Mainatchin, is the Chinese town Old Kiaakhta, the residence only of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; no officer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> stranger being permitted to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in it, according to an article in the treaty. The old town contains, according to Cochrane, forty-five dwellings, many of which are very superior edifices, and have within them very rich stores. Though situated in a dreary and sterile oasis, Kiaakhta, by means of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, possesses many comforts. It is 330 miles south of Irkoutsk. On one of the mountains by which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is surrounded are seen the boundaries of the Russian and Chinese empires, placed opposite each other; the Russian boundary being marked by a hillock of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> at the top; whilst that of the Chinese is marked by a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. This place is remarkable as the centre of all the trade which is carried on between the Russian and Chinese empires; the Chinese, by the jealous policy of their rulers, being prohibited from trading with Russia through any other place. It was fixed upon by the treaty concluded between these powers in 1728, as the only medium of their mutual intercourse; and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fair is accordingly held in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, when merchants flock thither from the most distant parts of the Russian empire. At this great commercial rendezvous are exchanged clothes; furs, namely, those of foxes, sables, river and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> otters, wild cats, beavers, and millions of squirrels, this latter fur, from its lightness, warmth, and durability, being a favourite with the Chinese; Russia and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; for nankeens, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, &c. Woollen cloths and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a> are also exported to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, as well as many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of curiosity and ingenuity, and some trinkets. The Russian and Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are quite separate from each other.

KIAMA

Pages 719-719
or KHIAMA, the capital of one of the four petty states or sultanries of Borgoo, a kingdom in the interior of Africa. It consists of a vast collection of thatched huts, built, as well as the town wall, of clay, and irregularly scattered over a considerable surface of ground. It is one of the towns through which the Houssa and Borou caravan passes in its way to Gouja, upon the borders of Ashantee. It has also a direct trade with Dahomey, Youri, Nyfei, and Youriba. The inhabitants, for the most part Pagans, may amount to 30,000 in number. They are governed by a king or sultan, whose domination is despotic. Kiama is situated in long. 5. 22. 56. E. and lat. 9. 37. 33. N.

KIANGNAN

Pages 719-719

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, which may be considered as the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, wealth, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> empire. It is bounded on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Shantung, on the west by Honan, and on the south by Tchekiang and Quangsee. This extensive province is well watered, being traversed by the great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Hoangho and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-kiang</a>, previous to their junction with the sea, and by their numerous tributaries, which give it an easy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with all the provinces and districts of the interior. It is also crossed by the great canal which leads to Pekin; and its waters are accordingly covered with a continuous line of barks, carrying to their various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> the different productions of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Nankeen is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which surpasses Pekin in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and even in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>. It contains many other cities, which, in point of size and wealth, might have been the capitals of empires. Industry and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> flourish to a great extent in this province; and the silks, japanned goods, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INK">ink</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, bear a higher price. There are manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> on the sea <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; and it contains also quarries of marble. The official estimate of the population given to Sir George Staunton was twenty-two millions, which is probably one of the boastful exaggerations of the Chinese.

KIANGSEE

Pages 719-719

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, consisting chiefly of lofty and precipitous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, with fertile valleys interposed. It extends southwards from Kiangan to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANGTONG">Quangtong</a>, and yields in abundance both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. Its mountains also contain various <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and minerals, and it has an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, forming <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> line of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> which reaches across the empire. A very extensive manufacture of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> is carried on in this province.

KIBBAN

Pages 719-719

a considerable town of Koordistan, situated at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, and surrounded by narrow passes and defiles. It is about one and a half <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and eighty miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>.

KIDDER

Pages 719-720

RICHARD, an English bishop, was born, according to Wood, at Brighton, but according to others, in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>. In 1649, he was admitted sizar in Emmanuel <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; in 1652, he took his bachelor's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; in 1655, he was elected a fellow; and in 1656, he took his degree of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. Having been presented by his college to the vicarage of Stanground, Huntingdonshire, he was ejected for non-conformity in 1662; but conforming soon afterwards, he was, in 1664, presented to the rectory of Raine, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> until 1674, when he was made rector of St Martin's Outwith, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1681, he was installed into a prebend of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>; in 1689, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> of Peterborough, on which occasion he took the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and, upon the deprivation of Ken, bishop of Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, he was promoted to the vacant see. In 1693, he delivered the Boyle Lecture, and afterwards inserted in his Demonstration of the Messias, the discourses preached by him upon that occasion. He also wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the Five Books of Moses, with a dissertation concerning the author <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> writer of the said books, and a general argument to each of them, which was published in 1694, in two vols. 8vo. To the first volume is prefixed a dissertation, in which he states and answers all the objections made against Moses being the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and, in particular, replies to one drawn by Leclerc from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> (xxxvi. 31), which he treats with some severity. This led to a correspondence between him and Leclerc, which the latter printed in his Bibliothèque Choisié. Dr Kidder likewise took <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the Popish controversy, in the course of which he published, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> between a Catholic Convert and a Protestant, showing why he cannot believe the doctrine of Transubstantiation, though he do firmly believe the doctrine of the Trinity; 2. An <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of Bellarmine's thirtieth <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> on the Confession of Adversaries; 3. The Texts which Papists cite out of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> for their Doctrine of the Sacrifice of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">Mass</a> examined; 4. Reflections on a French <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, printed at Bordeaux in 1686, pretended to be translated out of the Latin by the divines of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of this prelate was sudden and lamentable. In the night between the 26th and 27th of November 1703, he was killed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>, with his lady, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Wells, by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of a stack of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, occasioned by a violent storm which raged without. Dr Kidder was a clear and learned writer, and accounted one of the best divines of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

KIDDERMINSTER

Pages 720-720

a town of the hundred of Halfshire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, with a market, which is held on Thursday. It is 126 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the river Stour. It has <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufacturing industry. Formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> goods made were of worsted, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and worsted; then bombazeens, plushes, and poplins were introduced; but of late years the chief fabrics have been those of carpets, in which the Kidderminster <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> have excelled all others. The streets are clean, well paved, and well built. There is a fine old Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, many charitable institutions, and an endowed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school. By the late <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> this town has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of electing one member to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> Canal joins the town, and affords assistance to its trade. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 6110, in 1811 to 8039, in 1821 to 10,709, and in 1831 to 14,981.

KIDDLE

Pages 720-720
or KIDEL (Kidellus), a dam or weir in a river, with a narrow cut in it, for the laying of pots or other engines to catch fish. The word is ancient, for in Magna ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">Charta (cap. 24) we read Omnes kidelli deponantur per Thamesiam et Medueyam, et per totam Angliam, nisi per costeram maris; and, by King John's charter, power was granted to the city of London de kidellis amovendis per Thamesiam et Medueyam. A survey was ordered to be made of the weirs, mills, stanks, and kiddles, in the great rivers of England, by 1 Hen. IV. Fishermen corruptly call these dams kettles; and they are much used in Wales and on the sea-coasts of Kent.

KIDNAPPING

Pages 720-720

the forcible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDUCTION">abduction</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> stealing away of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, woman, or child, from their own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and sending them into another. This crime was <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> by the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. "He that stealeth a man and selleth him, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be found in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, shall surely be put to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>." (Exod. xxi. 16.) So likewise, in the civil law, the offence of spiriting away and stealing men and children, which was called plagium, and the offenders plagiarii, was punished with death.

KIDWELLEY

Pages 720-720

a market-town of South <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Carmarthen, 226 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is built on both sides the river Gwendraeth, which is navigable from Carmarthen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. It was formerly surrounded with walls, and there are still the ruins of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle. The neighbourhood abounds with coals, the export of which forms the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade; and for promoting which, excellent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> contrivances have been adopted for the most economical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of trans-shipping them from the barges to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-bound vessels. Near the town is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> foundery, and also a manufactory of tin plates. The town forms <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, but is governed by its own mayor and aldermen. There is a tolerable market on Friday, and three annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 1488, in 1811 to 1441, in 1821 to 1733, and in 1831 to 1631.

KIEL

Pages 720-720

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bailiwick of the same name. It stands on a beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, resembling a lake, on the Baltic, and has an excellent harbour. It contains near 800 houses, with 8000 inhabitants. It is a well-built city, containing a university of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character, with about 250 students, an <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and a library of 60,000 volumes. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade, both in the productions of the vicinity and in foreign commodities, and in ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 4. E. Lat. 54. 16. N.

KIELCE

Pages 720-720

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, and the seat of a bishop. It is, for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> like Poland, a well-built town, with the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, four churches, a nunnery, 800 houses, and 5100 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 55. E. Lat. 50. 52. N.

KIEV

Pages 720-720

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of European Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> formerly called Little Russia. It is situated between 28.30. and 32.20. east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and 48.26. and 51.34. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It extends over 15,466 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending sixty-eight cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 1304 parishes, with several villages and hamlets in each. The inhabitants are 994,830. It is divided into twelve circles, receiving the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns in it. It is generally a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> district, with undulations of hills proceeding from the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, whose elevations in this province are inconsiderable. There are many pleasant spots, though none very striking; but the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has a monotonous appearance. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally favourable to cultivation, and yields corn more than sufficient for consumption, so as to have 1,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> annually for the supply of less productive districts. It yields abundant crops of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. The cattle are numerous, and many are sold to Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and the internal provinces, to improve the breed. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Much spirit is distilled from grain, which, with coarse cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, forms the chief branch of trade. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river, the Dnieper, receives the waters of the smaller <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and conveys them to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Kiew, is on the Dnieper, is the seat of an archbishop, and has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, twenty-five other churches, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> seminary or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and other public institutions. It contains 3728 houses, in narrow and winding streets, and about 40,000 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. 22. 25. E. Lat. 50. 26. 19. N.

KILDA

Pages 720-721

St., <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Kirta, a solitary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>, belonging to the range of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, but removed to a considerable distance from the main cluster. The nearest <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> to it is Harris, from which it is distant sixty miles in a west-south-west <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and it is about one hundred and forty miles from the nearest point of the mainland of Scotland. It is about three miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> from east to west, and two miles from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and consists of a lofty and uneven ridge, fenced round on all sides by one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of rock, of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height except at a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> where is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> or landing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and even there the rocks have a considerable elevation. The surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is rocky, rising into four eminences, the highest of which, called Conachan, is 1380 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The general surface of the ground is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> loam, six or eight inches deep, and presents a nearly uniform, smooth, and green surface. Excepting some imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEAT">peat</a> upon the highest point, the whole is covered by a thick turf of the finest and freshest verdure. The island contains three <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, one of which gives rise to a considerable stream. Excepting a small tract in the vicinity of the little village in which the inhabitants live, the whole island is in pasture. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> would admit of cultivation to any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, but the violence of the west winds limits the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> to the south-east declivity, where there is most shelter. This tract is held conjointly by all the village, on the system of run-rig, the ridges being interchanged after three years; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> is performed by the spade and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>. The produce consists chiefly of bear, which is considered as very fine. The oats are of very inferior <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and are scantily cultivated; nor are potatoes raised to nearly the extent which is usual in Highland farming. A few horses are kept, together with some goats; but the pasture is chiefly occupied by sheep and black cattle. The breed of the former is Norwegian, and the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> which these animals produce is both thin and coarse. The cattle are small, and both the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> and cows are milked. The cheese, which is made from a mixture of these milks, is much esteemed. This article, along with wool and feathers, constitutes the exports of the island. The St Kilda style of husbandry is somewhat primitive and peculiar to the island. The soil is rendered extremely fertile by the laborious industry of the inhabitants, who manure it with great care. The inhabitants are all congregated in a village about a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the bay on the south-east. It consists of two rows of houses, with a pavement in the middle; and the habitations, like those of oriental countries, are nearly flat in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, in order to avoid injury from the storms which <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> over the island. The walls of the cottages are built of coarse free-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, without lime or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, but consolidated by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> layers of turf. All the houses are divided into two apartments, the interior one being for the family, and the other, nearest the door, being reserved for sheltering the cattle during winter. From their insulated situation, it is probable that the inhabitants of St Kilda have maintained the same manners, customs, and general style of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, for centuries. Previously to the reformation, there appears to have been three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> buildings on the island; but after that event took place, the inhabitants continued for ages unsolaced by the blessings of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, being only connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of South Uist by name. These disadvantages are now obviated by the establishment of a missionary and a schoolmaster, under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the Propagation of Christian Knowledge. The people live much upon the wild sea-fowl with which the precipices abound; and at certain seasons the whole sea is covered, and the very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is darkened, with feathered animals. Upwards of 20,000 solan geese are annually consumed by the natives, besides an immense <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eggs. St Kilda contains about twenty families, who, remote from the bustle of the busy world, and the luxuries of polished society, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> an easy, and even a comfortable life.

KILDARE

Pages 723-724

Kildare. a year; neither has he any episcopal residence, so that, in order to supply the deficiency of his revenue, he holds the deanery of Christ Church in commendam. The city of Kildare is a small, poor place, wholly unworthy of notice, except from the circumstance of being the seat of the bishopric, and from the cathedral, and some monastic remains still existing. This bishopric is one of those to be extinguished. After the demise of the present incumbent it is to merge into the archbishopric of Dublin. By much the greater part of the county is a flat, interrupted only by a range of low hills in the centre, the most northern of which is the hill of Allen, and the southern those of Dummurry; the land on the eastern boundary, toward Dublin and Wicklow counties, gradually rises as it approaches the adjoining mountain tracts. The general surface stands at an elevation of from 200 to 300 feet above the level of high water, giving birth to several rivers. The Boyne, with its tributary the Blackwater, rises in the bog of Allen in the northern part, as does the Lesser Barrow, which unites with the Greater Barrow near Rathangan. The Grees and Lane are small branches of this latter river, joining it near the southern extremity of the county. The Barrow forms the western boundary of the county, except in the neighbourhood of Athy, where the Meering embraces some land to the west of this river, which should more properly form part of the Queen's county. The Liffey enters the county from the west near Ballymore-Enstace, and after sweeping through it, at first in a western and then in a northern direction by Kilkullen Bridge, Clan, and Celbridge, receiving in its course the Morrel and the Ryewater, it quits the county at Leixlip. Numerous lesser streams, rising in the more elevated tracts, fall into one or other of these rivers. A great part of the bog of Allen lies in the northern part of the county. This bog is not an interrupted morass, but is intersected in many places by elevated tracts of firm ground, the largest of which, lying in its southern part, has obtained the name of the Island of Allen, in consequence of its being surrounded by an unproductive and half fluid mass. To the south of the town of Kildare is a tract of undulating ground, covered with fine sward, of a vivid green, uninterrupted by any plantation. It is called the Carragh. It extends nearly five miles in a south-eastern direction, having an average breadth of a mile, and containing 8000 acres. It is used principally as a sheep walk, for which it is peculiarly adapted, from the quality of its herbage and the dry elastic nature of its soil. The pasturage is held by the farmers of the surrounding lands, who pay large rents for the exclusive privilege of grazing sheep on it, in numbers proportioned to the quantity of land without its limits. The most celebrated race-course in Ireland is on the Carragh. The softness and elasticity of the turf render it peculiarly suitable for this sport. Races are held here periodically, at which two plates of £100 each are granted by the government, to encourage the breeding of running horses. The climate is moister than most other parts of the great limestone plain of Ireland. The soil of the county is generally a rich, heavy loam, on a bottom of limestone or limestone gravel, except in some insulated spots in the hilly districts. Copper ore is said to have been found in the central hills; but, either from deficiency of quality or quantity, or from a still more marked deficiency of fuel, none is now raised. The hill of Allen consists of a gritstone of which millstones are made. The population was as follows, according to the authorities stated beneath, at the respective dates. | Date | Boys | Girls | Sex not ascertained | Total | |------------|------|-------|--------------------|-------| | 1821 | 3398 | 2393 | | 6391 | | 1824–6 | 5118 | 3578 | 161 | 8857 | Of the number in the latter return, 1425 were of the established church, 7276 were Catholics, thirty-one dissenters, and 125 whose religious persuasion was unascertained. The number of schools was 214, of which twenty-five containing 1623 pupils, were maintained by grants of public money; twenty-nine, containing 1707 pupils, by voluntary contributions; the remaining 160 schools, containing 5527 pupils, were wholly supported by the fees paid by the parents or guardians of those receiving instruction. The diocesan school for the see of Kildare is held in Naas. The head master receives a salary of £60 per annum from the bishop, in addition to the pupils' fees. The lands are very unequally portioned out. There are a few large estates. That of the Duke of Leinster extends over nearly one third of the county. Many of the farmers hold large tracts; many others quantities scarcely sufficient for the sustenance of a family. The general average of farms is from 200 to ten acres.
