It stands on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Maine, over which is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> 1000 feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, connecting it with the suburb Etwashausen, both of which are surrounded with walls and ditches, and flanked by towers. It contains four churches, a convent, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and 784 houses, with 3850 inhabitants. It is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trading places on the river, with good wharfs and cranes. It has some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cotton, but its chief <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is wood, wine, corn, and other productions of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>.

KITTOOR

Pages 752-752

a town and district in the peshwa's territories, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bejaapoor, twenty miles southeast from Merritch. In 1804 the renter of the district complained that it was wasted by the neighbouring feudatories, and also by the peshwa's own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>; when, by the interference of the British, these grievances were redressed. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile.

KIU-TCHEOU-FOU

Pages 752-752

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in Tchekiang, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, situated on a fine river. It borders both on Kiangsee and Fotchien, from which last it is separated by a range of very rugged <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the ascent to which is by stairs. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 118. 39. E. Lat. 29. 2. N.

KIUN-CHEU-FOU

Pages 752-752

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAINAN">Hainan</a>. It has a port at two miles distance, formed by a river, and much frequented by Chinese vessels. It has also a considerable trade.

KIUTAIHA

Pages 752-752

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Anatolia. It is situated at the foot and partly up the sides of a cluster of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, bounded by a fertile plain on the south. It covers a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground. The houses are large and well furnished, and it contains handsome fountains conveyed from the hills by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>. It is not so populous as it was formerly, but it still contains between 50,000 and 60,000 inhabitants, of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 10,000 are Armenians, and 5000 Greeks. It contains thirty public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, fifty mosques, four Armenian and one Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and twenty caravanserais. It occupies the position of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Cotyceum, on the site of which there are still the ruins of a castle. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29. 52. E. Lat. 39. 25. N.

KIZILBACHES

Pages 752-752

a people of Asiatic Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Orenburg. They are not numerous, and consist chiefly of Persians who have been taken captive by the Kirghisses.

KIZILERMAK

Pages 752-752

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, which has its rise from Mount Argish, near Kaisarieh, and, after flowing a considerable space westwards, turns to the south, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> about forty miles south of Klaproth Samsoon, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 36. 10. E. lat. 41. 30. N. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>, and is the finest river in Asia Minor.

KIZILOZIEN

Pages 752-752
or golden stream, a considerable river of Persia, which is the natural boundary between the provinces of Irak and Azerbijan. According to Rennell, it is the Gozan of the Scripture, and has its source eight or nine miles to the north-west of Sennah in Kurdistan. It runs along the north-west frontier of Irak, and passes under the Kafatan Koh, or mountain of tigers, when it is met a few miles to the east of Meanna by the Karanku, which takes its rise to the westward of that town, in the mountains of Sahund. These two rivers combined force a passage through the great range of the Caucasus, and during their course form a junction with the Shahrood, a river formed by two streams, one of which comes from the vicinity of Cazween, and the other from the mountain of Elburz, behind Teheran. The collective waters, under the designation of Sifeed Rood, or White River, so named from the foam occasioned by the rapidity of its current, flows in a meandering course through Ghilan to the Caspian Sea.

KIZLAR

Pages 752-752

a fortified town and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, in Asiatic Russia. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEREK">Terek</a>, near its entrance into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It carries on a considerable trade, being a sort of entrepot for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Astrakan with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and the interior of the Caucasus. It exports considerable quantities of wine, brandy, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; also the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of sesamus, which answers the same purpose as the oil of olives. It was built in 1736, and is always garrisoned by two battalions, composed of the tribes who wander over the immense steppe between Kizlar and Astrakan. They are chiefly Nogays, Troukhmen, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KALMUCKS">Kalmucks</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 46. 29. E. Lat. 43. 31. N.

KLAGENFURT

Pages 752-752

a circle of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Illyria, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and the east by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEYERMARK">Steyermark</a>, on the south by Laybach, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VILLACH">Villach</a>. It extends over 1944 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cities with their suburbs, fourteen market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 1626 villages and hamlets, having 27,337 houses, and 163,759 inhabitants. It is generally a mountainous district, containing very lofty peaks and ridges, but having between them many valleys beautifully picturesque and highly fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> which gives its name to the circle. Near to it is a lake whose waters form the river Glan, on whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> it is built, and whence the northern canal is supplied with its <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is an open town, well built, containing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches, two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, an ursuline convent, and orphan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, besides an established lyceum and gymnasium, with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and physic. It contains 778 houses, and 9840 inhabitants, of whom some are employed in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of fine cloth, cotton goods, silks, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 55. 57. E. Lat. 46. 12. N.

KLAPROTH

Pages 752-752

Martin Heney, a celebrated Prussian chemist, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, member of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, foreign associate of the Institute of France, and of several other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and learned <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, was born at Berlin, on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1743. He had received from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> an observing, serious, reflecting mind, and a capacity of patient application which nothing could tire out <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> exhaust. After having terminated his classical studies, he applied himself wholly to that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a>, for which he had a decided predilection; but he felt that he could not make rapid progress therein without calling in the aid of chemistry, wherefore he devoted himself to these two branches of physical science. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of minerals appeared to him of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> importance with re-

KLEIST

Pages 752-753

EDWARD CHRISTIADEN, a German poet, and a soldier of distinguished bravery; was born at Zeblin, in Pomerania, in 1715. At <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was sent to pursue his studies at Cron, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; and he afterwards studied at Dantzig and Königsberg. Having finished his studies, he went to visit his relations in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, who invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there; and having in vain endeavoured to obtain preferment in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, at twenty-one years of age he accepted of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> in the Danish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He then applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of all the sciences that have a relation to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, with the same assiduity as he had before studied civil law. In 1740, at the beginning of the reign of Frederick <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Mr de Kleist went to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and was presented to his majesty, who made him <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry's regiment; and he was in all the campaigns which distinguished the first five years of the king of Prussia's reign. In 1749 he obtained the post of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; and in that year he published his poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>. Before the breaking out of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the king chose him, with some other officers at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POTSDAM">Potsdam</a>, as companions to the young prince Frederic William of Prussia, and to eat at his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>, in 1756, he was nominated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> of Hausen's regiment, which being in garrison at Leipsic, he had <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to finish several new poems. After the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Rossbach, the king gave him, by an order in his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, the inspection of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> established at Leipsic. On this occasion his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> was celebrated by the sick and wounded of both parties, and his disinterestedness was equally admired by all the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In 1758, Prince Henry coming to Leipsic, Mr de Kleist desired to serve in his army with the regiment of Hausen, which was readily granted. Opportunities of distinguishing himself could not be wanting under that great officer, and he always communicated his courage to the battalion under his command. He also served that prince at the beginning of the campaign of 1759, when he was with him in Franconia, and in all the expeditions of that army, till he was detached with the troops under General de Fink to join the king's army. On the 12th of August was fought the bloody battle of Kunnersdorf, in which he fell. His poems, which are greatly admired, are printed in the German tongue, in two volumes 8vo.

KLINOMETER

Pages 753-754
or Clinometer (from ξενος, which denotes inclination, and μετρος), the name of an instrument contrived by the late Lord Webb Seymour, a nobleman who devoted his life to the cultivation of science. This instrument is intended to be used by the geologist for measuring the inclination of stratified rocks, and the azimuth in which that inclination lies. If a plummet-level be applied to an inclined ass="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLANE">plane in that position in which the edge or base of the plummet-level is horizontal, and if the edge of the plummet-level be then turned round ninety degrees in the inclined plane, the angle formed by the plumb-line with the line which is perpendicular to the edge of the plummet-level is equal to the inclination of the inclined line to the horizon. On the same principle the inclination of a plane to the horizon is measured by the clinometer. In the clinometer represented at Plate XCIV. fig. 1, AC is a circular plate, the circumference of which is divided into 360 degrees; it has three short feet on its under surface, one of which is seen at S. The feet on the under side of the plate are of wood, which is preferred to metal, as less liable to slip when placed on an inclined surface. The ends of the feet are in a plane parallel to the upper surface of the circular plate. The fibre of the wood is set perpendicular to the plate, to diminish the derangement which may happen by the expansion of the wood from moisture. The arm CG is moveable round the centre of the circular plate. D is an oval hole, through which is moveable the catch of a sliding bolt; this bolt passes on the under side of the circular plate; the catch of the bolt is made flush with the surface of the circular plate. The bolt serves to fix the arm CG on the circular plate. When the instrument is to be used, C is the axis round which the arm CG turns. When the three short feet of the circular plate are placed on the inclined surface of a stratified rock, the arm which bears the spirit level EE is moved down to the lowest point of the quadrant DD, and the arm CG is moved round till the bubble stands in the middle of the level; the arm CG and the level are then in the intersection of the inclined stratum with a plane parallel to the horizon: the degree on the edge of the circular plate at which the arm CG now stands is noted, and the arm CG is to be moved round through ninety degrees of the circular plate upwards; when the arm CG is arrived at this second position, it is in the line of the greatest inclination of the stratified rock. The arm which bears the spirit level EE is then to be raised, by turning it on the centre of the quadrant; and when the bubble stands in the middle of the level, the arm will indicate, on the limb of the quadrant, the degree of inclination of the stratified rock. The magnetic needle in the box OO will, at the same time, show the magnetic azimuth, formed by the vertical plane, which contains the angle of greatest inclination; and this magnetic azimuth is to be converted into true azimuth by applying the number of degrees that the needle varies from the true meridian, at the particular time and place where the observation is made. The box OO has both the top and the bottom made of glass, so that the needle may be observed both when the instrument is placed on the upper surface, and when the instrument is applied to the under surface, of an inclined plane. When the instrument is not in use, the arm CG, with the quadrant and compass, are unfixed, and taken off from the circular plate, by withdrawing the catch of the bolt which is seen at d. The compass-box OO is turned round an axis, which is seen below the spirit level EE, so that the compass-box comes into the same plane with the quadrant, and then the quadrant, compass-box, and arm, CG, pack into a flat box. The circular plate ACS is now separate from the other parts of the instrument, and lies flat in another part of the box made for packing the instrument. Lord Webb Seymour's account of this instrument is published in the Transactions of the Geological Society, vol. iii. 1816.

KLOPPENBURG

Pages 754-754

a circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Oldenburg, in Germany. It extends over 612 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and contains one town and fifteen parishes, with 5023 houses, and 26,964 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, of the same name, is situated on the river Soste, containing 151 houses, and 860 inhabitants; but the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 4790.

KLOPSTOCK

Pages 754-754

Frederic Theophilus, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-QUEDLINBURG">Quedlinburg</a> in 1724, and one of the most celebrated of the German poets. His father was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an elevated character, and a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, who afterwards farmed a bailiwick in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>. Klopstock was the oldest of eleven children, and having received the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at home, he was put to the public school of Quedlinburg, where he soon became conspicuous both for bodily and mental exercises. He went to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the same place at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixteen, where, under the tuition of an able teacher, he obtained a knowledge of, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for, the beauties of the best classical authors. He composed some pastorals in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and even at this early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he conceived the bold <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> an epic poem, fixing at length, after much deliberation, on the Messiah, by which he has rendered his name immortal. He commenced the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at the University of Jena, in the year 1745, although in his retirement he was constantly ruminating on his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> projected <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> already mentioned, sketching out the three first cantos. They were first written in prose, as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of German verse did not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> with his own sentiments. Transported with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s strains, he determined to make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of German hexameters, in which he succeeded so entirely to his own satisfaction, that he fixed upon this majestic verse for the whole of his poem. By his removal from Jena to Leipzig in 1746, he became acquainted with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young votaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, who occasionally published their essays in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> called the Bremen Contributions, in which appeared the three cantos of Klopstock's Messiah, and a number of his odes, for which he was so applauded as to animate him to persevere. He quitted Leipzig in 1748, and resided at Langensalza, where he carried on a fruitless correspondence with a beautiful young lady, who discovered no inclination to return his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, which for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> threw a gloom over his mind. He now published ten books of his Messiah, by which he came to be known and admired all over Germany. It was an extremely popular work amongst all those who were at once the lovers of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. It was quoted from the pulpit by young divines, whilst others of a more stern deportment found fault with the author, as indulging too much in fiction on sacred topics. He travelled into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in 1750, to pay a visit to Bodmer of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an invitation, and was received with every token of respect. The sublime scenery of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the simplicity of its inhabitants, and the freedom they enjoyed, were admirably suited to the taste and sentiments of Klopstock. Here in all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> he would have breathed his last, had not Baron Bernstorff, who was charmed with his poetry, engaged <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Molke, after returning from France to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, to invite him to that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with assurances of such a pension as would make him independent. Our author accordingly set out for Copenhagen in the year 1751, by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, at which latter place he became acquainted with a young lady, Miss Moller, of literary abilities, and a heart susceptible of tender impressions. They were soon afterwards married, and seemed destined by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> to be one of the happiest couples upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but he was early deprived of her, for she died in childbed, and her <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was sacred to Klopstock to the last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his existence. He lived for the most part at Copenhagen till the year 1771, after which he resided at Hamburg in the capacity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> Danish legate, and counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, who gave him a pension, and engaged him to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the year 1775 at his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CARLSRUHE">Carlsruhe</a>. Such was the diffidence of our poet, that it required the most extraordinary condescension on the part of the great to make him easy in their presence. The decline of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> made no change on the habitual tranquillity of his mind; he contemplated his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> without any dismay, and his pious fortitude <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> unshaken amidst the severest sufferings. He died at Hamburg in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1803, being then seventy-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of age, and his funeral was attended with such honours as justly belonged to the greatest poet of the country. The character of Klopstock as a poet is that of exuberance of imagination and sentiment. His sublimity, which is nearly unparalleled, makes him almost lose himself in mystical extravagance. A great critic claims for the author of the Messiah a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> amongst the very first class of poets. His odes and lyric poems are much admired by his countrymen; and his dramatic works display great force and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, but are thought to be better adapted to the closet than the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. He was also an excellent prose writer, as is fully evinced by his Grammatical Dialogues.

KLOSTERNEUBURG

Pages 754-754

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Lower Ens. It is situated on the river Danube, and walled; but the fortifications are dilapidated. It is chiefly remarkable from an establishment for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, which is still maintained, consisting of seventeen professors, with a library of 25,000 volumes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. The houses are 479, with 3400 inhabitants.

KNAPSAK

Pages 754-755

in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a rough leathern bag which a soldier carries on his back, and which contains all his necessaries. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a> knapsacks are most convenient, and should be made with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> to hold the shoes and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> separate from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>.

KNARESBOROUGH

Pages 755-755

a town of the west riding of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WAPENTAKE">wapentake</a> of Claro, 215 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, and 202 by York. It is situated on the side of a hill, almost surrounded by the river Nidd. It was formerly fortified, and had a castle built in the reign of William the Conqueror. It was a burgage <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> borough, and sent two members to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, who are now chosen by the ten-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-keepers. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture, which is extensive. Near the town are some mineral <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of medicinal virtue, but they are not much resorted to. A dropping well, with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> petrifying power, is a curiosity, about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the town. There is a market on Wednesday, which is well attended; and there are eight <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, at which much business is transacted. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 3388, in 1811 to 4234, in 1821 to 5263, and in 1831 to 5296.

KNAVE

Pages 755-755

an old Saxon word, which had at first a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of simplicity and innocence, for it signified a boy: Sax. knapa, whence a knave child, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> a boy, distinguished from a girl, in several old writers; afterwards it was taken for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> boy, and at length for any servant <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>. It was also applied to a minister or officer who bore the shield or weapon of his superior; as field knapa, whom the Latins call armiger, and the French escuyer (14 Edw. III. c. 3). And it was sometimes of old made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> addition, as Joannes C. filius Wilhelmi C. de <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, knave (22 Hen. VII. c. 37). The word is now perverted to the hardest meaning, viz. a false, deceitful fellow.

KNEE

Pages 755-755

in a ship, a crooked piece of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, having two branches <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> arms, and generally used to connect the beams of a ship with her sides or timbers. The branches of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> form an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of greater or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, according to the mutual situation of the pieces which they are designed to unite. Knee of the Head, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, flat piece of timber, fixed edgewise upon the fore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a ship's stem, and supporting the ornamental <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or image placed under the bowsprit. The knee of the head is a phrase peculiar to shipwrights, as this piece is always called the cut-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> by seamen, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except a few, who, affecting to be wiser than their brethren, have adopted this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, probably on the presumption that the other is a cant phrase or vulgarism. Carling Knees, in a ship, those timbers which extend from the ship to the hatchway, and bear up the deck on both sides.

KNELLER

Pages 755-755

Sir Godfrey, a painter whose fame is well established in these kingdoms. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a> in 1648, and received his first instructions in the school of Rembrandt, but became afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Ferdinand Bol. When he had gained as much knowledge as that school afforded him, he travelled to Rome, where he fixed his particular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on Titian and the Caracci. He afterwards visited <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and distinguished himself so effectually in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> by his historical pictures and his portraits of the noble families there, that his reputation became considerable in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. By the advice of some friends he came at last to England, where it was his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Monmouth, by whose recommendation he more than once painted the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, who was so pleased with his skill in doing it, that he came to come and sit to him at his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Covent Garden <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Lely left him without a competitor in England, and from that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> his fortune and fame were thoroughly establish- ed. No painter could have more incessant employment, and no painter could be more distinguished by public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He was state painter to Charles II, James II, William III, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, and George I, and equally esteemed and respected by them all. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Leopold made him a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the Roman empire, and King George I created him a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a>. Most of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry had their likenesses taken by him; and no painter excelled him in a sure outline, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> in the graceful disposition of his figures. His works were celebrated by the best poets in his time. He built an elegant house at Whitton, near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, where he spent the latter <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and died in 1726.

KNIEPHAUSEN

Pages 755-755

a district, formerly an independent sovereign state, but now a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Oldenburg, in Germany. During the late <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> the greater <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Dutch vessels were rendered neutral by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of this district, and under the colours of Kniephausen were received in the English ports. It contains two parishes, with three churches, a strong castle, and 590 houses, with 3800 inhabitants. Though ceded to Oldenburg when mediatised, Count Bentick, the sovereign, has protested against the cession, and still maintains his claim to the dominion.

KNIFE

Pages 755-755

a well-known <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, and adapted in form to the uses for which it is designed. Knives are said to have been first made in England in 1563, by one Matthews, on Fleet <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The importation of all sorts of knives is prohibited.

KNIGHT

Pages 755-756

amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a person of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, following immediately that of the senators. Knight (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Cnecht, Germ.), in feudal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was originally an appellation or <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans to their youth after being admitted to the privilege of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms. See Chivalry. There is scarcely a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> who has not thought fit to institute an order of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>; and the simple title of knight, which the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> confer on private subjects, is a derivation from ancient chivalry, although very remote from its source. Knight-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">Service</a> (servitium militare, and in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> French chivalry), a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of feudal <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>. The knights created by this tenure differed most essentially from the knights of chivalry, though the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> seems not to have been accurately attended to by authors. The one class of knights was of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity, the other was not heard of till the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a fee. The adorning with arms and the blow of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> made the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of the ancient knight; the new knight was constituted by an investment in a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The former was the member of an order of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> which had particular privileges and distinctions; the latter was the receiver of a feudal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>. Knighthood was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, knight-service a tenure. The first communicated splendour to an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the last gave it strength and numbers. The knight of honour might serve in any station whatever, the knight of tenure was in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a soldier. By the tenure of knight-service the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the lands in England were helden, and that principally of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, till the middle of the seventeenth century; and it was created, as Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> expressly testifies, for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> purpose, viz. for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the realm by the king's own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subjects, which was judged to be much better than to trust to hirelings or foreigners. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> here given is that of knight-service proper, which was to attend the king in his wars. There were also some other species of knight-service, so called, though improperly, because the service or render was of a free and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and equally uncertain as to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of rendering as that of knight-service. proper, and because they were attended with similar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and consequences. Such was the tenure by *<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> serjeanty*, *per magnum servitium*, whereby the tenant was bound, instead of serving the king generally in his wars, to do some special honorary service to the king in person, as to carry his banner, his sword, or the like, or be his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">butler</a>, champion, or other officer, at his coronation. It was, in most other respects, like knight-service, only he was not bound to pay aid or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ESCUAGE">escuage</a>; and when tenant by knight-service paid five pounds for a relief on every knight's fee, tenant by grand serjeanty paid one year's value of his land, were it much or little. Tenure by *cornage*, which was to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORN">horn</a> when the Scotch or other enemies entered the land, in order to warn the king's subjects, was, like other services of the same nature, a species of grand serjeanty. These services, both of chivalry and grand serjeanty, were all personal, and uncertain as to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. But the personal attendance in knight-service growing troublesome and inconvenient in many respects, the tenants found means of compounding for it, by first sending others in their stead, and in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time making a pecuniary satisfaction to the lords in lieu of it. By the degenerating of knight-service, or personal military duty, into escuage or pecuniary assessments, all the advantages, either promised or real, of the feudal constitutions were destroyed, and nothing but the hardships remained. Instead of forming a national <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> composed of barons, knights, and gentlemen, bound by their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, their honour, and their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, to defend their king and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the whole of this system of tenures now tended to nothing else but a wretched means of raising <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to pay an army of occasional mercenaries. The military tenures, with all their heavy appendages, were at length destroyed at one blow, by the statute 12 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. c. 24; a statute which was a greater acquisition to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> than even *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>* itself, since that only pruned the luxuriances which had grown out of the military tenures, and thereby preserved them in vigour; but the statute of King Charles extirpated the whole, and demolished both root and branches. **Knights-Errant.** During the prevalence of chivalry, the ardour of redressing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a> seized many knights so powerfully, that, attended by esquires, they wandered about in search of objects whose misfortunes and misery required their assistance and succour. And as ladies engaged more particularly their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, the relief of unfortunate damsels was the achievement they most courted. This gave birth to knights-errant, whose adventures produced romances. These were originally told as they happened. But the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the marvellous came to interfere; fancy was indulged in the wildest exaggerations; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LENT">lent</a> her charms to the most monstrous fictions, and to scenes the most unnatural and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a>. **Knights,** in a ship, two short, thick pieces of wood, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> carved like a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head, having four shivers in each, three for the hauylards, and one for the top to run in. One of them stands fast bolted on the beams abaft the foremast, and is therefore called the *fore-knight*; and the other, standing abaft the mainmast, is called the *main-knight*. **Knight's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>,** in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>, the largest of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THREE_ISLANDS">three <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called the Snares by Vancouver. It was discovered in 1791. The south point is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 166. 44. E. Lat. 48. 15. S. **Knighthood,** a military order or honour, or a mark or degree of ancient nobility, or reward of personal virtue and merit. There are four kinds of knighthood; military, regular, honorary, and social. **Military Knighthood** is that of the ancient knights, who acquired it by high feats of arms. They are called *milites* in ancient charters and titles, by which they were distinguished from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> bachelors, and others. These knights were girt with a sword, and wore a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of gilt spurs; whence they were called *equites aurati*. Knighthood is not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, but acquired. It does not come into the world with a man, like nobility, nor can it be revoked. **Regular Knighthood** is applied to all military orders which profess to wear some particular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. Such were the knights <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEMPLARS">templars</a>, and such also the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. **Honorary Knighthood** is that which princes confer on other princes, and even on their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ministers and favourites; such are knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>, Bath, St Patrick, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, Thistle, and the like. **Social Knighthood** is that which is not fixed or confirmed by any formal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, nor regulated by any lasting statutes; of which kind many orders have been erected on occasion of factions, of tilts and tournaments, masquerades, and the like. **<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol9.html#article-KNIGHTON">Knighton</a>,** a market-town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Radnor, and hundred of its own name, in South <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. It is a well-built town, on the side of a hill, overlooked by a lofty mountain. An old intrenchment, called Ossa Dyke, which extends from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, runs at the bottom of the town, and is said to have formed the boundary between England and Wales. There is a market, which is held on Thursday. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 785, in 1811 to 952, in 1821 to 1000, and in 1831 to 1076. **Knittlingen,** a market-town of the bailiwick of Maulbronn, and circle of the Neckar, in the kingdom of Wirtemberg. It contains 304 houses and 2380 inhabitants. **Knolles, Richard,** was born in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a> about the middle of the sixteenth century, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, after which he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the free school at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. He composed *Grammatica Latina, Graeca, et Hebraica, compendium, cum ridiculos*, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1606, and sent many excellent scholars to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. He also spent twelve years in compiling a history of the Turks, which was first printed in 1610. It is called the General History of the Turks, from the first beginning of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to the rising of the Ottoman family. He died in 1610, and this history has been since <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; but the best continuation is that by Paul Ricaut, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, folio, London, 1680. Knolles wrote also the Lives and Conquests of the Ottoman Kings and Emperors to the year 1610, which was not printed till after his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1621, to which time it was continued by another <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and, lastly, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">Brief</a> Discourse of the greatness of the Turkish empire, and wherein the greatness of the strength thereof consisteth. **Knout,** the name of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted in Russia, with a kind of whip called *knout*, and made of a long strap of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> prepared for this purpose. With this whip the executioners dexterously carry off a slip of skin from the neck to the bottom of the back, laid bare to the waist, and, repeating their blows, in a little while rend away all the skin of the back in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> stripes. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> knout the criminal receives the lashes suspended on the back of one of the executioners; but in the great knout the criminal is raised into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> by means of a pulley fixed to the gallows, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CORD">cord</a> fastened to the two wrists tied together; a piece of wood is placed between his two legs also tied together; and another of a crucial form under his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. Sometimes his hands are tied behind his back; and when he is pulled up in this position his shoulders are dislocated. The executioners can make this punishment more or less severe; and, it is said, are so dextrous, that when a criminal is condemned to die, they can make him expire at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, either by one or several lashes.

KNOX

Pages 756-764

John, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reformer of Scotland, was born at the village of Gifford in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HADDINGTONSHIRE">Haddingtonshire</a> in the year 1505. His father is said, though perhaps without foundation, to have been descended from the family of Ranferly, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. The name of his mother was Sinclair; and some of his letters, written in seasons of danger, were subscribed John Sinclair. Whatever might be the lineage <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the situation of the father, the son was enabled to obtain the benefit of a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, such as his native <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> could then afford. After having been instructed in the Latin <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HADDINGTON">Haddington</a> school, he was in the year 1521 sent to the university of Glasgow, where <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> were taught by John Mair, a celebrated schoolman. The Greek and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> languages were not then publicly taught in Scotland; but the former of these he acquired when he was yet in the vigour of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the latter during the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his continental exile. It is not sufficiently ascertained that he took a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; but <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be correctly stated that he publicly taught philosophy in this university, and afterwards at St Andrews, we are perhaps to infer that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. He soon felt himself dissatisfied with the dry and barren speculations of scholastic philosophy and scholastic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and was gradually conducted to a more edifying course of enquiry. Not contented, as his excellent and lamented biographer has stated, with the extracts "from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors, which he found in the writings of the scholastic divines and canonists, he resolved to have recourse to the original works." In them he found a method of investigating and communicating <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, to which he had hitherto been a stranger, and the simplicity of which recommended itself to his mind, in spite of the prejudices of education, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of superior attainments in his own favourite art. Among the fathers of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, Jerom and Augustine attracted his particular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. By the writings of the former, he was led to the Scriptures as the only pure fountain of divine truth, and instructed in the utility of studying them in the original languages. In the works of the latter, he found <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sentiments very opposite to those taught in the Romish church, who, while she retained his name as a saint in her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, had banished his doctrine, as heretical, from her pulpits. From this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he renounced the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of scholastic theology; and although not yet completely emancipated from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, his mind was fitted for improving the means which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> had prepared, for leading him to a fuller and more comprehensive view of the system of evangelical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. It was about the year 1535 when this favourable change commenced; but it does not appear that he professed himself a protestant before the year 1542. The reformed doctrines had been preached to his benighted countrymen by Patrick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Ferne, who was allied to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, and who had the higher <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being the proto-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> of Scotland to the protestant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. On the last of February 1528, he was most inhumanly committed to the flames in the archiepiscopal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of St Andrews. But the seed which he had thus moistened with his blood, sprung from the ground with a degree of vigour which the foulest blasts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> were found incapable of withering. The new opinions were gradually adopted by men of learning as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Between the years 1530 and 1540, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of victims was doomed to a cruel <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, while others escaped the fangs of their persecutors, and sought refuge in England and on the continent. Several of these exiles, and among the rest George Buchanan and Alexander Aless, were men distinguished by their talents and learning, who obtained pre-ferment in foreign <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and there reflected <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> on their native country. During those times of persecution, Knox was engaged in teaching philosophy in the university of St Andrews, though it does not clearly appear that he held the office of a regent or professor. Several individuals of his acquaintance had embraced the reformed doctrines; the force of truth gradually affected his own mind, and he arrived at complete conviction in the year 1542, having then attained the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of thirty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. As he began to recommend to his pupils a more rational and edifying method of study, he excited some suspicions of heretical pravity; but when he proceeded so far as to expose certain corruptions of the church, he speedily found it necessary to change his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of residence. Having retired to the south of Scotland, and there avowed his adherence to the cause of reformation, he was declared a heretic, and was degraded from his orders. Nor was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Beaton satisfied with this more canonical form of procedure: he employed assassins to co-operate in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of supporting the church, but his intended victim found shelter and protection in his native country, under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of Hugh Douglas of Longniddry, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had adopted the same opinions. Here he was retained in the capacity of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; and the son of another protestant, John Cockburn of Orniston, was likewise committed to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He communicated religious instruction, not only to his pupils, but also to the other members of the family, and to the people of the immediate neighbourhood. He was accustomed to catechise them in a chapel at Longniddry, and there at stated times to read and explain a portion of the Scriptures. When religious instruction was so scanty, and access to the fountain of sacred knowledge so difficult, the services of so faithful a labourer must have been of no small value. About this period, he received a new impulse from the public and private instructions of George Wishart, who returned to his native country in the year 1544. He had been driven into exile by the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BRECHIN">Brechin</a>, for the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a> lectures on the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>, and during several years had resided in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. "Excelling all his countrymen at that period in learning, of the most persuasive eloquence, irreproachable in life, courteous and affable in manners, his fervent piety, zeal, and courage in the cause of truth, were tempered with uncommon meekness, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. In his tour of preaching through Scotland, he was usually accompanied by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gentry; and the people, who flocked to hear him, were ravished with his discourses. To this teacher Knox attached himself, and profited greatly by his sermons and private instructions. During the last visit which Wishart paid to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>, Knox waited constantly on his person, and bore the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, which was carried before him from the time that an attempt was made to assassinate him in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>. Wishart was highly pleased with the zeal of his faithful attendant, and seems to have presaged his future usefulness, at the same time that he laboured under a strong presentiment of his own approaching martyrdom." Wishart was brought to the stake at St Andrews on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1546, and his persecutor, the blood-stained cardinal, was not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> permitted to survive. On the 29th of the ensuing May, he was surprised in his castle by a small and resolute band of conspirators, whom his misdeeds had roused to acts of desperation. Having put him to death, they kept possession of his strong-hold, and procuring assistance from England, they sustained a regular siege from an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> collected by the regent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>. Many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a>, who had no participation in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, sought refuge in the castle; and among these were Sir <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Lindsay and Henry Balnaves, whose names are familiarly known to all who are acquainted with the literary his- --- M'Crie's Life of Knox, vol. i. p. 41, 6th edit. Edinb. 1831, 2 vols. 8vo. Knox, being among the number of the proscribed, was persuaded by Douglas and Cockburn to follow the example. He was accompanied by his pupils, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his religious as well as his literary instructions. In the chapel of the castle, he read lectures on portions of the Scriptures; and so favourable an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was formed of his talents and attainments, that he was earnestly solicited to officiate as the colleague of John Rough, chaplain to the garrison. It was not without much reluctance that he obeyed the call; but having undertaken this office, he acquitted himself with equal ability and zeal. He occasionally preached in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church, as well as in the chapel of the castle, and the popish clergy were at length roused to some degree of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-exertion: it was arranged that the most learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> and university should every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> preach in their turn, partly with the view of excluding the protestant ministers from the pulpit, and partly with that of conciliating the affections of the people, whose edification they had too long disregarded. Knox and his colleague were summoned to a public disputation, held in the presence of Winram the sub-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a>, who was <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>-general during the vacancy of the see, and who was secretly inclined to the reformed doctrines. He did not himself enter into much discussion, and he was very feebly supported by a Franciscan friar, named Arbuckle, who was finally driven to the desperate averment "that the apostles had not received the Holy Ghost when they wrote the epistles, but they afterwards received it, and ordained ceremonies." It was more easy for this father to abandon the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of the holy Scriptures, than to relinquish the vain ceremonies of the church: so customary has it generally been for mankind to adore the bungling <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. During the short period of his ministrations at St Andrews, many of the citizens renounced the errors of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, and publicly testified the change of their religious opinions, by partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> according to the rite of the reformed church. But the protestants could not long retain possession of the castle. At the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1547, a considerable reinforcement arrived from France, and enabled the regent to invest the place by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>: the garrison made a brave resistance, but after an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> was reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of accepting terms of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> from Leo Strozzi, the commander of the foreign auxiliaries. It was stipulated that their lives should be spared, that they should be removed to France, and that such of them as declined entering into the French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> should be conveyed to any other country except Scotland. Rough had previously emigrated to England, and there he suffered martyrdom in the year 1557. Knox, sharing the fate of his companions, was conveyed on board one of the French ships, which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>; but the terms of the capitulation were grossly violated, and, at the instigation of the pope and the Scotish clergy, they were treated as prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The principal gentlemen were committed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> custody in Rouen, Cherbourg, Brest, and Mont St Michael; while Knox and some others were sent on board the galleys, and after being loaded with chains, were compelled to labour at the oar. Here they were subjected to many other indignities; but in spite of every hardship and every threat, not one of their number could be impelled to renounce his faith. During the ensuing winter, the galley in which he was confined lay in the river <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1548, it sailed for Scotland, and during a considerable period lingered on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, for the purpose of intercepting English vessels. The hardships to which he was now subjected produced a very serious effect upon his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: he was seized with a violent fever, and no hope was entertained of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. He however regained his strength, and during his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> had sufficient energy of mind to compose more than one religious treatise. His treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, written during this season of affliction, was afterwards published. Having endured a captivity of nineteen months, he was restored to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in February 1549. Of the circumstances which led to this event, various accounts have been given; but according to Dr M'Crie, "it is more than probable that he owed his deliverance to the comparative indifference with which he and his brethren were now regarded by the French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, who, having procured the consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Scotland to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> to the dauphin, and obtained possession of her person, felt no longer any inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the quarrels of the Scottish clergy." Knox immediately directed his course to England, where his merits and his sufferings were neither unknown nor unregarded. Soon after he made his appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he received an appointment to officiate at Berwick, where he began to preach with his characteristic fervour and zeal. He exposed the errors of popery with an unsparing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and his labours seem to have been attended with no inconsiderable success. The tendency of his zeal was not however calculated to recommend him to the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, Dr Tonstall, who, although a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of elegant learning, was deeply infected with the ancient superstition. Having been accused of asserting that the sacrifice of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> is idolatrous, the preacher was cited to appear at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> on the 4th of April 1550, before the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, and to give an account of his doctrine. This prelate was attended by several of his clergy, as well as by various laymen, and a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> number of spectators was attracted by the peculiar circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. Knox entered into a copious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his opinions, and with the utmost boldness proceeded to demonstrate that the mass is a superstitious and idolatrous substitute for the genuine sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. The bishop, though he probably listened with surprize and indignation, did not venture to inflict any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> censure; and the fame of the obnoxious preacher was extended by this attempt to restrain the boldness of his attacks on the errors of the falling church. Having remained at Berwick till the close of the year, he was afterwards removed to Newcastle. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1551, he was appointed one of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward's chaplains in ordinary, with an annual salary of forty pounds, which at that period was no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> provision. The chaplains were six in number; two of whom were to be in constant residence at court, while the other four were employed in preaching in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In the course of this year, the Book of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> Prayer was subjected to a revision, of which it stood in considerable need; and Knox having been consulted among other divines, was chiefly instrumental in procuring a material <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the communion service, which at first was too favourable to the doctrine of the real presence. One deep vestige of this doctrine is still preserved in the kneeling posture of the communicants, which manifestly derives its origin from the popish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOST">host</a>. The freedom of his discourses in the pulpit gave offence to various individuals, and among others to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, warden general of the northern marches; and having been accused of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> misdemeanours, he was cited to appear before the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, which at that period possessed an extensive and ill-defined jurisdiction. But the malice of his enemies was altogether ineffectual, and this call to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> was followed by consequences very different from those which they anticipated. He was fully cleared from every imputation of blame; and having been employed to preach at court, he made so favourable an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the young king that he expressed his anxiety to promote him in the church. It was resolved by the council that during the following year he should preach in London and the southern counties. Having returned for a short time to Newcastle, he accordingly repaired to the metropolis in the beginning of April 1553. Archbishop Cranmer had previously been directed by the council to present him to the rectory of All-Hallows; but Knox declared that in the existing state of the church he could not conscientiously accept of any preferment. He was again summoned before the council, where he gave an unreserved explanation of his sentiments on that subject. Nor could the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of much higher promotion induce him to disregard the admonitions of a scrupulous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>: the king, with the advice of his council, made him an offer of a bishopric; but instead of availing himself of so favourable an avenue to worldly honours, he declared the office of a bishop, as exercised in the English church, to be destitute of divine authority. It is sufficiently evident that he considered that establishment as but imperfectly reformed from the errors of popery; and that, in his estimation, the new prelacy, retaining all the proud trappings, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> character of the old, was very widely removed from the simplicity of an evangelical church.
