The premature death of the king, on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1553, was fatal to the further progress of reformation, and a cloud of spiritual darkness again overshadowed the land. During his residence at Berwick, Knox had formed a lasting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Marjory Bowes. Her father was Richard, the youngest son of Sir Ralph Bowes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STREATHAM">Streatham</a>; her mother was <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and coheiress of Sir Roger Aske of Aske. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was cordially approved by the mother of the young lady, but having been opposed by her father, it was not concluded till after a considerable interval. After the king's death, he had some intention of settling at Berwick, or in the immediate neighbourhood; but he speedily discovered that he could not safely reside in a kingdom ruled by so bigoted and cruel a sovereign. He therefore sailed for France, and landed at Dieppe on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1554. Having lingered there till the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of February, he pursued his solitary way through France, and arrived in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; but in the beginning of the ensuing month of May, he retraced his steps to Dieppe with the view of obtaining intelligence from his friends in England. At that period, the intercourse between different countries was slow and precarious; nor was this the only occasion on which he returned to the same place for the same purpose. While he continued to reside on the continent, he received remittances from his friends in Scotland as well as in England, but his provision was neither certain nor ample. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> became for some time the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> place of his abode, and here his exile was cheered by the friendship of one of the most illustrious men of the age. Calvin had now attained to the summit of his reputation. They embraced the same opinions with respect to the leading doctrines of the Christian faith, and in their personal character they exhibited several conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of resemblance. In their notions of ecclesiastical polity they preserved the same agreement; and the authority of Knox, supported by that of Calvin, has contributed to establish in this country a simple <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and worship, to which our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> adhered with unconquerable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and in support of which many of them were found ready and willing to shed their blood. The leisure which he enjoyed at Geneva was profitably spent in study, to which he devoted himself "with all the ardour of youth, although his age now bordered upon fifty. It seems to have been at this time that he made himself master of the Hebrew language, which he had no opportunity of acquiring in early life." Many pious and learned men had now been driven from England by the unrelenting cruelty of Queen Mary, and most of them sought refuge in the protestant states of Germany and Switzerland. Those who resorted to the imperial city of Frankfort, were allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OCCUPANCY">occupancy</a> of a place of worship; and it was unanimously resolved to discontinue the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the surplice, the litanies, the audible responses, and some other superfluities which might rather excite the surprize than the approbation of their foreign brethren. Having determined to elect three pastors, they sent a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of invitation to Knox, subscribed by twenty-one of their number, at the head of whom stands John <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, the exiled bishop of Ossory. It was not without some degree of reluctance that he consented to leave his retreat at Geneva; he however repaired to Frankfort in the month of November 1554, and entered upon the duties of his new charge, but his connexion with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> proved a source of great uneasiness and mortification. Various dissensions which arose among its members, were chiefly occasioned by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of opinion as to the propriety of adhering to the English service; and those dissensions were greatly fomented by Dr Cox, who had been preceptor to King Edward, and who afterwards became bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>. In the progress of the controversy, Knox appears to have acted with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and moderation, but the ardent votaries of the liturgy were not easily diverted from their purpose; for when all other expedients failed, two of their number, with the approbation of others, sought a private interview with the magistrates, and accused him of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, his son <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, and his aunt the queen of England. This extraordinary charge was founded upon certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his tract published in 1554, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "A Faythfull Admonition unto the Professours of Gods Truthe in England." Of the futility of such an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> the magistrates were sufficiently aware; but they nevertheless deemed it advisable for him to withdraw from Frankfort, and he availed himself of the suggestion which they conveyed to him. On the evening of the 25th of March 1555, he delivered a farewell discourse to about fifty members of the congregation; and on the following day they accompanied him several miles on his journey. He immediately returned to Geneva, and he experienced a cordial welcome from Calvin. There he continued till the month of August, when he again proceeded to Dieppe; and having embarked in a vessel bound for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, he landed near the eastern border of the two kingdoms about the end of autumn. On reaching Berwick, he found his wife and mother living in comfortable circumstances. With them he remained for some time, and afterwards pursued his journey to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he took up his abode with a citizen named John Syme, to whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> the friends of reformation repaired as soon as they were aware of Knox's arrival. Notwithstanding the rigour of the penal laws, the votaries of the protestant cause were not entirely extirpated or dispersed. The queen dowager, Mary of Lorraine, having succeeded in her attempt to supplant the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Arran, had been appointed regent on the 10th of April 1554. She was sufficiently disposed to continue the corruptions of the church, but several prudential considerations restrained her from pursuing more violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. Some of the protestants who were driven from England by the atrocities of Mary, a worthy daughter of Henry the Eighth, were permitted to live in Scotland without molestation, and even to meet, though with some degree of privacy, for the purpose of worshipping God according to the dictates of their own conscience. William <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARLOW">Harlow</a>, who afterwards became minister of St Cuthbert's, is mentioned as the first preacher who returned from the south at this critical period; and, in different parts of the country, he continued his ministrations till the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> establishment of the reformation. His endeavours were ably seconded by John Willock, whom Knox found residing at Edinburgh as an envoy from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> duchess of Friesland; for he had been entrusted with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> for arranging the commercial relations between the two countries. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>, and had originally been a Franciscan friar; but speedily quitting his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> and renouncing the mass-book, he sought refuge in England, where he was appointed chaplain to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>. After the death of the young king, he was again compelled to change his place of residence, and he then settled in the town of Embden, and followed the practice of physic. He thus became known to the duchess, who was favourably inclined to the reformation of religion; and his mission to his native country afforded him peculiar opportunities of promoting that cause in which he felt so deep an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. He became known to the leaders of the protestant party, who privately resorted to him from the desire of religious edification. At this period, few individuals had openly renounced the Romish creed; and of those who were most inclined to the protestant doctrines, very few had ventured to discontinue their attendance at mass. Knox was deservedly scandalized at this want of firmness and consistency: a meeting, attended by William Maitland of Lethington and other leaders of the party, was held for the avowed purpose of discussing the lawfulness of such compliances; and Knox succeeded in his attempt to convince them that all participation in the worship of the Romish church was to be avoided by those who were convinced of her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> errors. Nor were his exertions confined to the metropolis. He accompanied Erskine of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUN">Dun</a> to his seat in the neighbourhood of Montrose; and during a visit of a month he preached every day, being attended by the principal persons of the adjacent district. On his return to the south, we find him residing at Calder-house, the seat of Sir James Sandilands, afterwards Lord Torphichen, an early, zealous, and consistent friend of the reformation. In the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of this baron, who was preceptor in Scotland of the knights of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, he preached and administered the communion. Here his ministrations were attended by several persons of distinction; and among these were Archibald, Lord Lorne, afterwards earl of Argyll, John, Lord Erskine, afterwards earl of Mar, and James Stewart, prior of St Andrews, afterwards earl of Moray; all of whom received religious impressions which influenced the future course of their lives. Early in the subsequent year, 1556, he was accompanied to the district of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KYLE">Kyle</a> by Lockhart of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAR">Bar</a> and Campbell of Kinaneleuch. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Ayrshire had been the principal seat of the Lollards in Scotland, and it then contained many friends of the purer religion. They were not therefore unprepared for his reception: he preached not only in the town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, but likewise in the houses of Bar, Kinaneleuch, Carnell, Ochiltree, and Gadgirth, and in several of these places the holy communion was now dispensed. Before Easter, he paid a visit to Finlayston, the residence of Alexander earl of Glencairn, one of the most strenuous friends of the reformation. In this baronial castle he also preached and administered the sacrament. Returning to Calderhouse, he next determined to visit his friends in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> residence at Dun, he was emboldened to preach in a more public manner. Many gentlemen of that vicinity made an open profession of the reformed faith; and, in order to strengthen their cause, they entered into a solemn engagement to renounce the communion of the popish church, and, to the utmost of their ability, to promote the pure preaching of the gospel. "This," says Dr M'Crie, "seems to have been the first of those religious bonds or covenants, by which the confederation of the protestants in Scotland was so frequently ratified." As he now began to preach more openly, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> felt a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> alarm for the safety of a tottering church; and the friars testified their zeal by urging the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> to proceed with rigour against such an offender. He was accordingly cited to appear before an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the clergy, to be held at Edinburgh in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a> church, on the 15th of May; but when they found that he did not shrink from this discussion, and that he was supported by some persons of influence, they sought a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for superseding the citation, on the ground of its informality. On the very day which had been appointed for his appearance, he preached in the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a>'s house to a much larger auditory than had previously attended him in Edinburgh; and during the ensuing ten days, he regularly preached twice a day in the same place, without being exposed to any molestation. About this period the Earl Marischal attended one of his evening discourses; and it may be regarded as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his favourable impression that he united with the earl of Glencairn in an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> request, that Knox would <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to the queen regent such a letter as might induce her to extend her protection to the protestant preachers. A letter was accordingly addressed to her, and it was delivered by the earl of Glencairn, but it does not appear to have produced any change in her sentiments. This letter he afterwards published, with some additions. In the mean time he received from the English congregation at Geneva an invitation to become one of their pastors. He readily listened to their call, and made arrangements for removing thither, accompanied by his wife, as well as by her mother, who had now lost her husband. He embarked them on board a vessel bound for Dieppe, and paid another visit to the several places where he had disseminated the truth of the gospel. He visited the earl of Argyll at Castle Campbell, and there he repeatedly preached to such an auditory as could be assembled. Having thus made no inconsiderable progress in preparing his countrymen for a more general reception of the reformed doctrines, he took his leave in the month of July 1556, and joining his family at Dieppe, he again directed his course to Geneva. His colleague in his new office was Christopher Goodman, B.D., an Englishman, who afterwards became a clergyman of the church of Scotland. Their congregation chiefly consisted of the exiles who had withdrawn from Frankfort in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the dissensions already mentioned. The two pastors lived together on terms of the greatest cordiality. Knox likewise enjoyed the friendship of Calvin and Beza; and the two years which he spent in this vocation are described as the most tranquil of his public life. At this period was published a directory for worship and discipline, frequently described as the Order of Geneva; but it had been composed at Frankfort by Knox, Whittingham, Fox, Gilby, and T. Cole. The same directory was afterwards adopted by the reformed church of Scotland. When the Scottish clergy were apprized of his having --- 1 Brook's Lives of the Puritans, vol. ii. p. 123. 2 The Forme of Prayers and Ministration of the Sacraments, &c. used in the English Congregation at Geneva, and approved by the famous and godly learned man, John Calvin. Imprinted at Geneva by John Crepsin, 1556, &c. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the volume consists of 93 <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>; which are followed by "One and fifte Psalms of David in English metre, wherof 37 were made by Thomas Sternhold, and the rest by others. Confirmed with the hebrew, and in certain places corrected as the text and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENS">sens</a> of the Prophet required." Next follows "The Catechisme, or manner to teache children the Christian religion, wherein the Minister demandeth the question, and the childe maketh answer." Made by the excellent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> and Pastor in Christes Church, John Calvin." The first Scottish edition, which contains some modifications and considerable alterations, bears the subsequent title: "The Forme of Prayers and Ministration of the Sacraments, &c. used in the English Church at Geneva, approved and received by the Church of Scotland; whereunto besides that was in the former booke, are also added somtric other prayers, with the whole Psalms of David in English metre." Printed at Edinbrugh by Robert Lekprevik, 1565, &c. The Catechisme has a separate title, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of 1564. Of this work there are many other editions, several of which were printed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. One edition is entitled quitted the kingdom, they renewed the citation for his appearance; and those who had no inclination to encounter such a disputant, now found themselves at liberty to proceed against him as a contumacious heretic. He was accordingly condemned to suffer death by fire; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> could not be executed on his person, it was executed on his effigy, which was in due form committed to the flames at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of Edinburgh. From this sentence he prepared an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, which was afterwards printed under the title of "The Appellation of John Knox from the cruel and most unjust sentence pronounced against him by the false Bishopopes and Clergie of Scotland." In the course of the year which followed his return to Geneva, two citizens of Edinburgh, James Syme, and James Baron, were the bearers of an invitation for him to resume his evangelical labours in his native country. They were furnished with credentials from the earl of Glencairn, and the lords Erskine, Lorne, and James Stewart. After consulting Calvin and the other ministers of Geneva, he determined to devote himself to this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and dangerous service; and he again pursued his way to Dieppe, where he arrived in October 1557. He had however the mortification of receiving letters which entirely disconcerted his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; for he was informed that some of the protestants already repented of the invitation which had been sent to him, and that the great body of them seemed to waver in their purpose. He lost no time in addressing a letter to the noblemen who had subscribed the credentials; and it may easily be supposed that he did not fail to upbraid them for their want of firmness and consistency. In a similar strain, he likewise wrote to Erskine of Dun, Wishart of Pittarow, and to some other individuals of the protestant party. He lingered in France to await the course of events; and as he was familiarly acquainted with the French tongue, his talents as a preacher were not in the mean time unemployed. About this period, he paid a visit to Lyon, and he is known to have preached at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. A protestant congregation had recently been formed at Dieppe; and he was now elected one of its pastors, being associated with Delaporte. So successful were their exertions, that some of the principal persons of the town were induced to renounce popery, and a general improvement began to be produced in the morals of the inhabitants. Discouraged by the aspect of affairs in Scotland, he at length determined to revisit Geneva, where he again made his appearance in the beginning of the year 1558. It was at this period that some of the most learned members of his congregation were engaged in preparing an English version of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and he is said to have had some share in so laudable an undertaking. The New Testament was printed at Geneva in 1557, and the entire Bible in 1560. This version, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Geneva Bible, is allowed by competent judges to possess great merit; and, in the opinion of Dr Geddes, it is generally superior to the version executed under the authority of King James. Of the former version, says Dr McReic, it is evident that his translators made great use; "and if they had followed it still more, the version which they have given us would, upon the whole, have been improved." In the course of the year 1558, Knox published three different works. One of these was the Appellation. Another, which has also been mentioned in a former page, was "The copie of a Lettre delivered to the Ladie Marie, Re- gent of Scotland." The third and most remarkable of these tracts bears the title of "The first Blast of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a> against the monstrous Regiment of Women." This anonymous work, directed against the political <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of females, attracted a very considerable degree of attention. It was speedily answered by John Aylmer, who in due time became bishop of London. The doctrine of Knox as to the inexpediency of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> rule was afterwards controverted by David Chalmers of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, and by John Lesley, bishop of Ross. Whatever opinion may be formed of his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, it must at least be admitted that, either in England or Scotland, he had seen nothing to reconcile him to the practice; and, in one of those countries, the regimen of a woman might with too much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> be termed monstrous. His literary labours were interrupted by the renewal of an invitation from the Scottish protestants; and at the beginning of the year 1559, he bade a final adieu to Geneva, having previously been presented with the freedom of the city. Leaving his family behind, he once more proceeded to Dieppe, where he arrived in the month of March; and having ascertained that he would not be permitted to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through England, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a> on the 22d of April, and was safely landed on the 2d of the following month. The popish church of Scotland was now approaching its crisis, which the presence of Knox had no small tendency to hasten. The queen regent, who for some time thought it necessary to dissemble her real sentiments, had lately evinced a fixed resolution to oppose the reformation with all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of her authority; and the fires of persecution had been rekindled by Hamilton, the profligate archbishop of St Andrews. Walter Mill, a venerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who had attained the age of eighty-two, was brought to the stake on the 28th of August 1558. This atrocious execution had such an effect in rousing the popular indignation, that the dread of the civil or ecclesiastical authority could no longer restrain the people from making an open avowal of their adherence to the reformed doctrines; while their spiritual guides, Harlow, Douglas, Methven, and a few others, began, with less fear of detection, to preach and to administer the sacraments. In the month of October, Willock again returned from Embden, and brought a new accession of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> and zeal. The death of the English queen, which took place on the 17th of November 1558, was another event that produced considerable influence on the affairs of the neighbouring states. The queen regent was however prepared to adopt the most violent measures. Several of the preachers, Willock, Harlow, Methven, and Christison, were cited to appear at Stirling before the high court of justiciary on the 16th of May, that is, eight days after Knox's return; and very soon after his arrival had been announced to Mary, he was proclaimed a rebel and an outlaw. The four preachers were outlawed for non-appearance, and a fine was levied on their sureties. After remaining a single day in the metropolis, he hastened to Dundee, where the chief protestants of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a> and Mearns were then assembled. They proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, and there he preached a sermon against the idolatry of the mass and of image-worship. After the conclusion of the service, a riot was casually excited among the common people; and, before it was terminated, the monasteries of the Dominican and Franciscan friars, with that of the Carthusian monks, "The CL. Psalms of David in prose and meeter: with their whole usuall Tunes, newly corrected and amended. Hereunto is added the whole Church Discipline, with many godly Prayers, and an exact <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KALENDAR">Kalendar</a> for xxv. yeeres: and also the Song of Moses in meeter, neuer before this time in print." Edinburgh, printed by Andro <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HART">Hart</a>, anno 1615, Svo. Instead of Calvin's Catechism, this edition includes "A Catechisme of Christian Religion. Appointed to be printed for the vse of the Kirke of Edinburgh." A more recent edition bears the title of "The Psalms of David in prose and meeter: with their whole Tunes in foure or more parts, and some Psalms in Reports. Whereunto is added many godly Prayers and an exact Kalendar for xxv. yeeres to come." Printed at Edinburgh by the Heires of Andrew Hart, anno Dom. 1635, Svo. 1 See Archbishop Newcome's Historical View of the English Biblical Translations, p. 68. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, 1792, Svo. were totally demolished. The queen, who was probably glad of such a pretext, collected a considerable army, and advanced upon Perth; but she found the protestants so well prepared for resistance, that she did not hazard an attack. She proposed and ratified terms of accommodation, which she speedily shewed a strong disposition to disregard. In order to ascertain the strength of their party, and to consolidate its union, they formed a religious bond or covenant, which received many signatures in different parts of the kingdom. From this period, they began to be distinguished by the name of the Congregation, and their noble leaders were commonly described as the Lords of the Congregation. On his return from Perth, he preached at Anstruther and Craill. Disregarding the admonitions of his friends, and the threats of the archbishop, he next preached in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of St Andrews, having selected the appropriate subject of our Saviour's driving the profane traders from the holy temple. On the three ensuing days he lifted up his warning <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the same place; and so signal was the success which attended his efforts, that the magistrates and the inhabitants resolved to establish the reformed worship in that city; the pictures and images were removed from the churches, and, on the 14th of June, the monasteries were defaced. He reached the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> in the end of the same month; on the day of his arrival he preached in St Giles's, and on the following day in the Abbey church. On the 7th of July, the body of the protestant inhabitants of Edinburgh elected him as their minister, nor did he decline the invitation. His wife followed him from Geneva; and her mother, after visiting her relations in England, likewise came to end her days in Scotland. But he was soon disturbed in his new functions, in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> occupation of the city by the troops of the queen regent. He now made an extensive circuit in the southern and eastern districts of the kingdom, visiting <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JEDBURGH">Jedburgh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>, Ayr, Stirling, Perth, Brechin, Montrose, Dundee, and St Andrews; nor can we doubt that the impressions produced by such a missionary were great and beneficial. After this period he was deeply engaged in the political as well as the ecclesiastical transactions of the Congregation; and the vigour of his talents, with the decision of his character, was conspicuously displayed in the steps which led to the establishment of the reformed religion. Knox, as well as Willock, concurred in advising the suspension of Mary from the office of regent. For the space of twelve months, the kingdom was infested with a civil war, in which French and English troops supported their respective allies. The contest, which had not been marked by many of the usual atrocities of intestine warfare, terminated in the month of July 1560. Parliament soon afterwards assembled; and in the course of a few days the reformed religion was established by the authority of the legislature. Knox, after officiating for several months at St Andrews, had returned to Edinburgh at the end of April, and continued to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his functions during the siege of Leith. Before the close of the year, he was visited with a severe domestic affliction in the loss of his wife, who left two children of tender years. The young queen returned from France on the 21st of August 1561. Not many days after her arrival, she sent for the reformer, of whose powerful influence she must have been fully aware; but neither this nor any of their subsequent interviews produced the effects which she seems to have anticipated. Such topics as Mary introduced he discussed with undaunted freedom, though it cannot with justice be affirmed that he treated her with incivility. She certainly did not overawe him with her royal presence, or render him less disposed to use his utmost endeavour in destroying the fabric of ancient superstition. The Scottish reformation differed in many respects from that of the neighbouring kingdom. In the one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the most essential trappings of a proud popish prelacy were left uncurtailed, nor was the church sufficiently purified from popish devices and observances. The sign of the cross in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, with the entire <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of godfathers and godmothers, some part of the funeral service, kneeling at the communion, the power of the priest to remit or to retain sins, and the power of the bishop to confer the gift of the Holy Ghost, ought to have been left in the sole and undisputed possession of those who still adhere to the mass and transubstantiation. Queen Elizabeth, the head of the church, was deeply tinctured with popery; insomuch that she was dissatisfied with the twenty-ninth article, as implying a denial of the doctrine of the real presence. She reluctantly permitted the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> and tapers to be removed from the altar in her chapel. It seems to have been by her private authority that a clause, unsanctioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, was added to the twentieth article; a clause which makes the averment that "the church hath power to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> --- 1 The genuine high-churchmen seem to feel some lingering regret for the discontinuance of the popish prayers for the dead. "In truth," says Mr Waddington, "to pray for the souls of our departed friends is the most natural and pardonable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of pieté; and although it be dangerous and improper to inculcate as a church doctrine the efficacy of such prayers, it would neither be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to discourage their private and individual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a>, nor easy to disprove the possibility of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>." (Present Condition and Prospects of the Greek or Oriental Church, p. 37. Lond. 1829, 8vo.) "Some persons," remarks Mr Palmer, "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps say that this sort of prayer is unscriptural; that it infringes either the Romish doctrine of purgatory, or something else which is contrary to the revealed will of God, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of things. But when we reflect that the great divines of the English church have not taken this ground, and that the church of England herself has never formally condemned prayers for the dead, but only omitted them in her liturgy, we may perhaps think that there are some other reasons to justify that omission." (Origines Liturgicae, or Antiquities of the English <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RITUAL">Ritual</a>, vol. ii. p. 94. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, 1832, 2 vols. 8vo.) This work, which is learned and curious in its way, might with a considerable degree of propriety have been entitled "The Conformity of the Church of England with the Church of Rome." Among other important facts, he is pleased to state that "the bishops who rule the churches of these realms were validly ordained by others, who by means of an unbroken spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of ordinations derived their mission from the apostles, and from our Lord. This continual descent is evident to any one who chooses to investigate it. Let him read the catalogues of our bishops ascending up to the most remote period. Our ordinations descend in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> unbroken line from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and Paul, the apostles of the circumcision and the Gentiles. These great apostles successively ordained <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Cletus, and Clement, bishops of Rome; and the apostolical line of succession was regularly continued from them to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CELESTINE">Celestine</a>, Gregory, and Vitalianus, who ordained Patrick bishop for the Irish, and Augustine and Theodore for the English. And from these times an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of valid ordinations have carried <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the apostolical succession in our churches even to the present day. There is not a bishop, priest, or deacon amongst us, who cannot, if he pleases, trace his own spiritual descent from Saint Peter and Saint Paul." (Vol. ii. p. 240.) To this last assertion it is only necessary to oppose another; namely, that there is not a single bishop, priest, or deacon, who can trace his own spiritual origin for one half of the requisite period. But what advantage could possibly result from their tracing it with the utmost certainty? Till they make an unequivocal display of their miraculous powers, we must totally disregard their extraordinary pretensions. By arguments equally logical and conclusive, the bishop of Rome undertakes to prove that he inherits all the spiritual gifts and graces of St. Peter, and to these is fully entitled to add all the temporal power and possessions to which he can extend his impious hand. This delirious dream of apostolical succession is disgraceful to the protestant name; and all those whom it bewilders would best maintain their consistency by returning to the bosom of their mother church. 2 See Archdeacon Blackburne's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONFESSIONAL">Confessional</a>, p. 368, and Dr Lamb's Historical Account of the thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">Articles</a>, p. 33. Cambridge, 1829, 4to. or ceremonies, and authority in controversies of faith." The king or queen superseded the pope as head of the church; and thus a protestant body might have, and in more instances than one has actually had, a popish head. Pluralities and non-residence, two manifest remnants of popery, have been closely interwoven with an establishment, in which the idle splendour of one class of ecclesiastics is placed in so indecent a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> with the laborious poverty of another. At this period, the metropolis of Scotland contained only one parish church. Knox was at first assisted by a reader, named John Cairns. It was then his regular practice to preach twice every Sunday, and thrice on other days of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; but in the year 1563, John Craig, minister of Canongate, was appointed his colleague. In 1562, he had for three successive days been engaged at Maybole in a public disputation with Quintin Kennedy, abbot of Crossragwell; and in the course of the following year, an account of it was printed at Edinburgh, under this title: "Heir followeth the coppie of the Resoning which was betweixt the Abbote of Crosgauell and John Knox." Another learned catholic, Ninian Winzet, addressed him a "Buke of fourscor thre Questionis," to which it was his intention to publish an answer, though he seems to have been prevented by his other avocations, which were sufficiently numerous. After this period he incurred the hot indignation of the queen for having, in one of his public discourses, aimed with great freedom on her intended marriage. During one of their interviews, she wept bitter tears of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>; and some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> historians have been not a little scandalized at his want of gallantry. In the month of December 1563, he was summoned before the privy council on a charge of high treason, for having written a circular letter to the protestant gentlemen, in reference to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of two persons who had been indicted for a riot in the chapel royal. Of this charge he was fully acquitted, to the great disappointment of Mary and the popish party. After having continued a widower for more than three years, he married Margaret Stewart, daughter of the good Lord Ochiltree. This marriage took place in March 1564, when he had attained the age of fifty-nine. The noble family with which he thus became connected was descended from Robert duke of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, second son of King Robert the Second. Knox was again brought before the privy council, for having, in a sermon preached in St Giles's on the 19th of August 1565, used certain expressions, or rather quoted certain texts, which gave great offence to the king, who was present, and applied them to himself. He was for a short time prohibited from preaching. Early in the following year, Mary subscribed the catholic <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> for the extirpation of the protestants; and if she had not been controlled by several prudential considerations, she seemed sufficiently prepared to adopt <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> measures. When she returned from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>, soon after the death of Rizzio, he retired from Edinburgh, and sought refuge in Kyle; nor does he appear to have resumed his pastoral care till after the final overthrow of her authority. Towards the close of the year he prepared to visit England, where his two sons were residing with some of their mother's relations for the purpose of receiving their education. He appears to have returned home soon after the queen had plunged herself into ruin by her marriage with Bothwell. He was a member of the general assembly convened at Edinburgh on the 25th of June 1567; and he preached a sermon at the coronation of the young king, which took place at Stirling on the 29th of the ensuing month. The assassination of the regent Moray, and the civil troubles which ensued, depressed his mind and affected his health: in October 1570 he felt a stroke of apoplexy, which however was of so mitigated a kind that he was able to appear in the pulpit; but his strength was greatly impaired by his unceasing exertions, and he never recovered any considerable degree of vigour. Before the end of that year, the freedom of his animadversions in the pulpit gave such deep offence to Kircaldy, governor of the castle, that at length he found it expedient to change his habitation. He quitted the metropolis on the 5th of May 1571, and retired to St Andrews, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his early labours. Here in the following year he published "An Answer to a Letter of a Jesuit named Tyrie." In a state of great debility he returned to Edinburgh towards the end of August 1572; and on the 24th of November he closed his most laborious and most honourable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, after having attained the age of sixty-seven. He left two sons by the first, and three daughters by the second marriage. Both his sons studied at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, Cambridge, and both of them became fellows. Nathaniel, the elder of the two, took the degree of A.M., and died in the year 1580. Eleazer, the younger son, proceeded B.D., and was one of the preachers of the university. Having been collated to the vicarage of Clacton-Magna, he died in 1591, and was buried in the college chapel. The three daughters, named Martha, Margaret, and Elizabeth, were married to three clergymen, James Fleming, Zachary Pont, and John Welsh. The widow of Knox became the wife of Sir Andrew Ker of Fadounside, who is described as a strenuous supporter of the reformation. The vigorous and ardent mind of Knox was lodged in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> and feeble body, which had been wasted by various hardships, and by intense mental exertion. His natural talents were improved by no mean attainments of learning, and he was eminently distinguished by an impetuous and impressive eloquence, which gave him a great ascendancy among his countrymen. That he was a man of fervent and habitual piety, will not be disputed by any one whose prejudices do not prevent him from forming a correct estimate of his character. From an early period of his life, he devoted his entire energies to the best of all causes; and, in the hand of Providence, he was the great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which rescued his countrymen from the fangs of papal tyranny and superstition; nor is any other name entitled to be mentioned with equal honour in the annals of Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Of civil as well as ecclesiastical tyranny he was a decided enemy; and his writings contain some bold speculations on the subject of government. No man was more upright in his intentions, or more disinterested in his motives. That the impetuosity of his character occasionally impelled him beyond the bounds of moderation may be fully admitted without any diminution of the re- --- 1 Bishop Lowth has stated that "there were some in England who, by the pope's authority, possessed at once twenty ecclesiastical benefices and dignities, with dispensation moreover for holding as many more as they could lawfully procure, without limitation of number." (Life of William of Wykeham, Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, p. 23, 3d edit. Oxford, 1777, 8vo.) In what protestant country, except England and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, is the system of pluralities and non-residence maintained to any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>? They are an intolerable nuisance, which even there must very speedily be abated. Even the regius professor of divinity at Oxford is convinced that there is a great and general demand for church <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>; and as Dr Burton is a man of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as well as learning, he must likewise be aware that, when there is a great and general demand for any commodity, it can in most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> be supplied. His notions of reform, as the reader may easily conjecture, are not extravagant; and some of his suggestions are not deficient in worldly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. It is notorious, as he avers, that many clergymen enjoy the income of their benefices, because the presentations have been bought and sold; and "if any legislative enactment should reduce their incomes, the patrons must in all fairness refund part of the purchase <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>." ("Thoughts upon the Demand for Church Reform," p. 38. Oxford, 1831, 8vo.) All the lay-dealers in such articles must therefore perceive the dangerous tendency of a reform in the church. spect due to his name: he was placed in a situation which required great energy and decision; and a person chiefly distinguished by the gentler virtues, would have been very indifferently prepared to encounter the boisterous elements with which he was destined to contend. It is not to be concealed that he was not exempted from that spirit of intolerance which, in a greater or less degree, belonged at that period to every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> and denomination of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. He was as little disposed to tolerate the mass as the mass-priests were to tolerate those whom they termed heretics. The principles of mutual toleration were little understood or relished; and almost every one who possessed the power betrayed the inclination of imposing, by very ungentle means, his own creed upon his neighbours. Beside the works which have already been mentioned, he composed various others, which are accurately enumerated by his biographer. "His practical treatises," says Dr M'Crie, "are among the least known, but most valuable, of his writings. In depth of religious feeling, and in power of utterance, they are superior to any works of the same kind which appeared in that age. The thoughts are often original, and always expressed in a style of originality, possessing great dignity and strength, without affectation or extravagance." The work by which he is best known as an author is "The Historie of the Reformation of Religion within the Realm of Scotland." So early as the year 1586, an octavo edition of it, to the extent of twelve hundred copies, was undertaken in England by Vautrollier, a well-known printer; but when ready, or nearly ready for publication, it was seized by the command of Archbishop Whitgift. Some imperfect copies, all of them wanting the beginning and the end, have however survived this visitation of the protestant inquisitor. An edition was afterwards published by David Buchanan, who has taken very unwarrantable liberties with the text. Lond. 1644, fol. Edinb. 1644, 4to. He has suppressed various passages, and interpolated others; and the fifth book, which has not been found in any manuscript, is perhaps his sole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. A genuine edition, "taken from the original manuscript in the university library of Glasgow," was at length published by Matthew Crawford, professor of ecclesiastical history in the university of Edinburgh. Edinb. 1732, fol. A collective edition of his works, executed with fidelity and elegance, might be preferable to any monument of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> or marble that could be erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this great benefactor of his native country. Knutsford, a town of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, in the hundred of Bucklow, 173 miles from London. It stands on the river Birken, is the place where the sessions for the county are held, and has a well-attended market on Saturday. The principal employment is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COTTON_MANUFACTURE">cotton manufacture</a>. It is an ancient town, said to have been in existence in the time of the Danish king Canute, who gained a victory, and gave its name, Canute's Ford, to the place where his army passed. The inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 2052, in 1811 to 2114, in 1821 to 2753, and in 1831 to 2823. Kodiak, an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the west coast of North <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, about fifty miles from the entrance into Cook's Inlet. It is about sixty miles in length, and, along with the smaller island of Atognak, is separated from the continent by the Straits of Cheligooff. The natives are robust, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and well skilled in all the arts connected with fishery. They have an ingenious manner of constructing their boats, which are almost entirely covered with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. The port of St Paul's on this island was long the chief seat of the trade of the Russians with north-western America. The natives having been found extremely serviceable, were removed in great numbers to the other Russian settlements along the coast. Koei-Tchoo, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, situated near the south-western extremity of the empire, bordering on Yunnan. It is of a much more unequal surface than the rest of the empire, and full of precipitous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, inhabited by barbarous and independent races, from whom the Chinese emperor is scarcely able to collect the moderate tribute which he exacts, even by the aid of all the forts and garrisons which he is obliged to maintain. The mountains yield <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. Sir George Staunton estimates the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> at 9,000,000. Koei-Tchoo-Fou, a city of China, of the first rank, in the province of Szechuan. It is situated on the great river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-kiang</a>, and has a very extensive trade. The neighbouring country is mountainous, but is highly cultivated, and abounds in fruit. Long. 109. 50. E. Lat. 31. 9. N. Kempfer, Engelbert, was born in 1651 at Lemgow, in Westphalia. After studying in several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, he went to Dantzig, where he gave the first public specimen of his proficiency, in a dissertation De Majestatis Divisione. He then went to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THORN">Thorn</a>, and thence proceeded to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, where he took his degree of doctor in philosophy; after which he went to Königsberg in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and staid there four years. He next travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, where he soon began to make a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and was appointed secretary of the embassy to the sophi of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. He set out from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a> with the presents for that emperor, and went through Aaland, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, and Ingermanland, to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, where he met Mr Fabricius the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, who had been ordered to take <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> in his way. The ambassador having ended his negotiations at the Russian court, set out for Persia. During their stay two years at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol9.html#article-ISPAHAN">Ispahan</a>, Dr Kempfer, whose curious and inquisitive disposition suffered nothing to escape him unobserved, took all the advantage possible of remaining so long in the capital of the Persian empire. When, towards the close of 1685, the ambassador prepared to return into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Dr Kempfer chose rather to enter into the service of the Dutch East <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of chief surgeon to the fleet, then cruising in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a>. He went on board the fleet, which, after touching at many Dutch settlements, reached Batavia in September 1689. Dr Kempfer here applied himself chiefly to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a>. From Batavia he set out for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, in quality of physician to the embassy which the Dutch East India Company send once a year to the Japanese court. He quitted Japan to return to Europe in 1692. In 1694 he took his degree of doctor of physic at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; on which occasion he communicated, in what are called Inaugural Theses, ten very singular and curious observations made by him in foreign countries. He intended to digest his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> into proper order, but was prevented by being made physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> la <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-LIPPE">Lippe</a>. He died in 1716. His principal works are, 1. Amenitates Exoticae, in 4to, a work including many curious and useful particulars in relation to the civil and natural history of the countries through which he passed; 2. Herbarium Ultra-Gangeticum; 3. The History of Japan, in German, for which the public is indebted to Sir Hans Sloane, who purchased for a considerable sum of money all our author's curiosities, both natural and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as likewise all his drawings and manuscript memoirs, and prevailed on Dr Scheuchzer to translate the Japanese history into English. Kohcraan, a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the north-western <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the province of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAHORE">Lahore</a>, situated between the thirty-third and thirty-fourth degrees of north latitude, on the western side of the Jhyhum or Hydaspes River. It contains no town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is extremely hilly and wild, possessed by petty chiefs, who are tributary either to the Seiks or Afghans. Kokaun, an independent state of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which is se-

KOLIN

Pages 764-765

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Kaurzim, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, contains 416 houses, and 4387 inhabitants, who are employed in cotton <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. Near to it is the field of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> where, in 1757, Daun defeated Frederick of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>.

KOLLBERG

Pages 765-765

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Pomerania, and the circle of Koslin. It is on the river Persante, about one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from its entrance into the Baltic. It has some foreign trade, and considerable establishments for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> ships; and near to it are some extensive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It contains four churches, 780 houses, and 7950 civil inhabitants, besides a garrison. It is chiefly remarkable for the strength of its position, and for its fortifications. It stands on a hill surrounded with morasses; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ditches can be with ease filled with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the river Persante. A strong citadel commands the city and the entrance from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and it has several strong out-works. From its importance as a landing-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it has been frequently attacked. The Russians besieged it in 1758, but were repulsed. In 1760, it was attacked by a combined fleet of Russian and Swedish ships and 15,000 <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> troops, but it was relieved by General Werner. Again, in the next year, it was attacked by the Russian general Romanoff, with fifty-five ships of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> and a powerful land force. It was ably defended during four months, and the Russians lost more than 3000 men in the trenches; but at length, from want of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, it capitulated on the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. The most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> was that in 1807, when most of the other strong places in Prussia had surrendered to the invading armies of Bonaparte. It was attacked by 18,000 men, commanded by Loisson, and defended by 6000 Prussians, including volunteer inhabitants. After a siege with constant bombarding, in which the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city was destroyed, it surrendered, having lost 1900 men. General Guiseneau, who commanded on this occasion, first displayed his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 32. N. Lat. 54. 7. E.

KOLOMENKA

Pages 765-765

a circle of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, extending over 1263 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehending three cities, twelve market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 204 villages, containing 30,618 houses, with 156,614 inhabitants, of whom 11,700 are Jews. It is an agricultural district, yielding corn and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> parts; but a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of it is mountainous and barren. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name situated on the river Pruth, with a Greek and a Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and 1890 inhabitants.

KOLUMNA

Pages 765-765

a circle in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Moskwa, which extends over 662 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and 269 parishes, with 65,650 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the city of that name, on the river Kolomenka, which runs to the Moskwa. It contains a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> and sixteen other churches, with 1150 houses, mostly of wood, and 6340 inhabitants. There is much tallow and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> produced, and there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and cotton goods. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 38. 25. E. Lat. 55. 20. N.

KOLYVAN

Pages 765-765

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Asiatic Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOMSK">Tomsk</a>, situated on the upper course of the Obi. It is chiefly distinguished by the abundant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> within its limits, containing a considerable proportion both of silver and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. These mines were discovered in 1727 by M. Demidoff, who, when he began to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> them in 1730, publicly extracted the copper, but was obliged clandestinely to separate the gold. This fraud being discovered by a German, the mines were confiscated to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the government; and, according to the accounts of the board of mines, these works, from 1725 to 1786, produced about 3,500,000 pounds of silver, and 48,000 pounds of gold. The town of Kolyvan is small, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Berda, near its junction with the Obi. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 81. 50. E. Lat. 54. 48. N.

KOMORN

Pages 765-765

a circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Farther Danube, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It extends over 1167 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, five market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 156 villages and hamlets, with 12,256 houses. The inhabitants are two-thirds Catholics, and one-third reformed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a city of the same name, at the junction of the Wang with the Danube. It is strongly fortified, and has five Catholic, one Lutheran, one Reformed, and one Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with 1400 houses, and 11,200 inhabitants. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by an earthquake in 1763, and again by another in 1783, but the damages were speedily repaired. Narrative of a Journey into Khorasan, Appendix, p. 106.

KONIGSBERG

Pages 766-767

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, on the river Roriké, in the circle of that name, and in the Frankfort <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>. It is walled, and contains 458 houses, with 4178 inhabitants, employed in making cloth and hosiery, and in distilleries and breweries. KÖNIGSBERG. In the recent division that has been made of those parts of the dominion of Prussia that are out of Germany; East Prussia has been formed into two governments, viz. Königsberg and Gumbinnen. The former of these is composed of the territory formerly called East Prussia, and a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lithuania. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Russia, on the east by the province of Gumbinnen, on the south by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and on the west by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> and the province of Dantzig. Its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is 8910 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It contains forty-eight cities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> places formerly walled, thirteen market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 3717 villages, and 76,949 houses. The inhabitants in 1826 were 683,925, of whom about 450,000 were <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, 110 Catholics, and the rest consisted of Jews, Moravians, and Mennonites. It is generally a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, presenting few elevations, and these scarcely higher than 200 feet above the level of the sea. It is a district in which are to be seen numerous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, some of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> extent. The largest of these, the Kurische-Haff, extends over 620 square miles; and the next in size, the Frische-Haff, is upwards of 500 miles. Besides these, there are others of various extent, amounting in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to near five hundred. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, but moderately productive, and yields good crops of rye and barley, and a small proportion of wheat. Its breeds of sheep and cows have nothing remarkable, either for their number or their qualities; but this province has been the repository from which the best and most numerous horses have been reared of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. The country is tolerably fertile; and from some of the districts of Polish Russia much corn is brought <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the navigable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The export of corn is, therefore, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> branches of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and has been as follows: An Account showing the Corn exported from Königsberg in each Year from 1818 to 1831. | Years | Wheat <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">Quarters</a> | Rye Quarters | Barley Quarters | Oats Quarters | Pease Quarters | Beans Quarters | <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TARES">Tares</a> Quarters | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a> Seed Quarters | |-------|----------------|--------------|----------------|---------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|--------------------------| | 1818 | 31,290 | 84,290 | 44,250 | 38,590 | 29,530 | | | | | 1819 | 12,320 | 73,600 | 29,520 | 15,130 | 19,910 | 1,360 | | | | 1820 | 28,610 | 67,690 | 8,180 | 55,650 | 12,100 | 410 | 4,390 | 24,970 | | 1821 | 15,590 | 14,590 | 2,150 | 8,640 | 2,334 | | 4,880 | 18,640 | | 1822 | 5,910 | 1,010 | 2,920 | 2,000 | 2,080 | | 780 | 31,730 | | 1823 | 4,280 | 10,300 | 210 | 1,160 | 2,150 | | 3,200 | | | 1824 | 10,020 | 3,930 | 2,980 | 15,660 | 4,120 | | 220 | 12,570 | | 1825 | 8,160 | 6,570 | 15,310 | 5,930 | 7,120 | | 9,260 | 10,160 | | 1826 | 14,830 | 6,920 | 2,010 | 53,210 | 8,030 | | 7,160 | 22,710 | | 1827 | 37,540 | 72,250 | 23,320 | 81,800 | 5,030 | 980 | 9,290 | 27,280 | | 1828 | 95,430 | 129,200 | 13,460 | 13,680 | 9,190 | 560 | 5,160 | 28,840 | | 1829 | 76,980 | 81,540 | 22,720 | 36,600 | 4,220 | 1,070 | 2,070 | 37,180 | | 1830 | 75,050 | 250,120 | 16,870 | 83,100 | 23,600 | 1,300 | 1,410 | 38,780 | | 1831 | 75,650 | 160,900 | 9,880 | 40,920 | 15,060 | 990 | 3,260 | 18,840 | The other exports in one year (1831) were as follow:— Bristles, 167,997 pounds; feathers, 13,860 pounds; flax, 75,280 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; hemp, 60,276 stones; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and skins, 53,707 pounds; wax, 31,955 pounds; <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, 118,008 pounds; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> yarn, 9000 bundles. The remaining exportable commodities are chiefly the produce of the extensive forests, consisting of ship-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, pot-ash, and tar. These are chiefly shipped at Memel, but some at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Some portions of flax and of flax-seed are also exported. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the province are merely of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and very inconsiderable. Konigsberg, the capital of the province, is a city standing on the navigable river Pregel, which empties itself into the Frische-Haff, about five miles below it. With the exception of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, it is the largest city in the Prussian dominions, and was formerly the capital. It is surrounded with walls defended by thirty-two ravelins, contains a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, eleven Lutheran, two Reformed, one Catholic, and one Menonite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, amongst which the domkirch or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is remarkable as containing the remains of the most distinguished individuals. It has several establishments for benevolent purposes, especially the great royal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, with nearly 1000 patients. The houses are 4503, and the inhabitants, including troops, 63,240, of whom more than 1500 are Jews. Konigsberg is the seat of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated university, containing twenty-two professors, having a botanic garden, an astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, and the other establishments for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of students in medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. It has, besides, institutions for the earlier stages of education. The trade is considerable, notwithstanding the shallowness of the river renders it necessary to load and unload ships by the aid of lighters. The manufactures are only for the consumption of the province.

KONIGSLUTTER

Pages 767-767

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, in Germany, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name. It is on the river Lutter, is walled, and contains a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, two churches, in one of which the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a> is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monument to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Lothario the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> and his empress. It contains 338 houses, and 2850 inhabitants, who carry on several extensive distilleries, and make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and other cloths.

KONIGSTEIN

Pages 767-767

a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, in the bailiwick of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIRNA">Pirna</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, situated on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, and containing 190 houses, with 1450 inhabitants. It is in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Saxon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and is remarkable for the impregnable fortress adjoining to it. The mountain castle overlooks the town, on a rock whose perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> towards the Elbe is about 900 feet. It includes, on the top of the rock, within its walls, fields, gardens, meadows, and a wood, and a well abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, 900 feet deep, so that sufficient provision for the garrison can be grown within itself; but there are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> storehouses on the rock, for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, ammunition, and all necessaries; amongst others, two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> casks of wine, capable of containing 1000 hogsheads. The casernes are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>; and, from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the rock, the castle can neither be assailed by traverses nor by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. In this fortress, the jewels, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, curiosities, and archives of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> have been deposited in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and were secure when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and its palaces were occupied by Frederick of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, as well as at a more recent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when Dresden was the head-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and assailed by the allied forces of Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, Prussia, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The castle contains also the state-prison. On the opposite side of the Elbe is the fortress of Lilienstein, on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> rock 1080 feet above the river. It is now dilapidated, but was occupied by the French in 1813, who added to the works.

KONINGGRATZ

Pages 765-766
