a circle of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, extending over 1536 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It contains forty-two cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 810 villages and hamlets, with 48,259 houses, and 271,080 inhabitants. It is moderately fertile, and produces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, wood, and has good pasturage. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, well fortified. It contains, besides the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, six churches, two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and an orphan-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with 624 dwellings, and 5903 inhabitants, employed chiefly in making woollen cloths. Lat. 50. 12. 38. N.

KONJEUR

Pages 767-767

a small district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORISSA">Orissa</a>, situated principally between the twenty-first and twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It is bounded on the north by the districts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SINGBOOM">Singboom</a> and Mohurbunge, and to the south by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTACK">Cuttack</a>. It was formerly tributary to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, but is now occupied by independent chiefs. It is fertilized by many streams, but is now in a neglected state. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Konjeur, Ogurapoor, and Andapoojurgur.

KONKODOO

Pages 767-767

one of the three independent states into which Bambouk, a considerable territory of Western <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, is divided. Latadoo and Bambouk are the names of the two other kingdoms, the latter having given its name to the whole territory. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is crowded with steep <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, but they are clothed with vegetation to the very summits; and the villages, which are built in delightful glens, present a most romantic appearance. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> is distributed in larger <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> smaller quantities throughout Konkodoo, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> occupation of the inhabitants seems to be the collecting of the precious metal, which they separate from grosser <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> processes. This <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is governed by a chief; but the Siratik, the regal <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the sovereign of Bambouk, enjoys an honorary superiority.

KOOKIES

Pages 767-767

a singular <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people, who inhabit the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the Chittagong district, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. They are little known to the inhabitants of the plain, and are seldom seen except when they visit the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> on the borders of the jungles in the Runganeah and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AURUNGABAD">Aurungabad</a> divisions, to purchase <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, dried fish, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. The Kookies are a stout, muscular race, but not tall; and have the peculiar Tartar features of the Asiatics in the east, namely, the flat nose, small eye, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, round <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>. They are divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of distinct communities independent of each other, and are all hunters and warriors. Their arms are bows and arrows, clubs and spears; and, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, they build their villages, which generally contain from 500 to 2000 inhabitants, on the most inaccessible hills. They are much addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in which they are almost constantly engaged; and, like most savages, they prefer ambuscades and surprises to regular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. They are vindictive in their dispositions, and always shed blood on a principle of retaliation. They <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> an intoxicating liquor distilled from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, which they drink at marriages, these being attended with much feasting. They have an idea of rewards and punishments in a future state, and they have also a saint <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> angel which they worship as the mediator between them and the Deity. They have no regular priests, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of each family instructs the children in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> knowledge which he thinks necessary. They sometimes engage in war with the Choomeas; but being in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dread of fire-arms, they are quickly driven back to their native mountains. They are, however, a great terror to the inhabitants on the borders of the Chittagong district, especially to the wood-cutters, on whom they frequently make incursions. They subsist partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>; and they have no religious <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> against any animal. An elephant is considered as a great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> by them, as it affords so great a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of food. Their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals are gags, goats, hogs, dogs, and fowls.

KOOM

Pages 767-768

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Koom. It stands on an extensive plain, and on the banks of a small river, which rises at no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance, and is lost in the great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a>. This city was built by the Saracens in the year 806, upon the site, as D'Anville supposes, of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Choona. It was erected from the ruins of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, which had composed a small sovereignty under an Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. It afterwards became one of the finest cities of Persia, and was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for the manufacture of silks. It was taken by the Afghans in 1722, when they invaded Persia, and completely destroyed it. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of it has since been rebuilt, but it has still the appearance of a vast ruin. There is a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, with a celebrated mosque and sanctuary erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Fatima, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Imaum Reza. In the mosque are still to be seen the tombs of Sofi the First and Shah Abbas the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a> is lofty, and has been gilded at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>. About ten miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the town is a very curious hill in the middle of the plain, called by some Nimick Koh, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the mountain of salt, and by others Koh Talism, the mountain of the talisman; for, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, no person ever succeeded in gaining its summit. Long. 50. 29. E. Lat. 34. 45. N.

KOONTASSEE

Pages 768-768

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a> and district of Morvee, near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> marshes called the Runn. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the neighbourhood is in a deplorable state, and the villages nearly uninhabited, owing to the tumult and confusion which pervade the whole district.

KOORANKOO

Pages 768-769

a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Western <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is bounded on the west by the Bullom, Limba, and Timanee countries; on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Limba, Tamiso, and Soolimana; on the east by Kissi, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, and countries little known; and on the south by those countries which border on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. These limits include a very extensive tract of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but the boundary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are somewhat indefinite; indeed they are continually fluctuating, according to the fortunes of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> as it is practised amongst <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> tribes of men. For our knowledge of Koorankoo we are indebted to the enterprise of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Laing, by whom it was visited and has been described. A chain of hills, sixty miles in length, runs in a north-easterly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> throughout the whole of the country. These are for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> clothed at their base with the camwood tree, which constitutes the staple article of trade. The range is composed of micaceous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a> slate, interspersed with veins of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> and laterite, so strongly impregnated with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> as sensibly to affect the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> at some inches distance. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> appear to be the Rokelle and the Kamaranka. The source of the former is set <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in Major Laing's map as in latitude 9. 45. north, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 9. 55. west, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> which lies in the Soolima country. It issues from the foot of a hill, by barometrical measurement 1470 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the Atlantic; and after receiving several tributaries, and traversing Koornkoo and other countries, falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, to which colony it is of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance. The Rokelle is the only river, says Major Laing, which bears one name from the source to the sea. The rivulets and longer streams which discharge themselves into it are picturesquely beautiful, dashing over rugged granite rocks several hundred feet in elevation. One of the tributaries, called Ba-Jafana, had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a> of about fifteen yards in breadth, though only about three miles from its source, which is in a mountain named Balakenko, where the natives procure the camwood in great abundance. The banks of the river are likewise lined with this wood, which grows to the height of about sixty feet. The Tongolelle, a rapid stream about thirty yards <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, also joins the Rokelle. It takes its rise in a sort of basin, surrounded with thick brushwood, and gives birth to a rich and luxuriant growth of wild canes in its centre, affording a cool retreat to the leopards which infest this part of the country. To such an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> are these rapacious animals dreaded, that Major Laing, "observed the sites of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> now in ruin, the inhabitants of which had been forced to move to the westward to avoid their attacks." The Kamaranka appears to be a river of the same size and general character as the Rokelle. It has also numerous tributaries. All the rivulets running south through the mountain chain already mentioned collect behind a lofty hill called Botato, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into it. About a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from Nyiniah, one of the largest and best-built towns in Koornkoo, is the source of a fine stream, which joins the Kamaranka. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> forms a basin ten yards in diameter, embanked with masses of granite, and overhung with lofty trees, clad with a foliage so thick as to bid defiance to the rays even of a vertical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Major Laing describes the scenery in this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> as occasionally very picturesque and beautiful. After crossing a range of hills to the eastward of Nyiniah, there presented itself to the eye of the traveller "an extensive valley, partly cultivated, and partly covered with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> grass about five feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, the cultivated part newly sown; lines of stately palm trees, as regular as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> laid out by art, with here and there a cluster of camwood trees, their deep <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> affording a relief to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> hue of the smaller herbage; these, with a murmuring rivulet meandering through the centre, exhibited the appearance of a well-cultivated and tastily-arranged garden, rather than a tract amid the wilds of Africa;" whilst, in the distance, mountain towered above mountain in all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and magnificence of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. There was also seen an extensive plain covered with short, thin grass; and our traveller having crossed a mountain ridge which separates the head streams of the Kamaranka, flowing southward, from those which reach the Rokelle, he ascended a lofty eminence called Sa Wolle. The summit of this mountain, according to barometrical measurement, was 1900 feet above the level of the sea, and the view from it was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and extensive in the highest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. A capacious circle of nearly two degrees in diameter, interrupted only by a hill to the eastward, which rose considerably higher, presented a landscape of the most rich and varied scenery. Camwood is the staple article of trade, and it is sent down the Rokelle and the Kamaranka to be bartered for various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. There is also a considerable advantage derived from the extensive manufacture of cloth. The loom in which this is wove is very narrow. The artisan sits under an open shed, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of which are suspended two frames of equal breadth with the roof, nicely divided with perpendicular strings. By a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the feet, these are made to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> one another alternately, and at each motion the shuttle is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> through. In this manner of working they exhibit much dexterity, and make good progress. Women are employed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> thread, but the sewing and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> are performed by men. Major Laing observes, "Koorankoo is the first country..." to the eastward of Sierra Leone where the manufacture of cloth is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; but it is generally of a coarse <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. As the traveller advances eastward, he finds the natives improve both in the texture of the cloth and the size of the loom. In <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANGARA">Sangara</a>, very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome cloths are manufactured." The Koorankos also cultivate a considerable portion of their ground; and in general intelligence and industry they <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> above the neighbouring tribes. Each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> has its enclosed garden, where are raised cassada, in the cultivation of which they bestow great care; spinach, small onions, and tankana, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERB">herb</a> which, when dried and beaten, answers as a cheap substitute for snuff. In <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> they are for the most part pagans, and they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in gree-grees (a sort of protecting spirits), for whom they have houses consecrated at the entrances of the towns. The head men are clothed in a long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, trousers, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, and sandals, but the women are contented with more scanty habiliments. They are great adepts in the art of dressing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and ornament each other's heads with great skill. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">Dancing</a> is a favourite amusement; and on the night of a funeral, which always takes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of the individual, they exhibit their skill in this art, brandishing hatchets <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> spears in both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The laws of this people are few and inartificial. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a> is the only crime punishable with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and even this can be compensated by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. There is a portion of the Koorankoo country inhabited by the tribe called the Soolimas. They have a territory of their own, which Major Laing describes as picturesque in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, being diversified with hills, extensive vales, and fertile meadows, belted with stripes of wood, and decorated with clumps of trees of the densest foliage. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is remarkably fertile, producing chiefly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, yams, which are planted like potatoes in England, and ground nuts, which are cultivated like our field peas. Bananas, pines, and oranges, are the principal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but the first only are found in any degree of perfection. The Soolimas have numerous herds and flocks, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. The elephant, the buffalo, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of antelope, monkeys, leopards, and wolves, are the wild animals. The principal towns of the Soolimas are all situated in the Koorankoo country. These are Falaba, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; Sangonia, a very large town on the borders of Footah Jallou, surrounded with a strong and lofty wall; Semba, a large, populous, and rich town near the southern frontier, situated on a very lofty eminence; Mousaijah and Koonko-doogore, a stage from Semba, in the hills. In all, these places contain a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of about 25,000 souls. Falaba derives its name from the river Fala, on which it stands. It is nearly a mile and a half in length, by a mile in breadth, and closely built compared with the generality of African towns. It was built in 1768 by the Soolima <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>, as a stronghold to protect him against his enemies the Foolahs; and the site is well chosen as a place of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, being on a gently-rising eminence in the centre of a large plain. The town is surrounded by a strong stockade of hard wood, and a deep and broad ditch, which renders it quite impregnable according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a> of the Africans. It contains about four thousand circular clay huts, having pyramidal roofs of thatch; and, being neat and clean, they present a very respectable appearance. The palaver or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-house stands in an open space, towards the southern extremity of the town, and is a place of recreation as well as of business. In the centre of the town a large piece of ground is left vacant, for the purposes of exercise, of receiving strangers, and of holding palavers. Formerly the Soolimas chiefly occupied themselves in war, but this is less practised amongst them now than heretofore. In person they are short and muscular, and well adapted to endure privation and fatigue. Their military weapons are the spear, the musket, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SLING">sling</a>, and the bow; in the management and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the two latter they are most expert. Where their predatory habits do not interfere, they seemed to Major Laing both mild and offensive in disposition. In their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> occupations the men and women appear to have changed places. The men attend to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a>; they also sow and reap; but all the other cares of husbandry devolve upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. They are masons, plasterers, surgeons, and the like; whilst the men employ themselves in sewing, and not unfrequently in washing clothes. In religion, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, dress, customs, and the like, the Soolimas resemble the Koorankos, so that these do not require a separate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>.

KOORBH

Pages 768-768

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-GUNDWANA">Gundwana</a>, district of Choteesgur, thirty-six miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from Ruttumpoor. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 83. 8. E. Lat. 22. 25. N.

KOOTAHE

Pages 768-768
or COCOA ISLAND, in the South Pacific Ocean, and separated from Neootabootaboo by a channel only three miles broad. It was discovered by Schouten and Le Maire, on the 10th May 1616. Long. 173. 48. W. Lat. 15. 55. S.

KOPAUL

Pages 768-768

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, belonging to the nizam, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bejaapoor, and district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJUNDERGUR">Gujundergur</a>. It is one of the strongest places in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The lower fort is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> at the bottom of a steep, rocky mountain, commanded by a middle and upper fort, the last overlooking the whole. It is chiefly formed of one immense rock, almost perpendicular, and of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height. In 1790, when it was possessed by Tipu, it was besieged by the nizam's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and capitulated after a siege of six months. It is 63 miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west from Bellary. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 6. E. Lat. 15. 28. N.

KOPYS

Pages 769-769

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Mohilew, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, on the river Dnieper. It contains a Greek, Catholic, a Lutheran, and a Unitarian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with 3800 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. 10. E. Lat. 54. 20. N.

KORAH

Pages 769-769

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLAHABAD">Allahabad</a>, situated in the doab, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the space enclosed between the Ganges and the Jumna, and between the 26th and 27th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is in general flat, except on the banks of the Ganges, where the villages are situated, being usually surrounded by mango trees. The whole territory is fertile, and in a progressive state of prosperity, under the administration of the British, to whom it was ceded in 1801. Korah is the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, in the province of Allahabad. The travelling distance is sixty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>, and 301 from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 40. E. Lat. 26. 6. N. This is also the name of a village in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTCH">Cutch</a>, situated about ten miles south from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCKPUT_BUNDER">Luckput <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUNDER">Bunder</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANDAVEE">Mandavee</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Cutch. Lat. 23. 38. N.

KORDOFAN

Pages 769-769

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Central <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated between the kingdoms of Darforo and Sennar. Little can be said of it, except that from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial an inveterate animosity has subsisted between the Foorian and Kordofanese, arising principally from mercantile jealousy, as the country of the latter lies in the route to Sennar and Suakem, the most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. The governors of Kordofan had for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> time been deputed by the Mek of Sennar; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the weakness and dissensions of the latter <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the power was usurped by the Foorian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>. But the enterprising ruler of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> having reduced all the provinces of Africa as far as Sennar, both Kordofan and Darforo were enumerated among the kingdoms which now acknowledge by a tribute the conqueror of Egypt and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. The country is of an arid character, destitute of any thing like a river <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> lake. The tropical rains, however, which <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at a certain season with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence, inundate a considerable portion of the country, and thus affording moisture to vegetation, agricultural operations are carried on. These are sufficient to produce wheat, and doka, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of millet. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> enjoys <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority, but policy compels him to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> his warriors, who, like those of Bornou, are invested in chain armour. What the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants occupying this rude tract of country may be, it is impossible to say.

KORDOS

Pages 769-769

the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Corinth, a town in European <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of the Morea, near the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Leptanto. It is the seat of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> archbishop, and contained about 500 houses, with 4000 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 3. 10. E. Lat. 37. 55. 54. N.

KORNA

Pages 769-770

a flourishing little village of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> Arabi. It is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and the Tigris, and carries on some trade with Bassora. It was recommended by Sir J. Malcolm as a fort which might Korotscha be occupied and fortified, and from which the predatory Arabs might be kept in check.

KOROTSCHA

Pages 770-770

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of European Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KURSK">Kursk</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle, and standing on a river of the same name. It contains six churches, 1033 houses, and 9600 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36. 57. E. Lat. 50. 45. N.

KOSCIUSZKO

Pages 770-771

Thaddeus, a Polish general, less celebrated for his exploits than for his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the independence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, was descended of a noble but not opulent family, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lithuania. He was educated in the school of cadets at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>, and made such progress in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, that he was named one of four pupils destined to travel at the expense of the state, in order to improve their talents by observation and inquiry. He consequently repaired to France, and having there passed several years devoted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, returned to his native country enriched with new acquisitions. He obtained the command of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and proposed to prosecute the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> profession in the Polish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, when the consequences of an unfortunate attachment for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the Marshal of Lithuania blighted his prospects, and forced him to leave his country. He proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> declared itself independent; served as adjutant to General <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> which the revolted colonies had to maintain against the mother country, was decorated with the order of Cincinnatus, and returned to his own country, where he lived in retirement until 1789. About this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he was promoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of general-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> by the Diet, which was then making vain efforts to restrain the influence of foreign powers. Kosciuszko was at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> little known; but in 1792 the affair of Dubienka, where with four thousand men he defended for six hours a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> attacked by fifteen thousand Russians, gained him much reputation. He served, with equal distinction, during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of that year, under the young Poniatowski; but the weakness of Stanislaus rendered fruitless the most generous efforts to maintain the independence of his country. He submitted to the conditions which were imposed upon him by Russia, and, under the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace, signed the ruin of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. The bravest officers of the Polish army, unable to support the disgrace thus incurred, gave in their resignation. Kosciuszko was amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; but having become an object of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> suspicion to the enemies of his country, he found himself obliged to quit Poland; a circumstance which added much to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> with the patriotic party, and caused him to be declared a French citizen by the Legislative <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> of France. He afterwards retired to Leipzig, where his friends in Warsaw, having decided to make a new effort against the Russians, apprised him that he had been chosen as their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. Kosciuszko did not refuse the perilous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> thus conferred on him; but, convinced that the means which his party had at their disposal were still insufficient, he resolved to proceed circumspectly, and, in order to avoid suspicion, undertook a journey to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he passed several months. At the beginning of 1794, however, having learned that it was no longer possible to restrain the impatience of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, he drew near to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of approaching <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and reached <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> at the moment when Medalinski had raised the standard of insurrection, and when he himself had just been declared <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of the national forces. Finding himself thus invested with dictatorial power, in circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty, he was careful not to abuse the trust reposed in him; and, by his conduct in every instance, he amply justified the choice of his countrymen. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Cracow, he published a manifesto, and immediately marched against the Russians at the head of a corps of five thousand men. He encountered the enemy, in number about ten thousand, at Wralawice, and, after a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of four hours, completely defeated them. This first success produced a general rising; Warsaw was delivered from the presence of the Russians; and Kosciuszko soon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself at the head of an army of fifty thousand combatants, including about twenty-five thousand regular troops. With this comparatively small force the Polish general-in-chief had to make head at once against the Russians and the Prussians. Frederick William II., who had just failed in his contest with the French, appeared desirous to avenge himself for this affront on the Poles; and, at the beginning of 1794, he marched against Warsaw, at the head of forty thousand men. Kosciuszko, who, upon this point, could not oppose to him more than fifteen thousand men, had, nevertheless, the courage to attack him at Szezekocin, on the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1794; but, after a murderous combat, in which he had two horses killed under him, he was obliged to retire to the entrenched <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> that covered the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, where, for two months, he resisted the most impetuous attacks and reiterated assaults. At the same time, he contrived to restrain and keep in order a furious populace, prone to give way to the greatest excesses. Scarcely had he been delivered from the Prussians, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the diversion which the insurrection of Great Poland operated in his favour, when Kosciuszko saw advancing against him the Russian army under Suworow, and also that commanded by Fersen. It was in vain that he attempted to prevent the junction of these two armies. On the 4th of October, being attacked at Macijowice, by very superior forces, he obstinately disputed the victory during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but at length he sank <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> pierced with wounds, exclaiming, as he fell, Finis Poloniae. He was about to expire under the sabres of the Cossacks, when being happily recognised, he was immediately surrounded with the respectful attentions of his enemies. Having been sent as a prisoner to St Petersburg, he remained two years confined in a dungeon, whence he was not liberated until after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the Empress Catharine. Paul I. immediately after his accession set him at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and loaded him with marks of esteem and regard. The first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which Kosciuszko made of his liberty was to proceed to England, and thence to America, where he passed several years amongst his old companions in arms. In 1798 he returned to France, where he was received with much distinction, and learned that a great number of his countrymen had enlisted under the banners of the new republic. Those who served in the army of Italy sent him the sabre of John Sobieski, which had been found in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CASA">Casa</a> di <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a>. From this time he lived either at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> at a country-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> which he had purchased near Fontainebleau. When <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> was about to invade Poland in 1807, he wished to avail himself of the name of Kosciuszko, in the hope of thereby inducing the people of that country to revolt against the Russians. But the Polish general had too much knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> not to divine the object for which recourse had been had to him, and he answered by positively refusing to comply with the imperial invitation. Nevertheless there was published in the journals a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> fabricated in his name, and addressed to the Poles. But although it was not till 1814 that he had an opportunity of denouncing this fraud, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> had <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been known in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of Poland had never ceased to be an object of veneration, even when the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Bonaparte treated him as a suspected person. When the Russians penetrated into Champagne in 1814, they learned with surprise that their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> enemy was living peaceably in the immediate vicinity. All those who had an opportunity of visiting his retreat testified their regard for him in the strongest manner; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Alexander himself had a long interview with the veteran and patriotic soldier. Nothing could induce Kosciuszko to return to his native country. In 1815 he made a tour in Italy, and afterwards established himself at Saleure in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, where he died on the 16th of October 1817. On the intelligence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>, the whole of Europe resounded with his eulogium; amongst all nations, and in every country, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was equally rendered to the brave soldier and the true patriot, who, without any other object than the independence and welfare of his country, had exposed himself to the greatest perils, and the most painful sacrifices. His mortal remains were interred in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> at Cracow, between those of John Sobieski and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Poniatowski. See POLAND.

KOSELSK

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KALUGA">Kaluga</a>, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name. It stands at the junction of the river Schibra with the Dragunka, and is the best built city of the province. It contains <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, a spacious market-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches, four of them of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and 559 houses, with 3800 inhabitants, who have considerable trade by the two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 35. 25. E. Lat. 54. 12. N.

KOSFELD

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the Münster <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Westphalia, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It stands on the river Berkel, has a fortress adjoining, and contains two churches, 490 houses, and, including the garrison, 5850 inhabitants. There are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 7. 17. E. Lat. 51. 57. 10. N.

KOSLIN

Pages 771-771

a circle of the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Pomerania, which extends over 5687 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending twenty-eight cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 1196 villages and hamlets, containing, in 1827, 303,836 inhabitants. It stretches along the shore of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, which contains the several boards of administration for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and 556 houses, with 6440 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 15. 55. E. Lat. 54. 12. 7. N.

KOSLOW

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Tambow, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORONESH">Woronesh</a>. It contains three wooden and five <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> churches, a convent, and 1237 houses, with 8060 inhabitants, who trade in salted fish, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, tallow, and other produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 40. 12. E. Lat. 54. 13. N. Koslow, a city of the Russian province of Taurien, the capital of a circle of the same name. It stands at the bottom of a deep <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It has been declared a free port ever since 1798, and has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUARANTINE">quarantine</a> station. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> quantities of produce are shipped from it, consisting of wheat, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, horses' tails and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, hides, and tallow. It contains 928 houses, and, according to Pallas, 11,500 inhabitants. It is considered to be unhealthy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> is not very good. Long. 33. 20. E. Lat. 45. 15. N.

KOSTENDIL

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Rumili. It is an open town, on the river Egrifu, at the foot of the mountain of that name. It contains many warm <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 8000 persons.

KOSTROMA

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of European Russia, to the eastward of Jaraslow, extending over 39,710 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It comprehends seventeen cities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 851 parishes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 1,422,000 souls. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> are numerous, and hold two thirds of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and of the peasants who <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon it. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> district, with a few elevations near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; and it is in many parts covered with forests, which yield excellent <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. The Wolga is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> river, and is navigable, as are the Kostroma and the Unscha. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is by no means fertile, but it produces sufficient corn for the inhabitants, and is enabled to grow good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The pastures maintain cattle, which furnish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and tallow. The rivers abound with salmon, sturgeon, and other fish. The females spin yarn in most of the cottages, and it is woven and bleached within the province. The several branches of industry enable an exportable surplus of hemp, flax, tallow, hides, dressed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fish, mats, bark, tar, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, and some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the Wolga is a source of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Kostroma, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the province, and of the circle of its own name, is at the junction of the Kostroma with the Wolga. It is the seat of an archbishop, and of the boards of revenue and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; is surrounded with walls, lately converted into promenades; and contains fifty churches, including the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> seminary, a gymnasium, several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and 1057 houses, with 8200 inhabitants. The leather made here is celebrated throughout <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and occupies eighteen considerable tanneries in preparing it. There is also a trade in sailcloth and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 41. 7. 31. E. Lat. 57. 45. 40. N.

KOSZOG

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Eisenburg, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Farther Danube, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It is sometimes called Guns, from the river of that name, on which it is built. It has some trade in internal productions, and contains 576 houses, with 3310 inhabitants, mostly of German origin. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 27. 58. E. Lat. 47. 22. 54. N.

KOTBUS

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of the same name, in the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, on the river Spree. It is a considerable manufacturing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with 739 houses, and 6430 inhabitants. It has a good internal trade by the navigable river.

KOTHEN

Pages 771-771

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Anhalt-Kothen, in Germany. It is the residence of the sovereign, and the seat of the civil and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> branches of the administration. It is on the river Ziathe, which runs to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, on a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and fertile plain. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, decorated with the arms and the proverbs of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Ludwig, built in 1617. It contains 740 well-built houses, and 5500 inhabitants. It has three churches and several public buildings, and the institutions adapted to a contracted independent state. The trade is mostly dependent on the wants of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>.

KOTTERUS

Pages 771-771

CHRISTOPHER, was one of the three fanatics whose visions were published at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1657, with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lux in tenebris. He lived at Sprotta, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and his visions began in 1616. He fancied he <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> an angel under the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who commanded him to go and declare to the magistrates, that, unless the people repented, the wrath of God would make dreadful havoc. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> palatine, whom the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> had declared <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, was introduced in these visions. Kotterus waited on him at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1620, and informed him of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. He went to several other places, and at last to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>. As most of these predictions promised felicity to the elector palatine, and unhappiness to his imperial majesty, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s fiscal in Silesia and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a> got him seized, set on the pillory, and banished the emperor's dominions. Upon this he went to Lusatia, and there lived unmolested till his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1647.

KOTTIAR

Pages 771-771

a district of Ceylon, situated on the eastern side of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, between the eighth and ninth degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">Cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BETEL">betel</a>-nuts, cocoa-nuts, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, form its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> produce.

KOTTILGHUR

Pages 771-771

a fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Northern Circars, situated on the summit of a very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and inaccessible hill. It consists of a fort and citadel, which is capable of making very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resistance; though it was taken by the British in 1817, with little resistance.

KOTZEBUE

Pages 771-772

Augustus Frederick Ferdinand Von, a prolific German dramatist and miscellaneous writer, was born on the 3d of May 1761, at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, where his father was a counsellor of legation. He early evinced a propensity to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and, whilst yet a boy, the representation of a play which he witnessed inspired in him such a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the drama as determined his future <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at his native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and when he was about sixteen years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he entered the university of Jena. Here he remained one year; but certain family circumstances occurred which induced him to remove to Duisburg, where he studied for a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> at the university, and returned to Jena in 1779. He was destined for the profession of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> predominated; and in gratifying his love of the drama, as well as literature in general, he consumed no inconsiderable portion of his time. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he did not display <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, he at least evinced wonderful versatility. Tragedy, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, ballads, essays, and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of literary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, came rapidly from his prolific <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. Their merits, however, he himself confesses in his autobiography, were exceedingly equivocal, although some of his plays were acted with applause. In his nineteenth year, he closed his studies at Jena with taking the character of an opponent at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Soon afterwards he returned to his native place, where he diligently applied himself to the pandects, and was admitted as an advocate. But his addresses to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> were still as assiduously paid as ever; and, in the ardour of his desire for distinction, he tried his skill in almost every species of composition, imitating, as caprice <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> admiration predominated, all the great writers of Germany, Schiller, Goethe, Wieland, Hermes, and others. In 1781, on the invitation, it is said, of the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, Kotzebue went to St Petersburg, where he obtained a situation under Von Bawr, general of engineers. The latter became his warm friend, and recommended him to the empress, who, on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Bawr, which occurred about two years afterwards, nominated him a counsellor. His imperial patroness first placed him in a judicial situation at Revel, and finally appointed him <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of Esthonia, on which occasion he was ennobled. His literary ambition kept pace with his growing fortunes, and drama succeeded drama from his pen, with great, if not increasing rapidity. In 1790, on a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PYRMONT">Pyrmont</a>, he published his Doctor Bahrdt with the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> Forehead, under the name of Knigge; a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which created a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> at the time of its appearance, but by which he lowered himself not a little in public estimation. Having received his dismissal from the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he retired for a time to an estate which he possessed at some distance from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>; but, in 1797, he returned to Weimar, with a pension of 1000 guilders. Three years afterwards, he was induced to pay a short visit to Russia; but he had scarcely crossed the frontiers of the empire when he was arrested by order of Paul I. and sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. This treatment of Kotzebue is said to have originated in a suspicion of the autocrat that he was the author of some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> pamphlets, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was personally attacked; but the exile was kept entirely ignorant of the cause of his banishment. He was, however, shortly afterwards recalled, and, as he informs us himself, well received by the emperor, who confided to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of St Petersburg. After the death of Paul I. Kotzebue returned to Weimar, and in 1802 was admitted a member of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. Some disputes which he had with Goethe and the Schlegels induced him to remove to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where the French literati flattered his love of adulation by the attentions which they paid him. It is not much to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> that he repaid their kindness by the publication of a calumnious work entitled My Recollections of Paris. The Italians were treated in the same spirit of illiberality in his Recollections of Rome and of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. About the end of 1803 he commenced, in conjunction with Merakel, a journal entitled Der Freymuthige, The Sincere, in which <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> was virulently attacked. In 1806 he went again to Russia, and lived from 1807 on his estate in Esthonia, never ceasing to write against the imperial usurper of France. Literature and politics <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to engage the pen of Kotzebue until 1813, when, as counsellor of state, he followed the Russian head-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of that year; and, in order more effectually to excite the nations against Napoleon, he published in Berlin the Russian-German National Gazette (Volksblatt). After the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> were decided by the victory of Waterloo, he went to St Petersburg; but was in 1817 commissioned by the Emperor Alexander to return to his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and report upon the state of literature and public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, for which he was to receive a salary of 15,000 roubles. He who had exerted himself so much in favour of Russia, sometimes, it is affirmed, at the expense of his native country, was not likely to be warmly welcomed on his return home. From the first he was looked upon as a spy; and the zeal which he displayed in his new employment soon confirmed this opinion, and prepared the way for his destruction. He established a literary weekly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in which judgment was passed on the publications of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and political opinions advanced, at once dishonourable and obnoxious to Germany, then awakening from its torpor, and heated with the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of concessions on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its rulers, and by delusive anticipations of representative systems. In his journal Kotzebue steadily ridiculed every attempt to form liberal institutions; and not only was every species of political amelioration opposed, but a marked enmity to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the press was exhibited. A private <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of his to the emperor of Russia, which had been obtained, it matters not how, was published in a German paper, and republished throughout the country; and its appearance excited a strong feeling of hostility and indignation against the author. Shielded as he was by the power of the autocrat, he found it necessary to quit Weimar for Manheim, where his literary and diplomatic labours were resumed with increased <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Unfortunately for him, he began to point his pen more directly against the enthusiastic anticipations and theoretical notions of liberty which had become the distinguishing characteristic of the great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the students at the German <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. A spark of dangerous enthusiasm caught the heated and disordered mind of a young student named Sand, who doomed the versatile dramatist and venal party writer to the death of a Caesar, under the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> that he was only performing an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of heroic virtue in the cause of national liberty. Having obtained admission into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his victim, he deliberately murdered him, on the 23d of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1819, after which he gave himself up to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and suffered on the scaffold. Kotzebue was three times married, and left thirteen children. He wrote about a hundred dramas, the best of which are the comedies, and even these are far from being first-rate productions. As a dramatist he is more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and more melodramatic and picturesque than profound in the knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, or happy in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of incident or illustration of manners. Some of his plays, however, have been translated into English, and adapted to the British stage with great success. His Misanthropy and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REPENTANCE">Repentance</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Stranger, is a stock piece; and his Spaniards in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, or the Death of Rolla, metamorphosed into Pizzaro by Sheridan, was the most successful play ever produced in this country. Kotzebue wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the German empire, and the Early His-

KOUANGNAN-FOU

Pages 772-773

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in Yunan, separated from the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> by frightful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The inhabitants are stigmatised by the Chinese as barbarous. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 106. 14. E. Lat. 30. 32. N.

KOUANGSIN

Pages 773-773

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, situated on a river which falls into the Poyang Lake. It is surrounded by lofty <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and carries on considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and candles. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 117. 44. E. Lat. 28. 27. N.

KOUBCABEIA

Pages 773-773

a considerable town of Darfoor, in Central <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It constitutes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the western <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and is the depot of all the merchandise brought from the west. A market is held here twice a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> medium for goods of small value being <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. The inhabitants obtain this article by collecting and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of those places where horses, asses, and other animals, have <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>. This market is celebrated for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of tokeos, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> coarse cotton cloths, here disposed of, and for the manufacture, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such it may be called, of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> sacks for corn, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and other purposes. The inhabitants are a mixture of Foorian, who speak their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; Arabs, Fellatahs, and individuals from Bengoo, and other western countries.

KOULI KHAN

Pages 773-773

Thamas, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Schah Nadir, was not the son of a shepherd, as the authors of the English Biographical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> assert; his father being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of a branch of the tribe of Affchars, and governor of a fortress erected by that people against the Turks. Upon his father's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his uncle usurped his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of taking care of it during the minority of Kouli Khan, or, more properly, young Nadir. Disgust at this affront made him commence adventurer. He entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the beglerbeg or governor of Muscada, in Khorassan, who, discovering in him strong marks of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> genius, promoted him to the command of a regiment of cavalry. In 1720, the Usbec Tartars having made an irruption into Khorassan with 10,000 men, the beglerbeg, whose whole force consisted only of 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 2000 infantry, called a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in which it was declared imprudent to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> the enemy with such an inferior force; but Kouli Khan proposed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against the enemy, and engaged to conduct the expedition, and to be answerable for the success of it. He was accordingly made general, defeated the Tartars, and took their commander prisoner. Hossein Beglerbeg received him at his return with marks of distinction; but growing jealous of his rising fame, instead of obtaining him the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of Khorassan, as he had promised, obtained it for another; which so exasperated Kouli Khan, that he publicly complained of the governor's ingratitude and perfidy, who thereupon broke him, and ordered him to be punished with the bastinado so severely, that the nails of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> toes fell off. This affront occasioned his flight, and his joining a banditti of robbers (not his stealing his father's or his neighbour's sheep). The rest of his adventures are too numerous to be inserted in this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. In 1729 he was made general of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> by Schah Thamas, and permitted to take his name Thamas, and that of Khuli, which signifies slave. His <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> therefore was The Slave of Thamas, but he was ennobled by the addition of Khan. In 1730, he fomented a revolt against his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, for having made an ignominious peace with the Turks; and having the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at his command, he procured his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a>, and his own advancement to the throne. In 1739, he conquered the Mogul empire; and from this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> growing as cruel as he was ambitious, he at length met with the usual fate of tyrants, being assassinated by one of his generals, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with his nephew and successor, in 1747, aged sixty.

KOUMA

Pages 773-773

a river of Asiatic Russia, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEREK">Terek</a> and the Cuban, and, taking an easterly course, loses itself in the sand before reaching the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>.

KOUMISS

Pages 773-773

a sort of Tartar wine, made of fermented mare's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. It is used by the natives as their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> during the season of it, and often serves them instead of all other food.

KOUMYKS

Pages 773-773
