a Tartar and Mahomedan tribe, who live in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TEREK">Terek</a>. They are nominally subject to Russia, though this does not restrain their predatory incursions into its vicinity. They carry on some trade on the Caspian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>.

KOUZNETZK

Pages 773-773

a small fortified town in Asiatic Russia, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOMSK">Tomsk</a>. It was founded in 1618; and the sable being here of peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of fur-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 500. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 87. 30. E. Lat. 53. 20. N.

KOWNO

Pages 773-773

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WILNA">Wilna</a>, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, on the river Wilna. It contains one Lutheran and ten Catholic churches, is an old, well-built town, with 608 houses and 3200 inhabitants. It has some trade in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and, by the river, which runs to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NIEMEN">Niemen</a>, in corn. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 53. 55. E. Lat. 54. 53. 30. N.

KRAILSHEIM

Pages 773-773

a town of Wirtemberg, in the circle of the Jaxt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bailiwick of the same name, which extends over 154 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and contains a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 22,500 persons. The town is on the Jaxt, contains two churches, 420 houses, and 2900 inhabitants, employed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>.

KRAKATOA

Pages 773-773

the southernmost <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> situated in the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a>, about ten miles in circuit. It contains a hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, used by the natives as a bath, and is esteemed more healthy than any of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The coral reefs with which it is surrounded afford abundance of turtle. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> peaked hill on the south, which lies in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 105. 15. E. lat. 6. 9. S.

KRAKEN

Pages 773-773

the name of an animal of a monstrous size, supposed to have been seen at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in the existence of which the weakness and credulity of the fishermen have excited the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of even respectable naturalists, and amongst others Bishop Pontoppidan, who describes it in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. It is probable that the whole depends on certain optical appearances arising from a peculiar state of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, which thus exhibits to the deluded fancy something of the form of a huge animal.

KRANTZ

Pages 773-774

ALBERT, a celebrated German chronicler, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> about the middle of the fifteenth century. Having finished his studies, he set out upon his travels, in the course of which he visited several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, attending the prelections of the most distinguished professors, cultivating the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the learned, and exploring public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, by which means he made acquisitions in knowledge equally varied and extensive. He took his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> at Rostock, and on that occasion supported several theses with so much distinction that he was retained to teach <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. Krantz was rector of this university in 1482. But being recalled to Hamburg, he was provided with a canonry in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and divided his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> between preaching and teaching theology. Elected <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYNDIC">syndic</a> of Hamburg in 1489, he assisted the same year at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of Wismar, where the interests of the Hanseatic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> were discussed. They deputed him to proceed to France in 1497 to demand a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, and to England in 1499 to solicit assistance against the pirates who infested the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. In these different missions he evinced so much <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, sagacity, and integrity, that John <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and Frederick <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, chose him, in 1500, to terminate the dispute which had arisen between them on the subject of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ditmarsen. Kranz, having been named <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> in 1508, laboured with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal to remedy the disorders which had been introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; but it is only by a forced interpretation of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his works, that <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOLF">Wolf</a>, and after him Bayle, have endeavoured to make him be considered as one of the precursors of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>. Kranz was witness to the first attacks of that reformer on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, and condemned them. He died on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1517, and was interred near the eastern gate of his cathedral. Kranz was a very learned <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and the historical works which he left behind him are useful, notwithstanding the errors by which they are disfigured. Some critics have accused him of plagiarism and of bad <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; but he has found numerous apologists, amongst whom may be mentioned Cisner, who places him in the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, not only for the elegance of style and the clearness of method, but also for the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Kranz was the author of: 1. Chronica Regnorum Aquiloniarum, Dania, Suecia, Novogiae, Strasburg, 1546, in folio; 2. Saxonia, sive de Saxonicæ Gentis vetusta origine, longinquis expeditionibus susceptis etc. libri xii. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, 1520, in folio; 3. Vandalia, sive Historia de Vandalorum vera origine, variis gentibus, crebris e patria migrationibus, etc. Cologne, 1519, in folio; 4. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">Metropolis</a>, sive Historia Ecclesiastica Saxoniae, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, 1548, in folio; and some other works of little importance.

KRASNOIARSK

Pages 774-774

a town of Asiatic Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOMSK">Tomsk</a>, situated on a small river tributary to the Yenesei. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Irkoutsk passes through this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, through which there is a considerable transit of commodities for the trade with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is remarkable for fertility, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are exceedingly cheap. KRAW. This isthmus connects the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> with the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and in the narrowest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> does not exceed ninety-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles across from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to sea.

KRASTAW

Pages 774-774

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUBLIN">Lublin</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of its own name, on a lake and the river Wieprz. It is surrounded with walls, and defended by a citadel, and contains 481 houses, and 3240 inhabitants, of whom many are Jews. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 1. 39. E. Lat. 50. 58. 46. N.

KREMENTSCHUK

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Pultowa, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of the same name. It stands at the mouth of the Kaganlik, where that river falls into the Dnieper. Its fortifications have been turned into pleasant walks. It contains 1200 houses, and 8600 inhabitants. It enjoys considerable trade on the navigable river, in native products, and has some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> on the Dnieper. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33. 23. 40. E. Lat. 49. 3. 10. N.

KREMNIITZ

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Barsch <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Bars, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. The city, with its extensive suburbs, contains 1200 houses, and 9678 inhabitants. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of mining, a mint where ducats are coined, a gymnasium, and a Lutheran <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment is in the working of the silver and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the surrounding district, and purifying these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 32. 35. E. Lat. 48. 42. N.

KREMS

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, in the circle of Manhartsberge, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Lower Ens. It is on the Danube, is well built, and contains a nunnery founded for English females. There are some manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, of mustard, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> goods, and some good wine is made. It contains 424 houses, and 3650 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 30. 42. E. Lat. 48. 21. 39. N.

KREMSIER

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Prerau, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. It is the seat of the Archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OLMUTZ">Olmutz</a>, whose castle is here, with a fine gallery of pictures and a library of 30,000 volumes. It contains, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINSTER">minster</a>, six churches, 420 houses, and 4100 inhabitants, who successfully cultivate vineyards.

KRESTXY

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Novgorod, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, extending over 372 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending one city, 730 villages and hamlets, with 47,387 inhabitants. The city is on the river Khalowa, contains 450 houses, and 1874 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. 28. E. Lat. 58. 20. N.

KREUZ

Pages 774-774

a circle in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Croatia, which extends over 664 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehends two cities, two market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 294 villages and hamlets, with 66,885 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, on the river Golkoniska, the seat of a bishop, with 302 houses, and 1819 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 26. 58. E. Lat. 46. 1. 16. N.

KREUZNACH

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. It is on the river Nake. It contains 700 houses, and 7205 inhabitants. It has fabrics of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, snuff, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, and very considerable establishments for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> refining, and has a lively trade in wine grown near it, and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, corn, spirits, and clover-seed. KRISHNA. See KISTNA.

KROMY

Pages 774-774

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Orel, in Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, on the river Kroma. It contains <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches and 300 houses, with 3100 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 35. 51. E. Lat. 52. 38. N.

KRONSTADT

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Siebenbergen denominated Sachsenland. It is on the frontier towards Wallachia, in a plain watered by numerous brooks, which unite to form the river Aluta. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>-built town, but surrounded with walls. It contains six Lutheran, two Greek, two Catholic, and one Unitarian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a Franciscan convent, with a church and cloth manufactory attached to it. It contains, including the suburbs, which are extensive, 3200 houses, and at the lowest estimate 25,000 inhabitants, among whom are Germans, Hungarians, Wallachians, Greeks, Armenians, and some Turks, who carry on a variety of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> for the supply of the home market. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28. 28. 25. E. Lat. 45. 56. 30. N.

KROSSEN

Pages 774-774

a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, of the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>. It is on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, near to where the Bober falls into that river. It contains 574 houses, and 3605 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are of cloth and hosiery.

KROTOSZYNN

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, in the circle of the same name, of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POSEN">Posen</a>. It is a frontier <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> towards <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, but now without fortifications, since the union of Posen with Prussia. It contains 535 houses, and 4860 inhabitants, speaking mostly the Polish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and employed in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>.

KRUINAU

Pages 774-774

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUDWEIS">Budweis</a>, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is on the river Moldau, is fortified, and, with about 300 villages around it, forms a dukedom belonging to the Schwarzenburg family. The castle and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> is near the city, which contains 696 houses, and 4291 inhabitants, some of whom are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>-makers, and others cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> manufacturers. Near to it are the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of Umloivitz, much frequented in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; and some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, but feebly worked.

KTEIFA

Pages 774-775

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in the pachalic of Damascus, on the borders of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a>. It is surrounded with walls of sufficient strength to defend it against the travelling Arabs. It is twenty-two miles east-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Damascus, and is supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Adarisi.

KUARA

Pages 775-775

a very mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> situated in the western <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. It is a rugged, unhealthy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> importance consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> which passes through it from the east. It receives a governor from Abyssinia when it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not to do otherwise.

KUBBEEES

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEISTAN">Seistan</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, situated on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Kerman to Herat, in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, 150 miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from Kerman, and 160 north-east from Yezd, and the whole intermediate space being an arid waste, intersected with one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> two ranges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. There is a path through this desert, by which couriers go; but the danger of perishing is so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that a person of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> demanded 200 rupees from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Pottinger, to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to his fellow-traveller, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Christie.

KUBBEER

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> lake, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> rather marsh, of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>. It runs from east to west about 150 miles, and is in some places thirty-five miles in breadth. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> through this morass, but they are not easy distinguished, and the unfortunate wanderer who misses them is in danger either of perishing in the swamp or of dying from thirst and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Koom to Tehran crosses a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this morass.

KUFFSTEIN

Pages 775-775

a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tyrol, on the river Inn. It is remarkable for the strength of its works, which, in conjunction with those of the fortress of Geroldstein, opposite to it, defends one of the important passes between <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and Germany.

KUILENBURG

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gelders, and circle of Thiel. It stands on the river Leck. It is surrounded with walls, and divided by the river into three parts, which are connected by handsome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bridges. It is an increasing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, containing, in 1830, 4299 inhabitants, who are occupied in making <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> goods, ribbons, and fire-arms.

KULM

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of West <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, on a hill, at the foot of which the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a> flows. It is the see of a Catholic bishop, and has an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> seminary for that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, with four professors and about 120 pupils. It contains 397 houses, and 3640 inhabitants. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> consideration, and one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, but has declined. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 20. 41. E. Lat. 53. 21. 6. N.

KULMBACH

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the bailiwick of the same name, in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. It is on the river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-Maine, in one of the finest situations of the circle. It is surrounded with walls, has a fine market-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, several public buildings, 437 houses, and 3420 inhabitants.

KUMBALIA

Pages 775-775

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, situated about five miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTCH">Cutch</a>, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of Nocanagar. It is a populous and well-built town, surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall, with round bastions, and four gates, which are sufficient to keep the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in awe. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the Gogia Brahmins, who are attendants on Ranchor, an incarnation of Vishnu and Dwarca. Having accumulated fortunes from the offerings of the pilgrims resorting to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a>, they have retired to Kumbalia, which is well adapted for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, to which they are much inclined. The port of this place is Sirreyah, at which vessels <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, and send up their cargoes in boats. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 69. 45. E. Lat. 22. 15. N.

KUNASHIR

Pages 775-775

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Eastern Seas, forming <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the small archipelago of the Kuriles. It is 100 miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and thirty-five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The Russians have erected a small fort on this island.

KUNCKEL

Pages 775-775

JOHN, a celebrated Saxon chemist, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sleswick, in 1630. He became chemist to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XI. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Counsellor in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">Metals</a>, and letters of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Louwensteing. He employed fifty years in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, in which, by the help of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> of a glasshouse which he had under his care, he made several discoveries, particularly those of the phosphorus of urine. He died in Sweden in 1702, and left several works, some in German, and others in Latin; amongst which, that entitled Observations Chemicæ, and the Art of Making Glass, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1752, are the most esteemed.

KUNDAL

Pages 775-775

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which is one entire forest, abounding with all sorts of wild animals. Seventy-four miles south-west from Dacca. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 91. 18. E. Lat. 23. 12. N.

KUNDAPOOR

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Canara, situated near the mouth of a river, which is the boundary of the northern and southern divisions of Canara. On the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the river, Tippoo formerly had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>, which is seldom used by the British. The town consists of 300 houses, and was formerly garrisoned by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of native infantry. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 74. 47. E. Lat. 13. 33. N.

KUNEE

Pages 775-775

town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, and district of Sirhind. It is surrounded by a mud wall and a deep ditch, but was taken by the British in 1809, without resistance.

KUOPIO

Pages 775-775

a circle in Russian <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, of the vast <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of 20,608 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, containing only one town and 4423 farms, with 144,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, of the same name, is a town in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the Lake of Kallavesi, containing 160 houses, and 920 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 27. 24. 55. E. Lat. 62. 53. 43. N.

KUPA

Pages 775-775

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> Arabi, once a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous city, founded by Omar after the ruin of Ctesiphon, and the residence of the caliphs, until, owing to the vices of the inhabitants, the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>. Little is left of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> but the mosque where <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> was assassinated, a plain edifice, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the centre, surrounded by a cloister. There is but one entrance, through an elegant gateway; and the walls being <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and flanked with bastions, give it more the appearance of a castle than a place of worship. The Mahommedans hold in high veneration the spot on which this mosque has been built; and their imams <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> priests, to add to its sanctity, have invented many wonderful stories concerning it. Four miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MESHED_ALI">Meshed Ali</a>.

KUPH

Pages 775-775

an extensive ruined village of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which appears to be the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town. The buildings appear like magnificent palaces. The style of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is of the fourth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> fifth century; and the crosses over the door show the buildings to have been Christian. Thirty-five miles south-south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>.

KURDA

Pages 775-776

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a>, situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west frontier, about three miles south of the town of Theraud. It is surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and unproductive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

KURGOMMAH

Pages 776-776

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-GUNDWANA">Gundwana</a>. It is situated in the middle of a very wild <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> inhabited by Goands, who are so uncivilized as not to know the value of the precious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, their only currency being cowries <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> shells. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82. 25. E. Lat. 23. N.

KURIL

Pages 776-776
or Kuriliski Isles, extending from north latitude 51. to 45. which probably once lengthened the peninsula of Kamtschatka before they were disjoined from it, are a series of islands running south from the low promontory Lopatka, which is distant one league from Shoomska, the most northerly of these. Of the twenty-one islands subject to the Russian empire, no more than four are inhabited. The rest of these islands remain wholly uninhabited, but are visited occasionally, for the purpose of hunting otters and foxes.

KURSK

Pages 776-776

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of European Russia, which extends over 15,430 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, comprehending seventeen cities, 137 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 1532 villages and hamlets, and containing a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 1,611,100 persons. It is between 50. 20. and 52. 26. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and is consequently in a temperate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. It is an undulating district, with no elevations entitled to the name of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Although well watered by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Donez and its tributary streams, it is neither swampy nor marshy, but enjoys a dry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It is fertile, and the increase of corn from the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of seed is greater than in any of the provinces to the north of it. As the greater portion of the people are occupied in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> surplus produce consists of corn, amounting in some years to upwards of 4,400,000 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. This forms the chief commodity for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, besides which, corn, spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and hemp <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, tallow, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, horses, and horned cattle, are supplied to the neighbouring provinces. From the want of navigable rivers, most of the commodities must be conveyed to the Wolga on wheel <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, which, as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> are bad, becomes very expensive. There are in this province a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, who among them possess 239,000 peasants <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> slaves. The province is divided into fifteen circles. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Kursk is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the province, as well as of the circle of that name. It is the seat of an archbishop. It stands at the junction of the rivers Kura and Tuskar, and has been fortified, but the walls are converted into pleasing promenades. It contains sixteen churches, two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> seminary, 2340 houses, and 21,500 inhabitants. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of extensive trade in wax, tallow, hemp, and the other productions of the soil, and the seat of some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and near it the gardens produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> not grow in the more northern parts of the empire. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36. 22. E. Lat. 51. 43. N.

KURZOLA

Pages 776-776

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, a portion of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is about 220 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is well wooded, and affords good ship <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. It yields good wine, and some corn, but is deficient in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The inhabitants are 6440, of whom 1800 live in the fortified <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the same name, in a narrow strait on the east end of the island.

KUSTER

Pages 776-776

Ludolf, a very learned writer in the eighteenth century, was born at Blomberg in Westphalia. When very young, he was, upon the recommendation of Baron Spanheim, appointed <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the two sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Schwerin, prime minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, who, upon our author's quitting that station, procured him a pension of four hundred livres. He was promised a professorship in the university of Joachim, and till this should become vacant, being then but twenty-five years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he resolved to travel. He read lectures at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, went to England, and thence proceeded to France, where he collated Suidas with three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> in the king's library, which furnished him with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many fragments that had never been published. He was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, which made him several advantageous offers to continue there, but he was called to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and there installed in the professorship which had been promised him. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; and being brought over to the Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he abjured that of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The king of France rewarded him with a pension, and ordered him to be admitted a supernumerary associate of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>. But he enjoyed this only a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, having died in 1716, at the age of forty-six. He was a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Latin, and wrote well in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; but his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellence consisted in his skill in the Greek language, to which he almost entirely devoted himself. He wrote many works, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Historia Critica Homeri; 2. Jamblicus de Vita Pythagorae; 3. An edition of Suidas, Greek and Latin, in three volumes, folio; 4. An edition of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, Greek and Latin, in folio; 5. A new edition of the Greek New <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, with Dr <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">Mills</a>'s Variations, in folio.

KUSTERDINGEN

Pages 776-776

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>, in the circle of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLACK_FOREST"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Forest, and bailiwick of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BABENHAUSEN">Babenhausen</a>. It contains 175 houses and 1230 inhabitants, who grow much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and convert it into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and diaper cloth.

KUSTRIN

Pages 776-776

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is a strongly fortified <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with a fortress on the river <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, surrounded by ditches and marshes, by which the approaches of assailants are impeded. It is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> defences on the east of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, is always strongly garrisoned, and well stored with ammunition and provision, and commands a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river 880 feet in length. It contains 562 houses, and 6220 civil inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 35. E. Lat. 52. 35. N.

KUTTENBURG

Pages 776-776

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZASLAU">Czaslau</a>, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is a well-built town, with a magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> and thirteen other churches, and containing 746 houses and 6417 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment is mining for silver, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for smelting the silver, another for refining <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and several establishments for manufacturing the several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>.

KUTUBDEA

Pages 776-776

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, thirteen miles in length by four in breadth, adjacent to the district of Chittagong, being separated from it by a narrow strait two miles <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, into which a vessel, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of distress, may safely run. In its vicinity are some valuable oysterbeds: the oysters are of an excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and are sent for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SALE">sale</a> to the Europeans at Dacca and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>.

KUTY

Pages 776-777

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the circle of Kolomea, in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, on the river Czerny. It contains a Greek and an Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with 430 houses and 4110 inhabitants, of whom 520 are Armenians. There is much occupation in the curing of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, in a way similar to that followed in Russia.

KYLE

Pages 777-777

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>, in Scotland. There are three districts in Ayrshire, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a> to the south, Kyle in the middle, and Cunningham to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Carrick is divided from Kyle by the river Doon. The boundaries of Kyle are the river Doon on the south, and the river <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a> on the north. See **AYRSHIRE**.

KYPHONISM

Pages 777-777

KYPHONISMS, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> CYPHONISMS, an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> frequently undergone by the martyrs in the primitive times, wherein the body of the sufferer was anointed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and so exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, that the flies and wasps might be tempted to torment him. This was performed in three ways. Sometimes they only tied the patient to a stake; at other times they hoisted him up into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and suspended him in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>; and at others, again, stretched him out on the ground with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> tied behind him. The word is originally Greek, and comes from *κυφός*, which signifies either the *stake* to which the patient was tied, the *collar* fitted to his neck, or the *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>* with which they tormented him. The scholiast on <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a> says it was a wooden lock, or cage, and that it was called so from *κυφός*, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, because it kept the tortured in a bent posture; but others take the *κυφός* for a log of wood laid over the criminal's head, to prevent his standing upright; and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a> describes it as a piece of wood on which criminals were stretched and tormented. In effect, it is probable the word might signify all these several things. It was a generic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, and these were merely the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Suidas gives us the fragment of an old <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which punished those who treated the laws contemptuously with kyphonism for the space of twenty days; after which they were precipitated from a rock, dressed in women's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>.

or KAIRABAD, a district of Hindustan, in the province of Oude, situated principally between the 27th and 28th degrees of north latitude, and bounded on the

KYRAHGUR

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rajahs tributary to the Nagpoor Maharrats, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-GUNDWANA">Gundwana</a>, eighty-six miles south-west from Ruttunpoor. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 81. 32. E. Lat. 21. 27. N.

KYRAUT

Pages 777-777

a district of Northern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, situated between the twenty-seventh and twenty-eighth degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It is bounded on the north by the Himalaya ridge, on the east by Bootan, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORUNG">Morung</a>, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEPAUL">Nepaul</a>, from which it is separated by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract little known to Europeans. The river Teesta is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river, and Damsong the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town. It was conquered in 1769 by the rajah of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GORCAH">Gorcah</a>.

KYREEGHUR

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Oude, situated on the east side of the Goggrah river, 102 miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 51.
